News.title: Man, 47, avoids jail after sexually assaulting five women during sick spree in World Duty Free shop at major UK airport
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

AIRPORT CREEP Man, 47, avoids jail after sexually assaulting five women during sick spree in World Duty Free shop at major UK airport

A MAN who sexually assaulted five women at a major international airport during a sick spree in a World Duty Free shop has avoided jail.

Slawomir Zieba, 47, inappropriately touched multiple women over several hours at Stansted after missing two flights to Poland.



The convict, a Polish national, initially missed his flight and went into World Duty Free before touching a woman on the bottom, a court heard.

He apologised and walked away before returning to the store later on.



After coming back to the shop, he touched a second woman’s bottom and squeezed it.

Zieba missed his second flight before going on to touch three other women inappropriately.



He was detained by World Duty Free security before being arrested by cops on suspicion of five sexual assaults.

When being quizzed by police, Zieba claimed the World Duty Free was “very busy” and that he couldn’t remember anything.

He denied touching the survivors deliberately and claimed the store was very “crowded”.

However, according to CCTV, he could be seen committing the depraved acts.



The sexual attacks were described as being “one off due to excess alcohol“.

His lawyers claimed he had an “unhealthy relationship with alcohol” but is receiving medical support.

These problems allegedly stem from loneliness while living away from his family, who are based in Poland.

He has since taken responsibility for the offences and demonstrated “genuine remorse and has expressed shame for his behaviour”.

Zieba has no previous convictions.



He was sentenced to a 12-month community service order, including 10 rehabilitation days.

The convict was also handed alcohol abstinence and monitoring requirement for 120 days.

He must undertake 80 hours of unpaid work plus pay £114 in surcharge, an £85 court cost and £75 of compensation to each of the victims.

Zieba will be subject to notification requirements for five years.

News.title: Teacher accused of gross indecency with a boy under 14 denies tying him to a bed and blindfolding him
News.content:
'SEX ACTS' Teacher accused of gross indecency with a boy under 14 denies tying him to a bed and blindfolding him

A TEACHER accused of several charges of gross indecency with a boy under 14 yesterday denied tying him to a bed and blindfolding him.

Deborah Franklin, 65, is accused of abusing the pupil between 1991 and 1995 at a prep school.

The pupil, now a man in his 40s, said he was nine when he joined her class at the Hertfordshire school and she became his private tutor.

He described “countless” encounters in which Franklin would tie him to her marital bed, blindfold him, tickle him with a feather and then have sex, the court heard.





At St Albans crown court, Aisling Byrnes, defending, asked: “Did anything sexual happen between you and him?”

She replied: “Never.”

Franklin, from Radlett, Herts, denies eight counts of gross indecency with a boy under 14.

The trial continues.

News.title: Raging wildfires are France’s biggest challenge since WW2, Macron says as he warns ‘coming weeks will be tough’
News.content:
FRANCE’S raging wildfires are the country’s biggest challenge since the Second World War, Emmanuel Macron has said.

The French president warned the coming weeks will be some of the toughest his nation has ever seen – with a 40C heatwave expected this week.



Macron told emergency workers at a crisis meeting in Bordeaux: “We have a situation that is more difficult than at any time since the Second World War.

“We must be realistic: the coming weeks will be tough, and we must persevere. The key is urgency, resilience.”



He made the comments in Gironde, the south-western area worst affected by the fire, on Monday evening.

Currently, 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel and around 1,200 police officers have been deployed to the region.

Officials say fire crews have been “overwhelmed” by the ferocity of the flames and remain “far from” bringing them under control.

Two people have died due to the wildfires so far with at least 88 injured.



Dozens of homes have been burnt to the ground with an estimated 220,000 people displaced and forced to live in shelters while the flames remain high.

On Monday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the flames that had decimated 42,000 hectares of land was stable but not contained.

Around 360,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France and Spain as infernos tear up neighbourhoods and forests.



Tens of thousands of hectares of land have been swallowed by vicious flames amid record-breaking temperatures.

Calling for unity, Macron also said: “The priority is obviously lives… when it’s necessary to relocate people, we relocate them.

“When it’s necessary to sacrifice forest or sometimes material goods, we do it.”



It comes amid fears Bordeaux could be reduced to ashes as authorities battle “apocalyptic” flames.

The fires are now less than seven miles away from the ancient city – with over 850,000 residents being warned Bordeaux is at risk of being reduced to ashes in the coming days.

Authorities in the Gironde region said they were banning holiday camps, including Scouts’ trips with overnight stays and holiday camps for people with disabilities.

Meanwhile in Spain, a new heatwave is set to begin on Wednesday.

Madrid earlier said temperatures would soar and humidity levels drop across Spain.



This would cause the fire risk to “surge to very high or extreme levels across almost the entire country”.

“This situation will persist, or may even worsen, in the following days,” it added.

Spain’s interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said: “Today and tomorrow are absolutely decisive days, because from Wednesday the weather forecasts become highly unfavourable for firefighting efforts.”

Reacting to the forecast, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said: “I ask for understanding and call on all citizens in all the country to exercise extreme caution and take every possible precaution.”

“We face difficult hours, complex hours” ahead, he warned.



The European Union said it would deploy additional aircraft to Spain to help combat the fires.

Over 284,000 acres have been burned due to wildfires since the start of the year, according to Nunez.

He told France 2 television that the country is battling 30 to 40 wildfires every day.

It comes after Gironde firefighting Chief Eric Brocardi compared the battle to contain the inferno as a “David-versus-Goliath scenario”.

Gironde authorities have now banned vacationers from entering the region by closing off several main roads and cancelling holiday camps for children and people with disabilities.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Some of the blazes in the Gironde wildfire are said to be so powerful they have now created a terrifying giant fire cloud which can create its own lightning.

The unprecedented “pyrocumulonimbus” is a dangerous weather system that whips flames around its own winds and can strike and ignite even more fires.

News.title: Hero bystander who tried to rescue dad and daughter killed in sea tragedy tells how he was lucky to survive himself
News.content:
A DAD who drowned with his daughter at Britain’s top surf beach is thought to have jumped in to the sea to try to save her.

A hero bystander heard shouts of help and dashed down a cliff to the shore, where he saw the daughter lying face down in the water at Fistral Beach in Newquay, Cornwall.



Her boyfriend was nearby trying to reach her after she apparently fell in by accident while walking — and her father followed in a failed rescue bid.

Bystander Jamie Stockwell, 47, threw himself in fully clothed to grab the woman, aged in her early 30s, who was being bashed against rocks in a strong swell.



He managed to push her to the shore where he and her boyfriend began trying CPR.

Jamie said: “I saw her head down in the water and her partner was trying to shout at her.

“I jumped in with all my clothes on. I didn’t realise how deep it was.

“It was very powerful swell and I was lucky I wasn’t another casualty.

“We were being hurled on to the rocks. I managed to push her up and her boyfriend pulled her up by the arms and started to try to give her mouth-to-mouth.

“She had swallowed loads of salt water. We tried to give her CPR for about ten minutes. I was trying to keep her partner calm as he was in pieces.”



The father, said to be in his 60s, was pulled out of the water a few hundred feet away and given CPR but also died.

Sand Phoenix, who was dozing on Fistral Beach, sprinted to help the man after hearing the commotion.

Sand, 33, said: “He’d been pulled out of the water but had been in there for about seven minutes. I had an adrenaline pen which I jabbed him with and tried to give him oxygen but his lungs were full of water and there was no response.

“The paramedics arrived and carried on trying to give CPR.



“He was still wearing his trousers so I don’t think he had been swimming. Apparently, he had gone in to try to rescue his daughter.

“It was an awful thing.”

He added: “I think she must have fallen in by accident because she was still wearing trousers and a bikini top.”

The dad and daughter, from Doncaster, South Yorks, died at the western edge of the beach underneath the clifftop Fistral Beach Hotel and Spa as the sun went down at around 9.30pm on Sunday.



A Coastguard helicopter, boats, police and ambulance services scrambled to the scene.

A woman, understood to be the mother of the female victim, was at the top of the cliff sobbing as their bodies were recovered.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The 750-metre beach is known as the home of British surfing because of its huge wave swells.

Earlier in the day, a man died after getting into difficulty at West Wittering beach in West Sussex.

News.title: Horror moment teen’s cliff jump goes wrong as he flies through the air before hitting rocks by the water
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a cliff jump goes horribly wrong as a teenage boy smashes into rocks before hitting the water.

Harrowing footage shows a teenager leaping off cliffs in San Diego as a crowd of spectators watch from a distance.



Instead of a smooth dive, the boy slams into the rocks before flipping into the water.

Several loud cries can be heard as the thrillseeker bounces off the rocks.



The teenager’s friend quickly jumps in and both boys come to the surface.

A further six people jumped in before authorities were called to the scene at around 4.30pm.

The stricken teenager was carefully pulled from the water using a technical rescue rig system.

The boy was then rushed to hospital where his condition remains unknown.



He was reportedly conscious and breathing when he was taken to hospital.

The city’s Municipal Code prohibits jumping or diving into the Pacific Ocean or Mission Bay from natural or human-made points higher than five feet above the water.

Local official Candance Hadley told NBC 7: “We want locals and visitors to enjoy San Diego’s coastline safely.

“Please stay back from cliff edges, follow all posted warnings and never jump from cliffs or other elevated areas into the water.”

Although there are repeated warnings, the spot near Sunset Cliffs Boulevard remains extremely popular for cliff divers.



People regularly jump from an arch above the crashing waves, despite the threat of fines and arrests.

Local resident Rae-Kwon Goldsmith told CBS8: “This is not a place for people who have never jumped.”

This comes after a 15-year-old boy died in 2019 after jumping at the same spot.

According to one report, there was an average of five deaths and injuries annually between 2005 and 2017.

The boy has not been publicly identified at this time.

News.title: Two top ex-generals issue a call to arms to stop Labour betraying our veterans
News.content:
WAR ON 'LAWFARE' Two top ex-generals issue a call to arms to stop Labour betraying our veterans

TWO of the nation’s most senior ex-generals have issued a call to arms to stop Labour betraying our veterans.

General Sir Peter Wall and General Sir Nick Parker demanded the government put safeguards in law to end decades-long legal witch hunts.



It comes after Sir Keir Starmer rowed back legal protections designed to shield troops from so-called “lawfare,” where enemies of the state – including IRA sympathisers – are free to wage war in the courts.

Scores of elderly veterans have been dragged through investigations decades after they were cleared of wrongdoing on operations in Northern Ireland.



Generals Parker and Wall said old cases must only come to court where there is “genuinely new and compelling evidence”.

They have urged Britain’s army of veterans to bombard their MPs with demands to change the Troubles Bill which is currently going through parliament.



Gen Wall, a former Chief of the General Staff, said changes to the bill would “prevent soldiers being betrayed”.

He said: “To prevent soldiers being betrayed now and in the future, we have to change the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill.”

In a joint statement with Gen Parker, he said: “Those who serve under lawful authority do so on one understanding: If they act lawfully, the State will stand behind them.”

It comes after Labour’s ex-Veterans Minister Al Carns warned the Troubles Bill was “unfit for purpose”.



Carns quit last month and accused Keir Starmer of “failing the very veterans” his government claimed to protect.

Carns, an ex-Special Forces commando, said: “I have worked to fix the Bill from the inside, but it remains unfit for purpose.

“It risks failing the very veterans it claims to protect.”

He added: “We ask soldiers to fight for this country. In return, we owe them the kit to do the job and the loyalty to stand by them when it’s done. We are failing on both.”

Generals Parker and Wall shared a letter for veterans to send to their MPs on a dedicated website shouldertoshoulder.uk.



They wrote: “This is not about immunity. Those who break the law should always be held to account.”

They added: “The issue is whether veterans who acted lawfully, under government authority and in accordance with the rules of engagement, should continue to face repeated investigations and legal proceedings decades later, even where there is no genuinely new and compelling evidence.”

General Parker, whose soldier son Harry lost both his legs to a Taliban bomb in Afghanistan, added: “We must let every MP know how important it is to support those who serve their country.

“Please help us by emailing your constituency MP and encourage all those who feel like us to do so as well.”

It comes after the SAS Regimental Association said veterans had been “hounded for doing their duty”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In a joint statement with the SBS and Special Reconnaissance Regiment associations, they also claimed Labour’s Troubles Bill was “not fit for purpose.”

The normally secretive associations said: “The Special Forces associations have never sought immunity from wrongdoing but are adamant that the mistreatment of veterans must end.”

News.title: Andy Burnham could water down Shabana Mahmood’s plan to make migrants wait ten years for permanent settlement
News.content:
ANDY Burnham could water down Labour’s flagship plan that would make migrants wait ten years for permanent settlement.

The PM said he wanted to bring “a new pair of eyes” to the row over Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s proposals and promised a “fair resolution”.



Mr Burnham inherited the policy from Keir Starmer’s government but stopped short of endorsing it when challenged on migration.

He told the BBC: “We’ll come to a fair resolution. I think the worry people have is the feeling it’s out of control and we don’t have a grip as a country and therefore we don’t have the right procedures in place.”



Asked again if he might rethink the proposals, Mr Burnham said he would look at the consultation and hinted NHS staff and care workers could be spared the tougher rules.

He said: “I see people contributing to our society by working in social care, who’ve in many cases come from around the world to work there or the NHS.

“I don’t think people actually say that is something that we don’t want.

“We want people when they’re here and making a contribution to be able to be, if you like, supported and welcomed here.”

The change would require most migrants to wait ten years rather than five years before applying for indefinite leave to remain.

Applicants would also have to meet stricter requirements including speaking English to A-level standard, having no criminal record and no debts.



Ms Mahmood’s allies insist changes are needed to stop the welfare bill ballooning as 1.6 million migrants who arrived from 2021 to 2025 become eligible to settle.

Reform UK claims it could add £622billion.

But Labour MPs say it is unfair to change the rules for migrants already here.

The Government is due to make its final decision on settlement reforms after considering responses to the consultation.

News.title: Benefit claimants face tougher hurdles to get cash as Andy Burnham pushes for more young people to get into jobs
News.content:
BENEFIT claimants face tougher hurdles to get cash after Andy Burnham vowed to “get really serious” about bringing down the ballooning welfare bill.

The PM yesterday signalled ministers could tighten rules ahead of a major push to get more young people into jobs.



It comes as analysis revealed some teens on sickness benefits receive around £100 a week more than others working part-time on minimum wage.

Today Mr Burnham will unveil a shake-up of secondary schools to better prepare youngsters for work.



From 14, pupils will combine English, maths and science with technical training, work experience and time spent at local employers.

Schools will be encouraged to tailor lessons to jobs available in their area, while Ofsted will start judging them on how well they prepare pupils for work.

The reforms are based on Mr Burnham’s Greater Manchester Baccalaureate, which combines GCSEs with technical education and work experience.

Mr Burnham said: “I want an education system based on parity between academic and technical which gives all young people a clear path in life.

“From today, Britain will value the hard hat every bit as much as the graduation cap.”

He added: “Fixing the youth unemployment crisis will require a major shake-up in how we do things — and that’s what this ­Government will do.”



The announcement comes as more than a million young people, known as Neets, are now not in work, education nor training — the highest number recorded.

Former Labour minister Alan Milburn, who is leading the review into youth unemployment, has warned Britain risks creating a “lost generation” unless more young people are given a clearer route into work.

Mr Burnham’s education reforms sit alongside a wider attempt to tackle Britain’s soaring welfare bill.

In an interview with the BBC, he signalled some benefits could come with tougher conditions, saying: “It’s about changing the nature of the support and making some of it conditional on people taking opportunities that are presented.

“So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits.”



But he insisted he was not blaming people already claiming.

Instead, he said many young adults had been “quite seriously let down” because they had not received the help they needed before falling out of work.

He added: “We’ve got to get really serious as a country at getting the welfare bill down.”

'FULLY FUNDED' By Jack Elsom ANDY Burnham insisted defence was a “top priority” as he welcomed Volo- domyr Zelensky in his first foreign leader reception. The PM vowed Britain would hit its Nato target of spending 3.5 per cent of its GDP on the military by 2035 — but has yet to set out a funding plan. At Portsmouth naval dockyard yesterday, he embraced Ukraine’s president, telling him: “You can count on the UK for as long as it takes.” He is Britain’s sixth PM since Mr Zelensky took power. Mr Burnham added: “It’s my job to keep the country safe and in the world that we’re living in, defence has to be right up there as a top priority. “I’ve already said I will fully fund the Defence Investment Plan.”

The number of young people claiming disability benefits continues to rise.



More than 87,000 16 and 17-year-olds now receive Personal Independence Payment, or PIP.

Analysis by The Times also showed a teen on the enhanced rate of PIP can pick up around £100 a week more than a 16-year-old working the maximum 12 hours allowed during term time on the under-18 minimum wage.

Overall, around four million people now receive PIP after claimant numbers doubled following the pandemic — with spending forecast to continue rising over the coming years.

The surge has prompted ministers to launch a wider review of the disability benefits system.

In an interim report, disability minister Sir Stephen Timms concluded PIP in its current form was “no longer fit for purpose”, with recommendations on possible reforms expected later this year.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The issue has already caused one of Labour’s biggest political headaches.

Last year Sir Keir Starmer’s ­Government attempted to overhaul disability benefits but was forced into an embarrassing climbdown after dozens of Labour MPs threatened to vote against the plans.

News.title: Newquay deaths: Bystander 'lucky to be alive' after trying to save dad and daughter
News.content:
'Cornwall locals dread moments like this'

Jeff Reines, the editor of the Mirror's sister title Cornwall Live, says the potential danger of even getting near the often turbulent tide is often underestimated at Fistral Beach.

He writes for The Mirror: "It's the occurrence Cornwall locals most dread - but sadly also most expect - when summer rolls around.

"While there is no doubt, and history proves, even people who live here and know the sea can lose their lives in seconds, because it can be THAT unpredictable.

"We lose friends and family members who we are convinced know what they are dealing with when they step into the water. Or even near the water, as in this tragic case.

"We wouldn't suggest at this stage that the man and woman are certain to be tourists; we just don't know yet and it's an unfair presumption, even if many locals would consider it a safe one.

"But the potential danger of even just getting near the often turbulent tide is commonly underestimated by visitors, and in the week the summer holidays have started, it's unfathomably sad to see it emphasised in this horrific way.

"And it's not like it's a remote corner of our county or unknown shore among our 300 beaches - this is unarguably one of our best known spots, largely for surfing but also for families - local and visiting - to enjoy the best of what Cornwall has to offer.

"Our thoughts are with the loved ones of this pair, and also on hoping it's not a scenario that repeats itself this 'silly' season, as we call it, albeit a term that feels flippantly insensitive given the gravity of what we have witnessed, and what our heroic emergency services have had to deal with once again."

News.title: Search for missing mum Elizabeth Waddell who disappeared on stunning holiday island
News.content:
Search for missing mum Elizabeth Waddell who disappeared on stunning holiday island

Elizabeth Waddell, 44, was staying with a friend at a popular tourist destination on a beautiful island when she decided to go for a swim but never returned

View 3 Images Elizabeth Waddell, 44, disappeared from a tourist hotspot (Image: Facebook/CailenWaddell)

A search has been launched for a mum who disappeared while out for a swim on a beautiful island in the Caribbean.

‌



Elizabeth Waddell, 44, was staying at the Grand Anse, a popular tourist destination in St. George, Grenada.

‌



The US woman was traveling with a friend when she decided to go for a swim, but never returned.

‌



After a few hours, her friend began to panic as Elizabeth did not have her phone with her. Amanda Romano-Harmon, another long-time friend of Elizabeth, told WRAL.

View 3 Images Elizabeth Waddell is missing (Image: Facebook/CailenWaddell)

"She had her swimsuit on, and she went outside their Airbnb," Amanda said.

‌



"They had a pool that overlooked the bay. Liz was set up out there just sightseeing from the pool, and her friend was taking her online course.

"When she got through with her course, she looked up and she didn't see Liz outside, so she went outside to walk around and see where she went, and she saw her towel down on the pier. So the only thing we can think is maybe she went for a swim."

A missing persons report has been filed.

‌



Elizabeth's husband, Cailen, has pleaded for anyone with information to please come forward.

"Facebook Friends. My wife Liz is missing in Grenada," he wrote in a post on the social media platform on July 24.

"If any of you have connections to the island – can you please share the following with your contacts there? Liz went missing in the afternoon on Wednesday.

‌



"I am on my way there now to help search.

"I expect nothing less than Liz's safe return – so please send your love, light, thoughts, and prayers our way."

Cailen and his daughter arrived in the country on Friday to help with the search.

‌



View 3 Images Cailen and Elizabeth Waddell (Image: Facebook/CailenWaddell)

"The police have been wonderful," he told WRAL News.

"The investigation is ongoing. [The police] have been incredibly communicative and have done everything it seems like they could be doing to help find her."

Article continues below

Amanda, the couple's friend of 25 years, said both Cailen and his daughter have split up to divide and conquer.

The Royal Grenada Police force are in contact with fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline in their search for Elizabeth's safe return.

News.title: France wildfires live: Inferno is country's 'most difficult situation since WW2' - Macron
News.content:
More than 220,000 people in south-west France's Gironde region have been evacuated as raging wildfires approach Bordeaux

French President Emmanuel Macron has claimed the raging wildfires are the 'most difficult situation' his country has dealt with since World War Two.

Fierce wildfires are currently burning seven miles from the French city of Bordeaux and its airport, with more than 220,000 people evacuated from their homes in the south-west of the country.

Firefighters are struggling to contain the flames, which have burned 42,000 hectares - an area four times the size of Paris - leaving two firefighters dead and 88 injured. Volunteers, including local farmers, are helping by towing huge water tankers to the scene.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez says the 'unprecedented' wildfires have developed a "life of their own," while Bordeaux's mayor has labelled the blaze the "fire of the century" that could take months to extinguish.

Meanwhile in Spain, 25,000 people have been ordered to evacuate and almost 40,000 have been told to stay indoors. Wildfires near Madrid "slowed their advance" overnight but remain active, the regional government said today.

News.title: Moment cruel carer screams ‘I hope you die’ to 81-year-old dementia-sufferer
News.content:
Moment cruel carer screams ‘I hope you die’ to 81-year-old dementia-sufferer

Louise Harris, 42, has been jailed for abusing Elizabeth, 81, and waving a kitchen knife around in her home - but the family of the victim say the sentence is unduly lenient

View 4 Images The moment carer Louise Harris screamed in Elizabeth Anne Shipton's face (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

A carer who screamed ‘I hope you die in your sleep you f***ing horrible cow’ in the face of a 81-year-old dementia patient has been jailed.

‌



Louise Harris, 42, is now behind bars after abusing Elizabeth Anne Shipton — the woman she was supposed to be looking after. Harris, of Cwrt y Waun, Rhydyfro, Pontardawe, Wales, answered a plea from Elizabeth’s family for help caring for the pensioner while a formal care package was put in place.

‌



Harris and Elizabeth’s daughter, Tracy Faram, agreed to a four-hour ‘trial’ shift at her family home in February. It was the only time Harris was left alone with Elizabeth.

‌



After Tracy left her mother an hour into the shift, Harris became infuriated when Elizabeth accidentally pressed her Lifeline button, which triggered a phone call to a crisis response helpline. Even though call operators ended the call once Harris told them it wasn’t intentional, the carer was enraged.

She started screaming abuse at Elizabeth, calling her a ‘horrible cow’. At one point, Harris knelt down and placed her arm on Elizabeth’s chest, while the pensioner was in bed, and demanded to know where her money was.

View 4 Images Elizabeth Anne Shipton just wanted to sleep in her own home, her family said (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



Elizabeth complained the arm was hurting her but the carer yelled: "I don't care, where's your money?"

Later, Harris began waving a large kitchen knife around while trashing the property, Swansea Crown Court heard. This was the moment Tracy leapt into action, witnessing the events on her CCTV cameras.

She called the police who had to break down the door. Cops found Harris ‘slumped on the floor’.

‌



View 4 Images The abuse was captured on CCTV cameras at home - which alerted Tracy to the danger her mother was in (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Sentencing Harris, Judge Huw Rees said elderly people were entitled to be treated with ‘respect, dignity, and humanity’ but that the defendant had been ‘heartless and cruel’, showing a ‘callous disregard’ for her welfare.

In mitigation, lawyer Andrew Evans said recovering alcoholic Harris found a bottle of vodka in Elizabeth’s home, and ‘gave into temptation’ after Tracy left, and downed the booze.

‌



View 4 Images Elizabeth, 81, with her daughter, Tracy (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

He added his client was genuinely remorseful for her ‘wholly unacceptable behaviour’. Harris was jailed for three months after pleading guilty to being a care worker who ill-treated the victim, and to criminal damage.

She had originally been charged with attempted robbery because of her demands about Elizabeth's money, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) dropped that charge.

Article continues below

Tracy has now launched a bid to review the ‘unduly lenient’ sentence. She said: “The judge's hands were tied by the sentencing guidelines. You could see he was raging.

"For her to be serving just over a month is unbelievable when you think what we've had since February. We've been living this day in, day out, with my mother getting worse.”

News.title: Donald Trump says Israel 'wouldn't survive' without US ahead of Benjamin Netanyahu meeting
News.content:
Donald Trump says Israel 'wouldn't survive' without US ahead of Benjamin Netanyahu meeting

The US and Israel are long-time allies and carried out joint strikes on several key Iranian sites on February 28, sparking a major conflict in the Middle East over the coming months

View 4 Images US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will meet for the eighth time since Trump took office last year (file image) (Image: AP)

US President Donald Trump has said a long-time ally "wouldn't survive" without America.

‌



Mr Trump made the claim hours before meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin "Bibi" Netanyahu at the White House on Tuesday, July 28.

‌



Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Mr Trump said: "Frankly we're being very nice to a lot of countries that would not survive without us.

‌



"And you know who wouldn't survive without us? Israel.

"Bibi's coming, he'll tell you."

View 4 Images US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The discussions between the allies on Tuesday will mark the eighth meeting since Mr Trump took office last year.

Mr Netanyahu said ahead of the talks that it would "first and foremost" be about Iran, but "all issues" will be discussed.

According to a source briefed on the matter Mr Netanyahu is going to Washington in "listening mode", the Financial Times reports.

‌



However, it is reported that the Israeli leader desires to expand military action in Iran.

The US and Israel are long-time allies and carried out joint strikes on several key Iranian sites on February 28, sparking a major conflict in the Middle East. Iran retaliated by striking sites across the region and closing the Strait of Hormuz waterway.

The source said: "Netanyahu wants it to be about more than just Hormuz."

‌



View 4 Images Three boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz, as a plume of smoke rises from an explosion in the background, off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 13, 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Razieh Poudat)

The source added that Mr Netanyahu will also raise concerns about Türkiye asking to buy F-35 fighter jets from the US, as he believes it will lessen Israel's military advantage over other countries in the region.

A White House official told FT that Mr Trump would "discuss the conflict in Iran, progress with the Trilateral Framework in Lebanon, and expanding the Abraham Accords".

‌



During his speech in Michigan on Monday, Mr Trump said he's making the "largest-ever investment in the United States Armed Forces", which he called the strongest military in the world.

View 4 Images The US and Israel are long-time allies (file image) (Image: Getty)

"We're winning big time with the Islamic Republic of Iran. We're ensuring that they're never having a nuclear weapon. It's very simple. If you understood the power of the nuclear weapons, you'd understand exactly what I was saying."

Article continues below

Mr Trump called Iran "the bully of the Middle East".

"You can't bribe them, you gotta beat them, and we're beating the hell out of them," he said.

"We'll see how it turns out. Right now there are very friendly negotiations going on."

News.title: Met Office maps show more than 50 areas set for rain on Tuesday
News.content:
Met Office maps show more than 50 areas set for rain on Tuesday

An orange rain cell is predicted to hit some as the week gets off to a wet start for millions following a damp weekend, although the south east will be hot

View Image The weather map for 3am on Tuesday, July 28, 2026 (Image: Met Office)

The Met Office forecast shows more than 50 areas of the country expected to see rain on Tuesday.

‌



Rainclouds will soak millions of Brits in the early hours of Tuesday (July 28) as a large band of rain will move north-eastwards, drenching Northern Ireland, swathes of Wales, south west England, and northern England.

‌



The heaviest rain will fall around 3am, when an orange rain cell is forecast to hit central Scotland and deliver 8-16mm of rain, the Met Office map shows. Once the heavy stops in mid-morning, scattered showers will persist for most of the day in Northern Ireland, north Wales, north west England, and Scotland.

‌



However, it looks like it will stay dry in the Midlands, East Anglia, and southern England.

The Met Office forecast for Tuesday said: “Heavy rain in the north will ease and move away northeastwards on Tuesday, replaced by sunshine and locally heavy showers. England and Wales mostly dry with some hot sunshine developing.”

According to the Met Office’s map, 53 council areas will see some form of rain. It’s estimated 12 Scots, four Northern Irish, nine Welsh, and 28 English top-tier council areas will be hit by precipitation.

‌



Temperatures are set to remain warm and typical for late July. In London, the mercury will hit 29C in the early evening, while it will remain hot in Cardiff and Manchester, both at 25C.

East Anglia will be warm at 27C, the same as Birmingham, the Midlands, and East Yorkshire.

North of the border, Glasgow will see 20C, Edinburgh 21C, and Aberdeen 22C. Over the Irish Sea, Northern Ireland’s high will be 23C in Newry.

News.title: US military helicopter with three on board crashes after 'aviation mishap'
News.content:
US military helicopter with three on board crashes after 'aviation mishap'

Officials say the crew was conducting routine flight training when the incident occurred and the chopper went down in a privately-owned field

View Image A helicopter from Fort Rucker went down near Opp (Image: Covington County Sheriff’s Office)

A military helicopter has crashed in Alabama, US, with three people on board.

‌



The helicopter from US Army base Fort Rucker went down near the city of Opp on the afternoon of Monday, July 28.

‌



Officials say the crew was conducting routine flight training when the incident occurred.

‌



Officials added the chopper was involved in an aviation mishap.

Sheriff of Covington County, Blake Turman, confirmed that a chopper crashed in a privately owned field on Cool Springs Road.

‌



Sheriff Truman told WDHN news outlet that he does not believe anyone was injured.

An instructor pilot and two student pilots were on board the chopper at the time. They are reported to be in stable condition.

All three were transported to a Dothan hospital for medical evaluation.

Article continues below

Officials say there are no reports of injuries to anyone on the ground and no reported damage to property.

It is being reported that the chopper was a UH-72 Lakota, but details on the crash are limited.

News.title: Hundreds of people turning up at A&E with eye complaints opticians would treat for free
News.content:
Hundreds of people turning up at A&E with eye complaints opticians would treat for free

Opticians on the high street provide free NHS clinics where you can be seen quicker for eye problems - but most people don’t know they exist and turn up in A&E instead

View 4 Images A host of eye injuries could be treated quickly without going to A&E (Image: Getty Images/Westend61)

Hundreds of thousands of people are turning up at A&E for eye complaints for which they could go to free clinics on most high streets.

‌



New analysis shows eye infections, such as conjunctivitis and dry eye, are among the conditions with which 400,000 people went to hospital with last year but could have been treated on the high street.

‌



The Association of Optometrists (AOP) estimates that between 62% and up to 78% of the 780,000 eye-related A&E visits in England could safely be managed by community opticians. It says up to 400,000 visits to over-burdened A&E departments could be saved by better use of those on the high street.

‌



View 4 Images A&Es are still struggling after a decade of funding cuts to services that keep people well (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

The AOP is calling for better funding of urgent and minor eye care services in optometrists so all can offer the NHS clinics as an alternative to A&E.

Chief executive Adam Sampson said: “Emergency departments should not be the default destination to manage eye problems. What this research tells us is that hundreds of thousands of patients each year end up in A&E because they conclude it’s their only option, but they could be treated by the highly trained optometry workforce based in the community.”

‌



A&E waits have remained stubbornly high since Labour came to power despite some progress on the elective NHS waiting list.

Waiting time standards collapsed under various conservative governments and the NHS target for 95% of patients to be treated or admitted within four hours of arriving in A&E has not been achieved in any month since July 2015.

Eye problems are among the top 10 most common reasons people attend A&E. Less serious eye abrasions can also be treated at NHS-funded clinics at optometrists.

‌



View 4 Images Opticians say they could do more for the NHS if paid to do so (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

Known as minor and urgent eye care services, they allow patients with conditions such as red eyes, infections, flashes and floaters, or sudden changes in vision to be assessed and treated for free. Patients can attend some on a drop-in basis but are usually advised to book ahead over the phone.

However not all opticians are funded by the NHS to provide these free NHS clinics and the industry body is calling for an end to this postcode lottery.

‌



AOP boss Adam Sampson added: “The challenge is not capability, it's consistency. It’s essential we have a service in place for everyone everywhere in England to treat eye problems in the community. The reality of the postcode lottery is that it deprives patients of access to care close to home.

“It is simply a no-brainer that the Government acts to ensure that every member of the public who has an eye problem should be able get the help they need on the high street, in the same way the public can go to a community pharmacy for a range of health issues, regardless of where they live.”

View 4 Images Adam Sampson, Association of Optometrists (AOP), has called an end to the postcode lottery

‌



A&E waits got steadily longer during over a decade of Conservative governments before which waits over 12 hours were unheard of. By December 2019 some 2,356 patients waited longer than 12 hours on a trolley until a proper bed became available and by December 2025 it was 50,775 patients.

Labour and NHS England have set an interim target of March 2026 for 78% of patients attending A&E to be admitted, discharged or transferred within four hours. Latest data shows 75.4% of patients in England were seen within four hours in A&Es and this has been improving in recent months.

Dr James Gagg, vice president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine said: “It’s no secret that emergency departments in England are under immense pressure at the moment, and we know our patients are being let down due to overcrowding and unacceptably long waits.

Article continues below

“We would welcome better-resourced community eye care, which could help deflect demand from A&E, accompanied by further measures from government to tackle the root causes of overcrowding and corridor care elsewhere in the system.”

News.title: Burnham says pupils in England need clearer pathway into work
News.content:
Children should be given a clearer pathway into work from the age of 14, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he unveils reforms that will allow pupils in England to study subjects like manufacturing and AI alongside core academic learning.

The government said the courses, available from Year 10, would be linked to local jobs and industries.

Data published earlier this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, or "Neet" - the highest level in more than 12 years.

While the government is describing it as a "fundamental change to the education system", there are few details behind the broad political vision.

The Association of School and College Leaders, which speaks for many secondary headteachers, said they welcomed the ambition of preventing young people falling out of education or work at 16.

With schools already asked to manage on tight budgets and support radical reforms to special educational needs, the union also said there was an issue of capacity.

Burnham said that "for too long" students had been told to take academic subjects to "do well and be respected".

"My message to young people is this - whether you choose construction, coding or classics, or maths, manufacturing or mechanics, you'll get the skills you need and be given the respect you deserve," he said.

The government, he added, was delivering the "major shake-up" required to fix the youth unemployment crisis in Britain, starting with improving the availability and quality of technical education.

Pupils, the government said, would be able to combine subjects such as English and maths with high-quality technical education linked to the jobs available in their area.

"They will be able to spend time with employers and gain real-world experience," it said.

In an Op Ed piece for the Times, external, Burnham wrote: "In the age of AI, practical and technical skills haven't become less valuable - they've become more valuable than ever. Britain will need brilliant engineers, electricians and cybersecurity experts more than ever before."

The reforms, he wrote, were about helping young people "build successful working lives from the start".

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Along with the changes to learning, Ofsted will change the way it measures performance and will inspect for technical education. It is not clear how this will fit alongside national measures designed to hold schools to account for the number of pupils taking core academic GCSEs.

News.title: Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled
News.content:
Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced.

It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places.

Separate wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have together burned about 297 sq miles (770 sq km), authorities estimate - an area larger than Madrid itself.

News.title: Reform UK reports Zack Polanski to police over guillotine T-shirt post
News.content:
Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top featuring the name "Nigel" alongside an image of a guillotine.

One of several images showed a man in a black t-shirt with a large guillotine below the words "We're only making plans for Nigel".

Sharing a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Once this image was brought to [Zack's] attention he immediately unshared the post. He unequivocally does not support this type of dangerous message."

Polanski had shared the photo with his 713,000 followers in a post containing several pictures of a Green Party event on Sunday, having accepted a request to collaborate with another account.

In a post on X, the Metropolitan Police said: "We received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media. We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter."

The words "We're only making plans for Nigel" are the same as the lyrics of a 1979 song by band XTC, external.

The Green Party spokesperson said: "Zack condemns the image on the T-shirt. He was tagged in a post with 20 images and clicked accept without realising there was more to it than he had seen.

"The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself.

"He and the Green Party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division."

The BBC understands Polanski has not been contacted by police.

News.title: BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murder
News.content:
A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez.

The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed photographic evidence.

BBC's North America correspondent Shaimaa Khalil was inside the courtroom.

Read more about the trial here.

News.title: Love Island UK crowns winners of twist-filled series
News.content:
This article contains spoilers for the Love Island final.

Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi have been crowned the winners of Love Island UK 2026.

The pair beat runners-up Jasmine Muller and Kavan Murphy, and Angelista Gunda and Simba Kudyiwa, who came in third, to take home the Â£50,000 prize.

A shocked Julia thanked all those who had voted for them, saying: "I just didn't think coming into Casa [Amor] I'd be stood here."

When host Maya Jama asked what they would spend the money on, Julia revealed she wanted Lorenzo, who appeared too stunned to speak, to move in with her after leaving the villa.

Talking to Maya ahead of the reveal during the live final, 28-year-old Lorenzo said he had "never met someone who feels so well matched to me" when reflecting on his relationship with Julia.

Business owner Lorenzo, who entered the villa on day one, said he felt like he "manifested" meeting Julia, 26, in Casa Amor, the alternate villa where relationships are tested by new arrivals.

Julia said she felt an "instant spark" when meeting Lorenzo and described their relationship as "seriously unserious".

News.title: 'I just found all the classified stuff downstairs' - Biden to ghostwriter
News.content:
Audio recordings that Joe Biden fought for years to keep private - in which he acknowledges possessing classified material after leaving office as US vice-president - have been released by Republicans in Congress.

The tapes contain interviews between Biden, now 83, and a ghostwriter working on his 2017 memoir, titled Promise Me, Dad.

"I just found all the classified stuff downstairs," Biden is heard saying at one point in the audio, recorded in February 2017, a month after he left the White House.

House Republicans and a conservative nonprofit, the Oversight Project, sued for the tapes, which were handed over for a 2024 justice department probe into Biden's handling of the records.

Biden's spokesman, TJ Ducklo, said in a statement that releasing the tapes was "just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DOJ for political retribution".

"It's wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today's decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy," he added.

The audio was recorded during the drafting of the 2017 memoir that Biden penned with co-writer Mark Zwonitzer.

At one point in the more than two hours of tapes released on Monday, Biden tells the ghostwriter: "The next thing I have here is, um, this is classified."

In an October 2016 recording, he tells Zwonitzer: "I have extensive notes over this period of timeâ¦ They [the White House] didn't know I have this."

At the time, Biden was still serving as vice-president to Barack Obama.

During Biden's tenure as president from 2021-25, the justice department declined to release the audio tapes.

In May, his personal lawyers sued the justice department in an effort to keep the tapes private, but after legal defeats they dropped their lawsuit.

The recordings contain significant redactions, which Republicans on the House Oversight Committee say "are intended to cover [Biden's] disclosure of classified information".

In 2024, Special Counsel Robert Hur obtained the recordings and transcripts while investigating Biden's handling of classified documents.

Hur found Biden improperly retained records, but he did not recommend charges, partly because of concerns that a jury would take his side and view him as "a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory".

Donald Trump was charged with illegally retaining the documents at his home in Florida, but the charges were dropped after he returned to the White House.

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of hundreds of prisoners.

Burnham announced last week that he was pausing the scheme, which would have seen about 700 prisoners freed in the first phase in September, following a backlash from survivors and victims.

But the Conservatives say the government's review will not stop offenders being released.

The scheme was part of a bid to stop unprecedented overcrowding, which Labour says was caused by Conservative governments failing to build new prisons.

A Labour spokesperson said: "It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess."

Early release was first used by the Conservative government, external in 2023 because of prison overcrowding, first for 18 and then 70 days, and 10,000 prisoners had been released early by June 2024 - before Labour came to power.

When Sir Keir Starmer entered Downing Street in July 2024, there were fewer than 100 spare prison places across the adult male estate, which is what prompted the Sentencing Act to release another 6,000 prisoners early from September.

While the act already excludes the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences, the eligibility for early release is based on the length of sentence, external, rather than the type of offence.

Badenoch is calling on Burnham to fast-track legislation to keep serious offenders behind bars.

"It's all well and good cutting bills and bus fares, but that pales into insignificance when paedophiles and rapists are about to be let out on our streets," she is expected to say at a press conference with victims on Tuesday.

"Burnham needs to show us he's ready to take the tough decisions."

Without emergency legislation, Badenoch says dangerous offenders will start to be released the day after MPs return to Parliament after the summer recess on Tuesday 1 September.

She is calling on Burnham to revoke legislation coming into effect on 2 September and if necessary recall Parliament to ensure the worst violent and sexual offenders are exempted from early release.

Conservative shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Victims should not have to live in fear all summer waiting for a review.

"The clock is ticking. Thousands of rapists, paedophiles, and other serious criminals are set to be released in September.

"Labour must act now and stop the mass release of dangerous criminals."

Earlier this month, the Conservative front bench sought to put pressure on the government to rethink the earlier release plans, saying that it would mean some rapists would leave prison sooner than expected.

The government stood by the plan, saying it was a political choice to manage offenders on strict conditions in the community, rather than see the collapse of the system, leaving sex offenders and others to act with impunity.

Burnham's decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added.

PC Harper's widow Lissie called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

Defending the review of the Sentencing Act that has been announced by Burnham, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives have some nerve.

"During their 14 years in office, they shut 23 prisons, created just 482 jail places, and granted early release to 10,000 prisoners - leaving the criminal justice system teetering on verge of collapse.

"It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess. We have already delivered over 3,000 prison places and we're investing billions to deliver thousands more."

Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The reality is that in a properly functioning justice system, no victim or loved ones should ever be told that their perpetrator is being released earlier than expected.

"Unfortunately, the Conservatives left our prisons on the brink of collapse, creating a capacity crisis that required emergency action to keep the system functioning and the public safe.

"Now that the government claims to have increased prison capacity, there is a clear opportunity for Burnham to correct some of the mistakes made by his predecessors with this scheme."

Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the "disastrous" policy had been introduced by the Tories, and Badenoch had in 2024 supported efforts to expand it.

"It's clear that only one party has consistently opposed early release and proposed strong law and order reforms to ensure hardened criminals are locked up for the full duration of their sentences," Yusuf said in a statement.

"Only Reform UK will fix lawless Britain," the party's Home Affairs spokesperson added.

News.title: Burnham appoints Phillipson as Labour Party chair
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Bridget Phillipson as Labour Party chair.

A Labour spokesperson said Phillipson, who is also minister for women and equalities, will work closely with deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell to modernise the party ready for the next general election.

Phillipson and Powell went head to head for the deputy leader position last year, after a race triggered by Angela Rayner's resignation, with Powell emerging victorious following 54% support from the party membership, external.

Phillipson had been education secretary under Sir Keir Starmer but that job was also handed to Powell by Burnham when he appointed his cabinet last week.

Announcing Phillipson's appointment, Burnham said she would help the party focus on preparations for a new digital campaigning environment.

"She will play a vital role in ensuring the Labour Party is match fit for the next election," he said.

She replaces Anna Turley who was made a minister in the Home Office last week.

The leadership team, which also includes chief whip Anneliese Midgley, is expected to focus on culture change, and building the infrastructure and policy platform needed by 2029, which is the latest an election can be held.

Posting on X, Phillipson said she was honoured, external to take on the role.

"I joined our party as a teenager and saw first hand the difference a Labour government makes," she said.

"I'll work with members to build the election-winning machine that sees off Reform [UK] for good and secures a second Labour term."

Welcoming her, Powell said: "Working together, we will ensure the party continues to lead the way in campaigning, with the strongest ground operation in British politics as we prepare for the next general election."

News.title: Funeral director who left people unburied breached families' trust 'on industrial scale', court hears
News.content:
A funeral director who failed to bury people and gave out wrong ashes has breached the trust of bereaved families "on an almost industrial scale", a court has heard.

Some 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024.

Owner Robert Bush previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities.

At the start of his five-day sentencing hearing on Monday, family members watching proceedings at Hull Crown Court gasped and were in tears as details of the "horror scene" at the parlour were described by prosecutors.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

Chris Paxton KC told the packed court bodies had been discovered "on the racks" of a cold storage area and one was found on a stretcher on the floor.

The vast majority were "uncovered and in varying states of decomposition", including one of a stillborn baby.

Bush, 48, was "entrusted by hundreds of bereaved families" but had "breached that trust on an almost industrial scale in a myriad of ways", Paxton said.

News.title: Very strong tide led to West Mersea drownings, relative says
News.content:
A mother and daughter who drowned off the Essex coast were swept out to sea by a "very strong" tide, a relative has said.

Shahin Ahmed said six members of his family were paddling at West Mersea beach when they were knocked off their feet on Wednesday afternoon.

Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died in the tragedy, while Ahmed's seven-year-old son Musa was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

Ahmed said his son, who is from east London, remained on a life support machine at a hospital in London.

Three others were also taken to another hospital by ambulance after the incident. Ahmed said 12 of them were visiting West Mersea that day.

"This was 20 minutes before we were going to go home. The whole day, alhamdulillah (praise be to God), was really nice," Ahmed told Bangladeshi newspaper Surma News.

News.title: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10.

Burnham said the visit of the Ukrainian president was designed to "send a very clear message" about the UK's continued support.

"To put it simply, Volodymyr, I want you to know that we've got your back, you can count on me and you can count on us. You can count on the UK for as long as it takes," he said at a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday.

Zelensky, meanwhile, said Ukraine's relationship with the UK was "stronger than ever".

Addressing Zelensky, Burnham said: "I am personally with you 100%, Mr President, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Burnham added that he intended to visit Ukraine "soon" following the "very warm meeting" between the pair.

The PM also announced the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.

Burnham said: "It will help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives."

The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.

The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.

Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.

It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.

During Monday's visit, the two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.

Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.

Burnham also said the UK would support Ukraine to get a "full and unconditional ceasefire".

"We will keep up the pressure, pushing for a ceasefire and a resumption of negotiations which must have Ukraine at the table and include a strong voice for Europe too."

News.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
News.content:
TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie has died at the age of 85, his agent has said.

Oddie became a household name in the 1970s as part of zany TV comedy trio The Goodies, before concentrating on his love of wildlife, as one of the original hosts of BBC TV's Springwatch and other shows about birdwatching.

In a statement, David Foster said: "It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country's best-loved birder.

"Bill was a multi-talented celebrity â wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued. Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment."

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and there were "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Teen denies endangering lives of 165 people on migrant boat crossing
News.content:
A teenager accused of endangering the lives of 165 migrants by allegedly piloting a record-breaking dinghy crossing of the English Channel is to stand trial.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally of Sudan, appeared at Margate Magistrates Court earlier, where he denied endangering lives at sea during the attempt which set off from France last Thursday.

He appeared with the aid of an Arabic interpreter and when asked how he wished to plea, denied having piloted the dinghy.

Atak was then remanded into custody and will next appear at Canterbury Crown Court on 24 August.

Prosecutor Lucie Fish told the court that, on Thursday, a rigid hulled inflatable boat departed the French coast headed towards Dover carrying the migrants.

The vessel was intercepted by Border Force and Atak is alleged to be one of two people controlling its speed and travel.

The boat was poor quality, overcrowded and "appeared to be deflating upon interception", the prosecutor added.

Pictures of Border Security Command towing the dinghy into Dover showed to be about the same size as a standard bus, at 13m (42ft) long.

During the hearing, the court heard that the French authorities had recovered the body of a man who had suffered head injuries - but there was no indication in court whether his death was related to the record-breaking dinghy.

A spokesman for the National Crime Agency told BBC News: "We are aware of an incident on Thursday 23 July in which an individual died in French waters. French partners are leading the investigation into the circumstances".

Endangerment at sea is a new offence that was created by the government under Sir Keir Starmer to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the English Channel.

In June, two men were the first to be jailed for the crime, each receiving sentences of more than two years.

The previous record arrival in a single vessel was 128 people.

Home Office figures show that while the overall number of arrivals this year is down by about 45% on 2025, the number of migrants per boat has gone up.
