When Nokx Majozi told people in her Durban community that she wanted to spend three years at college learning how to cook, they thought the idea was ridiculous.

Her family had never encountered the idea that cooking could be studied formally. “They said, ‘No, that’s not a course’,” she says. “Even the community, it was very difficult to explain this to them. I was like a joke within the community, like, ‘You don’t know how to cook’.”

In a place where cooking was something learnt at home, needing lessons could look less like ambition than evidence that your parents had failed to teach you properly.

“It was like a failure from your parents, that they didn’t teach you how to cook,” she says.

Majozi went to college anyway.

That decision would take her from a hotel kitchen in Durban to a Disney resort in Florida, then into some of London’s best-known kitchens. Now, having once been laughed at for taking cookery seriously, she has written the book she always hoped to make.

The South African Cook Book: Authentic Flavour-Packed Recipes from Cape Town to Durban is intended both as an introduction to a cuisine that remains surprisingly unfamiliar overseas and as encouragement for the young cooks following behind her.

“I always believe my story begins at home,” Majozi says. “I want to transport people to where I come from, to the beginning, and to inspire the young women or the young chefs in South Africa that, sometimes, the beginning may not be great, but look at me now.”

Home, in Majozi’s case, was Durban, on South Africa’s east coast, where she learnt by watching both of her parents cook. Her mother’s food was traditional; her father was more inclined to experiment, drawing on flavours and ideas he encountered through his work at the harbour.

She remembers her mother’s dumplings and her father’s fish curry as particular specialities, but it was the process of cooking beside him that first showed her what a chef might be able to do.

open image in gallery ‘The South African Cook Book’ travels from Cape Town to Durban through bold, accessible recipes ( Bloomsbury )

“When I was having that moment with my dad when he was cooking, I was chopping or doing something to help him, that’s when I realised you can take something so simple and elevate it,” she says. “That’s how my love of cooking started.”

The difficulty came when she tried to turn that love into a profession. Her family understood cooking as a domestic skill, not something that required qualifications, tuition fees or three years of study.

“I realised I just want to learn. I just want to go to college and learn how to cook – and that’s where the problem started,” she says.

After graduating, she found work at the Riverside, a four-star hotel in Durban. It was there that Nokuthula became known as Nokx. Then came the opportunity that changed how her ambitions were regarded at home: Disney recruited her to cook South African food at its resort in Florida.

“That’s when the community and everyone started to understand and say, ‘Wow, this can get you a job, you can go overseas’, and I was the first one in the community to do this,” she says. “It was something very rare, especially where I come from, for someone to go overseas for work.”

Majozi moved to the UK in the early 2000s and went on to work at the InterContinental in London and The Pie Room at Rosewood London. She has since appeared on Sunday Brunch and James Martin’s Saturday Morning, was selected as one of Jay Rayner’s Rising Stars in 2022 and recently joined Fallow as chef in residence.

open image in gallery Majozi’s kitchen career took her from Durban to Disney and some of London’s best-known hotels ( Russell Clamp )

The cookbook is the culmination of that journey, but it also has another job to do. South African wine may be familiar to British drinkers; South African food, Majozi believes, has not travelled nearly as successfully.

“Our food is very vibrant with colour, it’s got bold flavours – we are not scared to go for it – and it’s very diverse and inspired by different people,” she says.

It was only when she began travelling that she fully appreciated how many cultures had shaped the food she grew up eating.

“I never actually knew until I started to travel and I realised, ‘Oh, this is from Australia, this is German, this is Polish food’,” she says. “It’s multicultural, South Africa, and the food as well.”

That diversity runs through the book, which moves between provinces, traditions and the foods of different communities rather than presenting South African cooking as a single, fixed cuisine.

Among Majozi’s favourite recipes are bunny chow, one of Durban’s best-known street foods, and the seven colours meal, which she says “represents togetherness, family and a celebration of food and heritage”.

The recipes may be rooted in tradition, but she has deliberately made them possible to cook outside South Africa. Most of the ingredients can be found in supermarkets or ordered online, and she is comfortable making small adjustments where they help a dish travel.

Two of her favourite meals in the book are bunny chow, a type of street food, and the seven colours meal, which she says “represents togetherness, family and a celebration of food and heritage”.

open image in gallery The cookbook is the book Majozi says she always dreamed of writing ( Handout )

Speaking about why she loves cooking, she explained: “It’s a joy. You can have the same ingredients, but you can do 20 or 60 things with them.

“The beautiful thing is the more you work with different people – especially in London, you have different people of different countries and culture – there’s so much you learn from them.

“We can talk about food any time, with any stranger, and when you’re cooking and people are enjoying your food, for me that is just the best thing ever. It puts a smile on my face in a different way.”

For those wanting to cook South African food at home, Majozi advises people to have maize meal (similar to polenta), tomatoes, a chutney such as Mrs HS Balls, rice and a medium curry powder.

She says the salads are a great place to start in the cookbook for beginners, along with the mango chicken wings or the Malva pudding, which is “South Africa’s answer to sticky toffee pudding”.

Sharing her main hope for her cookbook, she adds: “I just want people to be able to cook something that they’ve never tried before.

“Not a lot of people know about South African food, but with this book, it can help people try something new, understand our culture and our food, and how food varies across provinces when visiting.

“Everyone knows about wine, but we can’t forget about the food – pair the wine with some food.”

Baked butterfish with herb crumb

open image in gallery A crisp herb crust gives tender butterfish a simple but special finish ( Yuki Sugiura )

“I love preparing this recipe so much!” Majozi says. “One of my all-time favourite ways to enjoy butterfish is by baking it with a crispy herb crust. The fish is tender and flaky, and the herbs create such a beautiful, fragrant coating and a pleasant crunch.

“I love how simple yet elegant this dish is – perfect for when I want something light but flavourful. Whether it’s a weekend family meal or a quick dinner on a busy weeknight, this baked butterfish always feels like a special treat.

“I like serving it with a fresh salad or roasted vegetables for a complete, satisfying meal.”

Serves: 4

Ingredients:(Serves 4)

60g unsalted butter

60g panko breadcrumbs

Small bunch of parsley, chopped

Small bunch of lemon thyme, leaves picked

1 lemon, zest and juice

35g Parmesan, finely grated

4 butterfish steaks (or black cod fillets)

1 tbsp vegetable oil

Sea salt and black pepper

Method:

1. Preheat the oven to 200C/fan 180C.

2. In a small pan over a low heat, add 30 grams of the butter. Remove from the heat as soon as it has melted and leave to cool for a few minutes.

3. In a small bowl, mix the breadcrumbs, parsley, lemon thyme, lemon zest, Parmesan, the just-melted butter and a good pinch of pepper.

4. Season the steaks with a little salt on one side. Heat an oven-proof frying pan over a medium–high heat, add the oil and place the steaks seasoned side down into the pan. Fry for about four to six minutes until there is a good colour on the underside of the fish, then take the pan off the heat.

5. Using a spatula, carefully turn over the fish so the cooked side is facing up and divide the breadcrumb mixture between the four steaks.

6. Place the pan in the oven for five minutes until the herb crust is golden. Transfer the fish onto individual plates.

7. Add the remaining 30 grams of butter and the lemon juice to the pan and use a wooden spoon to scrape up any toasted bits of fish and herb crust. Drizzle the lemon-butter sauce over the fish to serve.

Grilled peri peri chicken

open image in gallery Bold, smoky peri peri chicken made for the braai or the oven ( Yuki Sugiura )

“I’m generally a huge fan of peri peri,” Majozi says. “The heat from the spices, combined with the smoky flavours from grilling, makes every bite exciting.

“If you have time, marinate the chicken for a few hours, letting it soak up all those bold flavours, then throw it on the grill for that perfect crispy skin.

“It’s spicy, it’s tangy, and it’s just full of flavour – exactly the kind of dish I crave when I’m in the mood for something with a bit of a kick.

“Whether it’s a weekend braai or a quick weeknight dinner, this chicken never fails to deliver.

“If lighting the braai is too much of an effort, it is also fabulous in the oven. Simply roast at 200°C/fan 180°C for 40–50 minutes, turning once halfway through cooking.”

Serves: 4

Ingredients:

1 free-range chicken, about 1.5kg

For the peri peri marinade:

10 bird’s eye chillies, deseeded

4 garlic cloves, peeled

2 red peppers, deseeded and roughly chopped

1 red onion, roughly chopped

Large bunch of coriander, roughly chopped

Large bunch of basil, roughly chopped

1 tbsp dried oregano

3 tbsp smoked paprika

120g olive oil

2 lemons, zest and juice

Sea salt and black pepper

Method:

1. Start by making the marinade. In a food processor, put the chillies, garlic, peppers, onion, coriander, basil, oregano and smoked paprika and blend until smooth. Stir in the oil, lemon zest and juice and salt and pepper, to taste, until combined.

2. To spatchcock the chicken, turn it breast side down on your chopping board. Using kitchen scissors, cut along both sides of the spine and discard. After removing the backbone, place the chicken breast side up. Press down firmly to flatten. Pat the chicken skin dry using a piece of kitchen paper and season with salt and pepper.

3. Put half the sauce into a dish large enough to hold the chicken. Add the chicken and coat well with the peri peri sauce, then cover and leave to marinate in the fridge for at least an hour, or ideally overnight.

4. Light the braai 30 minutes before you want to cook.

5. When you’re ready to cook and the coals are hot, lightly brush the grill with oil. If you can adjust the height of your grill, raise it to a medium height, otherwise move your coals to one side and place your chicken away from the coals so it cooks slowly.

6. Place the chicken on the grill, skin side down for 20 to 25 minutes, then turn and baste with the remaining marinade. Grill until the juices run clear, turning every 10 to 15 minutes. It should take around 50 to 60 minutes in total.

Rainbow salad

open image in gallery A bright, crunchy salad that brings every colour to the table ( Yuki Sugiura )

“This rainbow salad is a showstopper in every sense,” Majozi says.

“It’s packed with every colour of the vegetable spectrum, from crisp peppers and radishes to leafy greens and shredded red cabbage, as well as Hispi cabbage, also known as pointed cabbage or sweetheart cabbage, whose leaves are delicate and sweeter than regular green cabbage.

“I love how it’s not just a feast for the eyes, but for the taste buds too. Each veggie brings its own crunch, freshness and flavour, and the tangy dressing ties it all together beautifully.

“This is the salad I make when I want something vibrant, healthy and guaranteed to brighten up my day. Every bite feels like a celebration of what nature has to offer.

“Ditch the regular leafy greens and make this your new middle-of-the-table salad!”

Serves: 6-8

Ingredients:

2 carrots, grated

125g butternut squash, peeled and julienned

1 red pepper, deseeded and julienned

¼ green cabbage, such as Hispi or Savoy, thinly sliced

¼ red cabbage, thinly sliced

100g baby spinach, thinly sliced

5 radishes, thinly sliced

20g parsley, chopped

60g mixed seeds, such as sunflower, pumpkin, linseeds

For the dressing:

1½ tbsp apple cider vinegar

1 lemon, zest and juice

3 tsp runny honey

3 tsp Dijon mustard

6 tbsp olive oil

Sea salt and white pepper

Method:

1. Start by making the dressing. In a blender or bowl, add the cider vinegar, lemon zest and juice, honey and mustard. While the blender is running or you are whisking by hand, slowly add the olive oil in a thin steam until it’s all incorporated. Season to taste with salt and white pepper.

2. In a large bowl, mix all the vegetables, the chopped parsley and the seeds.

3. Drizzle over the dressing and toss to coat everything thoroughly. Serve on a large platter.

This article was edited by The Independent.

‘The South African Cook Book: Authentic flavour-packed recipes from Cape Town to Durban’ by Nokx Majozi (Bloomsbury Publishing, £26).

Most people employ diets to lose weight and get in shape. But what if your meals, and the times at which you eat them, could keep your brain healthy too?

New research suggests eating all of your day’s meals and snacks within a nine-hour window, and eating your last meal four or more hours before bed, could slow down cognitive decline and reduce your risk of dementia.

You may recognise this as a form of intermittent fasting – a general protocol made famous by Michael Mosley and his 5:2 diet. But does this mean we should all be intermittent fasting for optimal health?

Sadly, as with anything in the health and fitness space, the answer is not so clear cut.

What the study says

The trial enrolled 47 overweight or obese women aged between the ages of 50 and 79. They were all guided to reduce their calorie intake by 500 per day. Of the 47, 26 women consumed their daily calories within a window of nine hours or less, while the remainder ate over a typical 12-hour period.

On average, the women lost 6.8kg after six months. But those with the nine-hour eating window enjoyed bonus benefits for their brain.

“There was a modest effect of time-restricted eating to improve spatial planning and problem-solving, and on reducing errors related to memory and learning,” says Sue Shapses, professor of Rutgers University and the study’s lead investigator.

“These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks, and reduced mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving. Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements.”

However, researchers add, the trial was relatively small and further studies are needed to confirm the findings. They also hope to identify why these benefits occur, and how time-restricted eating interacts with circadian rhythm, nutrient-sensing pathways, inflammation and metabolic health.



open image in gallery A nine-hour eating window has been linked to several benefits for your brain, but fasting expert Dr Valter Longo has warned against it being any longer than that ( Getty/iStock )

Should I be intermittent fasting?

The study above is interesting, suggesting a nine-hour eating window could deliver improvements in cognitive performance alongside weight loss in overweight people.

But 2026 research published in the Cochrane Library found that “compared to regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting may result in little to no difference in weight loss or quality of life”.

Any reduction in calories can lead to weight loss. This is no different to any other diet Vassiliki Sinopoulou, registered dietitian and lecturer

If you consume less energy than you burn, you will lose weight – this is the first law of thermodynamics in action. If you have less time to eat in your day, you tend to eat less, tipping this equation in favour of those looking to shed pounds. This is why intermittent fasting works for weight loss. But the common denominator – creating an energy deficit – is why pretty much every other type of diet does too.

As registered dietitian and University of Lancashire lecturer Vassiliki Sinopoulou puts it: “Any reduction in calories can lead to weight loss. This is no different to any other diet.”

The most important aspect of any diet is adherence – can you follow it sustainably for a prolonged period of time? If so, it will invariably have the desired effect.

If the structure and clear guidelines of intermittent fasting fit your routine and mindset, it could be a good option for helping you manage your weight. If it doesn’t, eating an appropriate number of calories for your activity levels in any way, shape or form will still do the job.



open image in gallery Intermittent fasting could work for some people – but not everyone ( Getty/iStock )

The bonus benefits of intermittent fasting

Fasting may not be provably superior to any other form of diet for weight loss. But some say it offers bonus perks that are worth pursuing.

“There is research to suggest fasting can lead to improvements in cholesterol levels, improvements in blood pressure and lower inflammation in general, which is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease,” says Heart Research UK nutritionist Amie Leckie.

“Digestion also takes a lot of energy. Many people eat all day long without realising, and I think a lot of that comes down to people not balancing their meals properly – they’re not eating enough protein or fibre, so they feel hungry an hour after a meal.

“When we do intermittent fasting, we give the body a break. We give it time to work on things at a cellular level and repair, so we do see certain benefits from that such as reducing CRP (C-reactive protein) levels, which are a marker of inflammation, and cognitive benefits as well.”

Many people eat all day long without realising, and I think a lot of that comes down to people not balancing their meals properl Amie Leckie, nutritionist at Heart Research UK

Dr Valter Longo, the longevity pioneer who inspired many of Dr Mosley’s fasting-related endeavours, is leading research into its extended benefits. When I spoke to him last year, he was understandably supportive of some forms of fasting. But he also stressed the need for nuance – and opposed 16-hour fasting windows, similar to those seen in the study above.

“People shouldn’t think that anything you do [with regards to adopting a diet] is right, because a lot of people are doing things they think are good for them that are actually associated with a shorter life; a ketogenic diet, a low-carbohydrate diet, 16 hours of fasting, skipping breakfast, there is a long list of things,” he said.

“There is 30 years of data indicating that you are going to live a shorter life and you will have more [risk of] cardiovascular disease [if you skip breakfast].”

One potential mechanism for this is the impact of 16-hour fasts on cholesterol levels, Dr Longo says.

“You may view [16-hour fasts] as an anti-statin – it’s increasing your cholesterol rather than lowering it,” he said.

“We know that statins lower your risk of cardiovascular diseases, heart attacks and cardiovascular events. It makes sense that if you did the opposite, that should increase your cardiovascular disease and events. And of course, we know that bad cholesterol levels correlate with cardiovascular disease.”



open image in gallery A Mediterranean diet contains many of the hallmarks of healthy eating ( Getty/iStock )

How should you eat for better health?

With the internet at your disposal, you can easily find data, articles and information to support almost any dietary approach. Therein lies the confusion.

Some people will report life-changing results from intermittent fasting; some will experience little change. The same can be said for research in many cases – some studies are for intermittent fasting, others are against it. This applies to almost any type of diet.

A 2020 review sought to put the “best diet” argument to bed, comparing research around several popular strategies including low-fat, low-carbohydrate, ketogenic, high-protein, Mediterranean, paleo, low GI, Nordic, vegetarian and intermittent fasting.

It concluded: “There is no single best strategy for weight management. Reducing daily calorie intake is the most important factor for weight loss.

“...Except for energy deficit, there seems to be no significant difference between macronutrient composition-based diets. Improvement in cardiometabolic factors strongly depends on the degree of weight loss.

“However, as in the Mediterranean diet, increasing consumption of fruits and vegetables and intake of healthy fats (including monounsaturated as well as polyunsaturated fats) can be a healthy strategy for weight loss and maintenance.”

This aligns fairly well with Dr Longo’s “longevity diet”, which follows a 12-hour eating window in line with your body’s circadian rhythm – or in-built body clock which follows natural night-day cycles.

“It almost completely eliminates red meat, it keeps white meat very low, and fish is eaten maybe three or four times a week,” he says.

“There are lots of vegetables, lots of legumes, lots of tree nuts, wholegrain cereal and some fruits. These are some of the ingredients that, consistently all over the world, have been associated with living a longer, healthier life.”

The study’s results also agree with the insights of the nutrition experts I interview weekly.

It seems that, when in doubt on how best to eat, we can fall back on tried and trusted advice that has outlasted innumerable trends, fads and crash diets.

Focus on whole foods, eat your greens, swerve late-night snacking – pretty much everything your parents told you to do as a child. Perhaps “mother knows best” is more than just a phrase, after all.

News.title: I ditched my iPhone and went ‘analogue’ for a trip to Lisbon – this is how it changed the way I travel

I have almost 120,000 photos on my phone, dating back to 2011. It sounds like an insane amount, though not unusual for a millennial like me, who grew up in tandem with ever-improving camera phones and has a deeply rooted fear of losing my digitally captured life.

Now, I’m as tired of the digital admin of safeguarding my photos as I am of my snap-happy habits. I decided to try the trend flooding my Instagram declaring 2026 as “the year of analogue” – an irony not lost on me – and use a film camera for my trip to Lisbon with my friend Rebecca.

Gen Zers are popularising film photography again in their search for offline activities, and research shows the wholesale film market grew by 127 per cent between 2020 and 2026, with more than 300 new film labs opening globally to keep up with demand.

Famed for its miradouros (viewpoints), bright yellow trams and pretty azulejos-clad (glazed patterned tiles) buildings, I imagined Lisbon would translate beautifully onto film. I hoped going analogue would make me more thoughtful about what I chose to capture from my travels.

open image in gallery A wall of plates outside Museu de Lisboa ( Emma Henderson )



To do it, I ordered a simple and cheap 35mm reusable plastic film camera, but over two weeks later, it still hadn’t arrived. Instead, rather resentfully, I picked up a Fujifilm disposable camera from Argos. It meant I had just 27 shots on one film instead of the three films I’d ordered. With a limited number of pictures available, I really had to think about what I was going to capture.

After dropping our bags off at the hotel in the artsy Santos neighbourhood in the early afternoon, our first stop was nearby natural wine bar, Insaciável, for wine and small plates. While roaming Santos' pretty streets with colourful tiled villas and the pretty pastel-pink Church Santos-O-Velho, I was already regretting not having two disposable cameras.

The following morning, we hopped on the Tram 28 and headed to one of the city’s miradouros, Jardim Júlio de Castilho in the historic centre. From the high vantage point, I took one of the trip’s best photos; overlooking the Tagus River, where the sky’s electric blues faded to a light pastel blue and contrasted the reddish rooftops. It looked like a painting.

open image in gallery Emma found the perfect viewpoint from which to pap the Tagus River ( Emma Henderson )

As I listened to a group of musicians perched on the wall of blue and white azulejos, beneath a pergola covered in bougainvillaea yet to bloom with the river behind, I wished my camera had the ability to do video too.

Instead I soaked in the moment among the growing crowd. The singer had wonderful gravelly harmonies as she strummed the guitar, and a man played the flute while another tapped the cajón he was sitting on and the drum in front of him.

Later, we walked down to the Rua Augusta Arch that commemorated life after the city’s 18th-century earthquake. It’s flanked by the Praça do Comércio’s sunny Lisbon-yellow buildings – and a blue sky backdrop made it another one of my favourite photos.

Near the water’s edge of the Praça do Comércio square, a man was feeding seagulls, and I thought it would be a great photo, so I clicked the button on my camera again.

That afternoon, I wanted to stock up on conservas (tinned fish), which Lisbon has many shops dedicated to. In Loja Das Conservas, more than 300 varieties of colourful tins line the walls, with different shapes and bright packaging. It was a great shot in my mind, but it came out very dark. I’d also tried to cut out the staff member on the left – not so easy to do without using the crop tool on your phone.

The next day, we headed to the region of Belém to eat Pastéis de Belém’s delicious custard tarts, where I realised mastering food photography with film isn’t easy.

open image in gallery Emma (left) and Rebecca take a selfie at the Belém Tower ( Emma Henderson )



At nearby Belém Tower, I managed a selfie with the landmark behind, but hadn’t accounted for a passer-by coming into shot and ruining it.

By now, remembering to use my camera had become second nature. But I wish I’d been able to take more abstract photos and close-ups of the many beautiful tiles. I did notice that I was appreciating the slower pace with this simple camera, as I really needed to look closely in the tiny viewfinder to get my subject lined up.

Heading back to the centre via the modern trams, we stopped off at the LX-Factory in the Alcântara neighbourhood, a former textiles factory turned creative hub. I tried to photograph the wall of books inside Ler Devagar bookshop, where the industrial-looking metal staircases appeared almost suspended mid-air. My photo is unintentionally moody, despite using the flash.

I began to realise that I'd quickly forget what I’d taken a photo of, as I was unable to scroll back through a digital camera roll, à la iPhone. And with such precious few snaps available, it felt a shame to potentially repeat any – but then again, I did want my own shot of the iconic mustard-yellow Tram 28 on the city’s steep roads.

To try and get it, I perched on the smooth steps of the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene, at a three-way crossroads traversed by many of the old trams while eating my lunch; a hefty bifana – a bread bap stuffed with slow-cooked shredded pork and topped with mustard. These photos, once printed, were blurred, probably due to me moving too quickly in my excitement while holding my food. Though they still tell a story – one of me trying to get a perfect shot.

We finished the day walking up and down the cobbled hilly streets of Rua da Bica de Duarte Belo to find the famous yellow funicular. Rebecca and I took some photos of us next to it.

As much as I loved my return to film, it’s an expensive hobby. The camera and development cost just under £33. And it’s risky – I had four blanks, while only a few of my photos were perfect. Though it did make me realise how many of my adventures are seen directly through a screen, and reminded me how analogue photography can be tangible and intentional – all elements of travel that are being ebbed away in our digital world.

Being forced to slow down and having a time-lapse between the trip and receiving my photos made it clear that the photos were the real souvenirs of my trip.



Where to stay

As Janelas Verdes Inn – in the quieter and slightly bohemian Santos neighbourhood – is easily walkable to trams and the main sites.

How to get there

EasyJet’s direct flights to Lisbon take around two hours 45min from the UK’s major airports.

An adaptation of a revolutionary science-fiction book previously considered “unfilmable” finally has a trailer, promising fans “the next chapter”.

Apple TV’s Neuromancer is based on the 1984 cyberpunk classic by author William Gibson. Set in a near-future dystopia, the story follows a computer hacker enlisted into a crew by a powerful artificial intelligence and a traumatised former soldier to complete a high-stakes heist.

The first official trailer for the show was released at Comic-Con on Sunday (26 July), and it showed off what looks to be another cult hit for the streamer, as well as a release date of 22 January 2027.

open image in gallery Callum Turner leads new cult series 'Neuromancer' ( Apple TV )

British star Callum Turner takes centre stage in the neon-soaked trailer, in which his character Henry Case can be heard saying: ”I’m the best console man around – I steal data in cyberspace,” before being transported through a trippy digital matrix.

Ten episodes were ordered in February 2024 from showrunner Graham Roland, whose previous credits include cult hits Lost and Fringe, and director JD Dillard.

The complex nature of the experimental novel, which often confounds new readers, has led many to believe an adaptation would have been too challenging to pull off. But for those wondering if Gibson had approved it: the 78-year-old writer is on hand as executive producer and creative consultant.

open image in gallery William Gibson's 'unfilmable' novel 'Neuromancer' is getting adapted ( Ace Books )

There’ll be more eyes on Neuromancer than ever before, thanks to the casting of Turner, an actor whose profile has risen considerably in the last year. Turner recently married pop star Dua Lipa and is a hotly tipped contender to become the new James Bond.

He leads the series as computer hacker Case alongside rising star Briana Middleton, Mark Strong, Clémence Poésy, Emma Laird, Peter Sarsgaard and Dane DeHaan.

The initial teaser trailer, released earlier this month, didn’t give much away, but it set up the vibe of the ready-made cult hit. It shows a computer monitor emblazoned with the opening words of the novel: “The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.”

open image in gallery Callum Turner is leading new Apple TV series ‘Neuromancer’ ( AFP/Getty )

The teaser’s description enigmatically states: “42 years ago, William Gibson introduced the world to Neuromancer. Now, the next chapter is loading.”

This could mean that the series will be going beyond the pages of Gibson’s source material, which is part of the Stream trilogy. However, the plot description remains loyal to the book: “A hacker and an assassin are thrust into a web of high-stakes crime as they take aim at a corporate dynasty.”

Should the show become a success for the streamer, the other two novels in the series – Count Zero and Mona Lisa Overdrive – could also be adapted.

Jack Draper has pulled out of this week’s Mubadala DC Open with an arm injury, tournament officials have announced.

It is the latest setback for the 24-year-old, who has been dogged by fitness issues throughout the year and missed the first three grand slam events.

The former world No 4, who has now fallen to a ranking of 147, had been due to play American Alex Michelsen in the first round.

A statement on X read: “Jack Draper has withdrawn from the tournament with a left arm injury. He will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Mackenzie McDonald.”

It is understood that Draper has withdrawn to focus on next month’s ATP Tour events in Montreal and Cincinnati, although he would need a wild card in both, and the US Open, for which he would probably need to qualify.

Cameron Norrie, meanwhile, light work of American Aleksandar Kovacevic with a 6-4 6-1 win at the Miffel Tennis Open.

Fifth seed Norrie ended a six-match losing streak stretching back to April as he progressed to the last 16 in one hour and 22 minutes.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

Playing in the Los Cabos event where he won his first ATP Tour title in 2021, Norrie lost on serve in the opening game of the match but immediately broke back and converted his second set point.

A one-sided second set lasted just 32 minutes as Kovacevic held serve only once, and that after saving two break points.

Norrie will face either Australian James Duckworth or American qualifier Aidan Mayo in the last 16.

In Washington, Katie Boulter failed to build on a promising start as she lost to Ashlyn Krueger.

open image in gallery Katie Boulter suffered defeat to Ashlyn Krueger ( Getty )

The 29-year-old, who married Australian world No 5 Alex De Minaur earlier this month, dominated the first set and went a break up in the seventh game as Krueger sent a backhand long.

Boulter, making her first appearance since a first-round Wimbledon exit, broke again two games later to clinch the opening set.

American Krueger turned things around – having made 16 unforced errors in the first set, she made only 10 more as she completed a 3-6 6-2 6-2 victory to set up a last-16 clash against Naomi Osaka.

An illegal, high-quality copy of The Odyssey was leaked online over the weekend, reaching over two million views.

The post from an X account, which has since been suspended, went viral after being re-shared by a separate account. “Someone uploaded The Odyssey full movie on X,” the person wrote. “Can you believe it?”

The message included the entirety of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s epic poem, according to Variety. The video amassed 2.1 million views before it was removed and replaced with a takedown notice.

Universal Pictures, the film’s studio, has since vowed to “pursue all appropriate remedies to protect our content and intellectual property rights.”

“We became aware of the unauthorized posting of the film and immediately initiated takedown protocols,” the studio told Variety in a statement. “We take copyright infringement seriously.”

open image in gallery ‘The Odyssey,’ starring Matt Damon, is out now in theaters ( Universal Pictures )

open image in gallery It also features Tom Holland as Telemachus, the son of Odysseus ( PA )

The Independent has contacted Universal Pictures for further comment.

Several other lower-quality bootleg copies have been circulating online, but many have also been taken down in “response to a report by the copyright owner.”

The millions of views of the pirated version certainly have not affected The Odyssey’s enormous box office haul. The acclaimed film, which premiered in theaters July 17, has already earned $639.6 million worldwide. It is projected to cross the $1 billion mark globally, matching his highest-grossing movie, The Dark Knight Rises, which earned $1.085 billion worldwide in 2012.

The Odyssey stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, the King of Ithaca, on his perilous journey home after the decade-long Trojan War. It also features Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Odysseus’s wife, and Tom Holland as Telemachus, Odysseus’s son, alongside Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Lupita Nyong’o, Robert Pattinson and Elliot Page.

It has received rave reviews and is expected to be a major Oscar contender, perhaps earning Nolan his second Best Director and Best Picture awards, following Oppenheimer (2023).

open image in gallery Anne Hathaway’s ‘dazzling’ performance as Penelope has been lauded by critics ( Universal Pictures )

“Christopher Nolan’s massive, fearless adaptation is his best film to date,” The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey proclaimed in a five-star review.

“There are touches of Oppenheimer, Memento and even his Batman movies in this enormous condensing of the British filmmaker’s fixations, brought to life by a cast of seemingly thousands,” Loughrey added, “but it’s the women (among them Anne Hathaway and Samantha Morton) who steal the show.”

Last week, Nolan said it would be at least three years before he made another film as the scale of The Odyssey took a toll on himself and his crew.

“I definitely hit the limits of my own stamina and everybody’s stamina, I think,” he told Today’s Kaylee Hartung. “I mean, it’s The Odyssey, of course it should be difficult. We are not doing the job right making a film of The Odyssey if it doesn’t seem difficult.”

News.title: Human first, athlete second: Ramsay-Peaty finds peace despite second bronze
News.content:
So a pair of bronze medals for the man who once only dealt in gold. Not that Adam Ramsay-Peaty thinks that is necessarily such a bad trade when he also computes the wider price of sporting domination.

“I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it,” Ramsay-Peaty said after his return to international competition continued in his now favoured 50m breaststroke with a second podium place at these Commonwealth Games. “That period of time, where I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human,” he added. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”

Aged 31, and with a baby girl on the way with wife Holly Ramsay, Ramsay-Peaty’s order of priorities might be understandable, but it was still another performance to raise questions over whether he can again climb to the top of a major podium.

Swimming is not kind to the over-30s – Michael Phelps was the first man in 2016 to win an Olympic gold in the pool even at the age Ramsay-Peaty is now – and we still have another two years until the Los Angeles Olympics. It would be the greatest achievement even of the Englishman’s extraordinary career to win his third individual Olympic title.

He trailed from the start here and was almost exactly a second outside his world record – set almost a decade ago – as Australia’s Sam Williamson completed a breaststroke double ahead of South Africa’s Michael Houlie in second. “As you get older, it gets harder,” said Ramsay-Peaty, before adding a crucial caveat, “but I’m enjoying it more…in my head, I’m getting fresher.”

News.title: Musk passed ‘slow death sentence’ on HIV patients by cutting US spending, says head of UNAIDS
News.content:
The world’s richest man has passed a “slow death sentence” on an untold number of people with HIV by cutting US spending on the disease, according to the head of UNAIDS.

In an interview with the Telegraph, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the UN body, said Elon Musk’s claim that the cuts made to US aid had resulted in “zero” deaths was born of ignorance.

“I do not know where Elon Musk gets his data from, but he [is] showing ignorance of the disease”, Ms Byanyima told the Telegraph at the opening the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro.

“This disease is not like a bullet shot in the head and you die. This is an attack on the immune system.” Withdrawing medication is a “a slow death sentence,” she said.

Data released by UNAIDS show that reductions to international funding and cuts to HIV prevention and community services threaten a resurgence of the epidemic.

In 2025, 1.2 million more people became infected with HIV and 570 000 more people died of Aids-related illnesses as the world fell short of global targets.

Although new HIV infections and Aids-related deaths are at their lowest levels in more than 30 years, an 18 per cent cut to total international funding means previous gains are now at risk, say experts.

News.title: Europe faces energy crisis as gas stockpiles sink
News.content:
Britons face a winter of surging energy bills as Europe struggles to secure enough gas to fill its storage tanks.

A squeeze on Qatari gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed European gas stockpiles into “energy crisis territory”, analysts at Wood Mackenzie warned.

The Continent’s storage tanks are barely 50pc full, a historical low for this time of year. Fresh tension between the US and Iran has cut the chances of more tankers sailing anytime soon.

Wood Mackenzie now forecasts that Europe will enter the winter with its gas storage tanks no more than 75pc full, compared with a five-year average of 90pc.

This could drive up prices, as Europe competes with Asia to buy extra gas, mostly from America on the spot market.

“Europe is approaching energy crisis territory,” Wood Mackenzie warned on Monday.

Meanwhile, Britain, which no longer stores significant amounts of gas, faces paying even more than rival buyers.

“The UK’s market model is that we’ll always pay more than anyone else, rather than relying on storage,” said David Lewis, an energy analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

“If other markets are going to struggle, it just means that the UK price will be even higher.”

Last week British Gas boss Chris O’Shea warned the country risked shortages over winter because of low levels of storage.

European gas prices fell at the fastest pace in a month on Monday after a pause in attacks between the US and Iran over the weekend, dropping to about €58 per megawatt hour.

Goldman Sachs expects the price to remain at about this level for the next three months, which is 80pc higher than the pre-war price of €32.

But the US investment bank warned the price could hit €100 next year if Middle East energy exports were slow to get back to normal.

The pressure from lost Qatari supply is being compounded by the EU’s plan to prohibit imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) from next year.

This will leave Europe in a bidding war with Japan and China for US LNG supplies.

Britain produces half its own gas and imports the rest, mostly via pipeline from Norway. But the Norwegian gas will largely track global LNG prices.

Laura Page, of the analysis firm Kpler, said Britain’s heavy reliance on Norway left it perilously exposed to any supply interruption.

“If there was a pipeline outage in Norway, or a problem with the gas field, that could cause prices to increase,” she said.

Mr Lewis said the Norwegians were postponing as much maintenance on their gas rigs as possible, to keep the supply flowing for Europe’s depleted stockpiles.

“But the problem is the same as in the UK: these are mature fields, they require a lot of maintenance, a lot of careful management,” he said.

Goldman Sachs said Europe had “only small room for error” in its gas stockpiling, and capacity could be as low as 28pc by the winter’s end.

Mr Lewis said the Netherlands and Germany were particularly exposed. “They might struggle to actually deliver the gas during peak demand days,” he said.

The El Nino weather pattern that will prevail for the rest of this year might come to Europe’s aid, delivering a milder winter than usual.

“It’s going to be an expensive winter unless we have a mild winter, which is what everybody’s hoping for at the moment. Fingers crossed,” Mr Lewis said.

News.title: Amazon has ended support for pre-2013 Kindles. What to do if you’re affected (and what to avoid)
News.content:
It seems like a lot of devices, but Amazon told Engadget that the move will affect around three per cent of current users. In theory, if you’re using a device that’s affected, then Amazon should already have notified you via email. If in doubt, however, the company has a support page with pictures and specifications of every Kindle ever released. If you’re still unsure, entering the model number into Google should reveal the exact version you’re using. This can typically be found on the back of devices.

For Kindle Fire tablets, the process is simpler. Open the Settings menu and select “Device Options”. You’ll find the model you’re using either under “Device Model” or “About Fire Tablet”.

Why did this happen?

Nobody expects electronic devices to be supported forever, but it’s disappointing that the Kindle’s most enthusiastic early adopters got cut off. Given the basic functionality of e-book reader technology, there doesn’t appear to be a technical reason behind the decision, making it appear like an anti-consumer move to push older customers towards the purchase of newer devices where existing Kindles would become an e-waste casualty.

When asked why these devices were losing support, we received a response defending the (admittedly impressive) longevity.

“These models have been supported for at least 14 years – some as long as 18 years – but technology has come a long way in that time, and these devices will no longer be supported moving forward,” an Amazon spokesperson said. “We are notifying those still actively using them and offering promotions to help with the transition to newer devices.”

At the initial time of writing, the promotions mentioned appeared to be 20 per cent off “select new Kindle devices” alongside a £15 eBook credit. While the latter was welcome, the highlighted discount is somewhat disappointing for a number of reasons. Firstly, according to the promotion’s terms and conditions, the “select” caveat excludes the most expensive model, the Kindle Scribe. It doesn’t apply to Fire devices for those tablet owners looking to replace like-for-like, either.

More importantly, the prices aren’t all that impressive considering happy owners of older Kindles weren’t budgeting for this purchase. Amazon frequently discounts its own-brand devices like Echo smart speakers and Fire tablets, and 20 per cent isn’t that unusual. Last year’s Black Friday sale saw discounts of over 30 per cent on the basic Kindle and Kindle Colorsoft, and the price-tracking site CamelCamelCamel shows that the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition has been as low as £183 in the past – a 32 per cent discount on its current price of £269.

There was added time pressure, too. Amazon said the discount and credit offer was only valid until June 20, one month after support for the older Kindles ended.

Additionally, owners of the earliest UK Kindle will see that prices have gone up over the past decade. The £109 they paid in 2010 is some way off the £159.99 Kindle Paperwhite, even with a 20 per cent discount, let alone the £219.99 Kindle Colorsoft. That said, at £94.99, the basic Kindle 12th Generation remains a bargain for no-frills readers, with a 20 per cent discount taking it down to £75.99.

Possible upgrades

If you’re affected by this news, the silver lining is that while e-book technology moves relatively slowly, things have still advanced significantly in the past 14 years. Resolutions are higher; most are backlit for bedtime reading; there’s support for audiobooks; and storage has increased. There are also optional extras like colour screens, blue-light filters to prevent eye strain and waterproofing.

As outlined in our guide to the best Kindles, our pick for most people is the 12th Generation Kindle Paperwhite, which costs £159.99 with lockscreen ads or £169.99 without. The seven inch screen with warm lighting makes for a comfortable reading experience, and it’s waterproof for bathtime or poolside reading.

At £94.99 (or £104.99 without ads), the basic 11th Generation Kindle is a great budget pick, however. It’s slightly smaller at six inches, and like the Paperwhite, can hold around 8,000 e-books with support for audiobooks through Audible. It lacks the warm light and waterproofing, however, and its battery life is around half that of the Paperwhite — albeit still a generous six weeks of normal use.

The two remaining Kindles occupy specific niches. The Kindle Colorsoft has a colour screen, making it well suited to those who enjoy graphic novels. The Kindle Scribe, meanwhile, has a bundled stylus for note taking.

Can I still use my old Kindle?

Yes, Amazon said users would be able to “continue to read books already downloaded on these devices”. If you factory reset your older Kindle, however, or you deregister it, you won’t be able to use it anymore.

News.title: Lando Norris comes in from the cold with dominant Hungarian GP victory
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix from the Hungaroring. This is the 40th anniversary of the race at this track and the 41st edition. I think over the years this track has had a bit of an unfair reputation but we have certainly had some interesting and exciting races over the years. Even over the last few years.

The nature of the track means it is a bit of an outlier. And that means you often get results that go away from the norm of the season. Mercedes took a couple of poles here in the ground-effect era whilst Charles Leclerc did so last year. We have had a handful of first-time winners at this track, too: Damon Hill, Fernando Alonso, Esteban Ocon, Jenson Button and… errr Heikki Kovalainen.

So far that has been true this weekend. Although McLaren and Ferrari have been closing in on Mercedes, the SIlver Arrows have usually had the edge or found it when it comes to qualifying. That was not the case yesterday: Lando Norris took the first non-Mercedes grand prix pole of the season, pipping the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton by just 0.012sec.

Hamilton, though, takes a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri in Q3. Kimi Antonelli, who had qualified fourth, takes the same penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. It was Ferrari who had been expected to be the team to beat but they were the team that dropped the ball. In fairness Norris, in the upgraded McLaren had looked competitive throughout qualifying and was simply able to deliver when Ferrari could not.

The grid is slightly mixed up because of the penalties. George Russell’s season did not get any easier after qualifying seventh but he at least moves up because of those grid drops. The Mercedes’ race pace is expected to be strong but will it be enough to put them into contention with the McLarens and the Ferraris? And let’s not forget Max Verstappen in fourth, either…

We find out at 2pm BST, when the race gets under way.

News.title: Anthony Joshua knocks out Kristian Prenga after worst round of his career
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Anthony Joshua’s heavyweight clash with Kristian Prenga, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom plays host to yet another major boxing event, and this is the second part of a weekend that serves as a build-up to a potentially huge match-up later this year.

Prenga’s 20 wins have come against pedestrian opposition, and if he wins tonight then it would be such an upset as to probably finish Joshua’s career as a real name in the sport.

Joshua, the former unified champion, has plenty of defeats to his name. Oleksandr Usyk, twice, as well as Daniel Dubois and Andy Ruiz Jnr.

Tonight should show us where he is. After his loss to Dubois in 2024 he did not fight again until December 2025, when he rearranged Jake Paul’s ability first to stand up, and second, to chew.

A win for Joshua tonight means that all eyes turn to the end of the year, when he is expected to finally meet Tyson Fury in the ring to settle their rivalry.

Now both are deposed champions, the interest has waned a tad, but it remains the biggest all-British clash that anybody could conceive.

Fury, for his part, had little trouble against Mariusz Wach last night, the 46-year-old journeyman who he fought in Thailand. While that was not broadcast live, the clips online hardly suggested it was a classic, but it was enough to keep Fury active as he maintained his focus and avoided his own banana skin.

Joshua now needs to show that he is capable of finishing a fight. If he struggles, he invites pressure for the next four or five months in the build-up to meeting Fury.

Sports.title: How Chelsea could line up with Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson as Xabi Alonso rips up transfer strategy
Sports.content:
CHELSEA have ripped up their youth movement and are targeting good old fashioned Premier League experience instead.

For years Blues fans have had to Google plenty of little-known teenagers from far flung corners of the globe as their club swooped for various wonderkids.



Following last season’s disastrous 10th place finish, however, things are looking a little different at Stamford Bridge.

And the club are now targeting two England internationals in their mid-30s – Jordan Henderson, 36, and Danny Welbeck, 35.



Chelsea‘s last two bosses’ only experience of managing in England had come in the Championship; Enzo Maresca at Leicester and Liam Rosenior at Hull and Derby.

Their hotseat’s latest incumbent Xabi Alonso, however, was last seen at Real Madrid.



And there’s no need for Google when it comes to most of Alonso’s targets.

The Spaniard has already splurged £117million on England star Morgan Rogers.



Today it emerged that the Blues want Henderson and Welbeck in order to add top professionals with vast experience of operating at the highest level.

Should the Blues land both targets, how will they fit into Alonso’s new look team?

BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

THE LEVERKUSEN APPROACH

Alonso enjoyed easily the most successful spell of his career as Bayer Leverkusen boss – completing an unbeaten 2023-24 season to win the Bundesliga title while also collecting the DFB Pokal.

The Spaniard utilised a 3-4-3 formation during his time in Germany, although curiously ditched the approach for his less successful stint in Madrid, but more on that later.



Should he decide to revert back to that system in West London, both Henderson and Welbeck should be helpful.

The latter, who scored 13 Prem goals last term, can slot into the middle of an attacking trident flanked by Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer.

This approach will likely be towards the end of games as Joao Pedro tires, or if the Brazilian is ever unavailable.

Henderson, meanwhile, will add steel next to Moises Caicedo when selected, which may be more than initially expected should Enzo Fernandez leave the club.



THE REAL MADRID APPROACH

As mentioned above, Alonso primarily reverted to a 4-3-3 during his short tenure at the Bernabeu.

The tenure can by no means be called a success, although the 44-year-old did win 24 of his 34 games in charge before the club’s hierarchy gave in to player power and got rid.

It would not seem far fetched that Alonso could stick with the 4-3-3 at Chelsea, rather than going with the back three.

In this scenario, Welbeck would still be able to slot in up front between Rogers and Palmer when required.



Henderson, meanwhile, could potentially sit in front of the back four, giving his midfield partners more license to get forward and join attacks.

This would be particularly beneficial should Fernandez stay at Stamford Bridge, given the Argentine’s eye for goal.

A NEW APPROACH?

Towards the end of his Real Madrid tenure, Alonso did begin to dabble with a 4-4-2 system.



And particularly when chasing games, this could allow him to stick Welbeck on alongside Pedro.

The pair know each other well, having been Brighton team-mates for two years.

Henderson may also be useful for this attacking scenario.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

His disciplined presence can allow the likes of Palmer and Rogers to attack without too much fear of being exposed defensively.

Both Henderson and Welbeck may prove to be useful impact subs for Alonso, if not regular starters.

Sports.title: Italian football hits new low as Paolo Maldini QUITS after just 16 days in charge over refusal to appoint Pirlo as boss
Sports.content:
PAOLO MALDINI has quit as Italy’s technical director after just 16 days in the job after his bosses refused to hire Andrea Pirlo as the new manager.

Italian football was plunged into chaos as Pirlo, 47, was axed from the running to take over at the Azzurri helm due to links with a Russian betting company amid the war in Ukraine.



That led to Maldini, 58, and his advisor Leonardo resigning from their respective roles.

This comes after the former Italy duo flew to Barcelona last week to meet Pep Guardiola and offer him the job just two months after he rolled credits on a glittering ten-year stint at Manchester City.



Guardiola, 55, kindly declined as he didn’t feel ready to return to management even on a part-time capacity that international football can offer.

Thus, Pirlo emerged as the leading candidate to succeed former team-mate Gennaro Gattuso, who quit in April after Italy missed out on World Cup qualification for the third time in a row.



However, the legendary midfielder’s role as global ambassador for Russian bookmaker Fonbet prompted objections from some Italian Football Federation officials and politicians.

The AC Milan and Juventus icon, who won the World Cup with Italy in 2006 along with Maldini, defended his involvement with the company in an Instagram post.

Pirlo is currently working in the United Arab Emirates where he manages Dubai United.

The former Juve boss signed an ambassadorial agreement with Fonbet in October and said the collaboration was exclusively commercial and sporting in nature.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Pirlo posted: “After learning last night that I am no longer the candidate to lead the Italian national team, I believe it is my duty to clarify a few points.

“In the last few days I have witnessed with great bitterness the debate that has developed around my name and the possibility of taking over the role of head coach of the Italian national team.

“During my career, first as a football player and now as a coach, I have always carried out my activity in full respect to the laws of the countries I worked in and the contracts I signed.

“To attribute a political meaning to such a collaboration means to attribute convictions that I have never expressed and that do not belong to me.”

Maldini was appointed on July 11 to help rebuild the national side and lead a decade-long project that would include radical youth development after claims the lack of grassroots talent is what caused Italy’s recent woes.



The fallen football giants have embarrassingly failed to qualify for the last three World Cups, although they did win the Euros in 2021 against England.

Antonio Conte, Roberto Mancini and Thiago Motta are now among the favourites to take over at the helm.

Sports.title: John Stones on verge of shock Inter Milan free transfer as Italian giants beat Chelsea and Arsenal to England ace
Sports.content:
INTER MILAN are on the verge of winning the race to sign free-agent John Stones.

The centre-back, 32, left Manchester City when the season finished and has been without a club since.



Stones won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, five League Cups, three Community Shields, the Club World Cup and the Uefa Super Cup during his time at City.

However, appearances have been limited in recent years due to injury issues for the former Everton defender.



He only managed 18 games for the Etihad club last season as he was either left on the bench or struggling with niggles including a thigh problem.

But he showed he still has plenty to offer in five games at the World Cup as England made the semi-finals.

Juventus made a move over the weekend but appear to have lost out to Serie A champs Inter, with a two-year contract close to being finalised.

Premier League rivals Arsenal and Chelsea have been linked with the Barnsley Beckenbauer.

But the Blues look to have gone for Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix instead.

Stones’ old Etihad centre-back partner Vincent Kompany — the boss of Bayern Munich where Stones’ Three Lions pal Harry Kane plays — has also had a look, while Napoli were reported to be interested.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Juventus need a new centre-half with Gleison Bremer, 29, expected to join Galatasaray.

Stones’ England team-mate Jordan Henderson is also on the verge of a surprise move.

The midfielder, who is recovering from the broken arm he suffered at the World Cup, is in being lined up for a free switch to Chelsea from Brentford.

Henderson, 36, joined the Bees on a two-year deal ahead of last season following 18 months at Ajax.



Keith Andrews‘ side could now grant him a free transfer to Chelsea as he prolongs his career at the top level.

Sports.title: Arsenal stars cool off in pool as Gunners jet to Girona for pre-season training camp and first friendly
Sports.content:
ARSENAL stars cooled off in a swimming pool after jetting to Girona for their pre-season opener.

The Gunners will take on the second tier Spanish side at their diminutive Montilivi home this Saturday.



Ahead of the match, boss Mikel Arteta has taken his side over to Catalonia for a training camp.

On day one of the trip, the Gunners completed a session on the pitch in addition to further gym work.



To cool down at the end of the day, Arsenal stars enjoyed themselves in the pool.

The group splashed around with a ball playing head tennis – with plenty of stars laughing and beaming during the recovery session.



Players that went deep in the World Cup, including England stars Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze, are still on holiday.

But high-profile players including Kai Havertz, Viktor Gyokeres and Gabriel Jesus are on the trip.



Boss Arteta has been able to run the rule over new signings Christos Tzolis and Illan Meslier.

And forgotten men Reiss Nelson and Fabio Vieira are also on the trip following loan spells last season.

BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Following Saturday’s Girona clash, Arsenal will play further friendlies against Real Betis, Borussia Dortmund and Como.

They will then take on FA Cup winners Manchester City in the Community Shield on August 16.

Sports.title: England star James Trafford closing in on £40million transfer after just 17 games with Man City
Sports.content:
JAMES TRAFFORD is closing in on a £40million move to Leeds.

The Manchester City goalkeeper is Elland Road-bound just a year after arriving at the Etihad in a £27million move from Burnley.



Trafford, 23, will become Leeds’ third summer signing following the arrivals of Tarik Muharemovic and Harry Wilson.

Karl Darlow’s move to Man Utd had left Daniel Farke on the hunt for a new goalkeeper, with Alex Cairns set to be Trafford’s deputy.



Newcastle had also been interested in signing him, but their interest faded with the signing of £18.5m Ewen Jaouen from Reims.

Trafford cast doubt on his Man City future while away with England at the World Cup.

Though he played every match in both of City’s domestic cup wins, he made just four Premier League appearances following Gianluigi Donnarumma’s arrival.

Asked if he would be leaving the Etihad, Trafford said: “It’s obviously been very challenging the past season, but looking back, I’ve learned so much, I’ve developed so much.

“I thought I’d had a lot of experiences up to this point in my career, but this was a new experience for me in everything.

“It was obviously very tough. Some days were harder than others.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Trafford also noted the need to be a No1 somewhere if he wishes to overtake Jordan Pickford as Thomas Tuchel’s go-to man between the sticks.

Tuchel handed Trafford his Three Lions debut in March, and was part of the World Cup squad, but failed to make an appearance.

Sports.title: Chelsea lead race to sign Jordan Henderson in shock free transfer as two more clubs battling for England star
Sports.content:
CHELSEA are plotting a shock swoop for Brentford star Jordan Henderson.

The Blues are aiming to add more experience this summer and see the England veteran as an ideal addition.



Henderson, 36, joined Brentford on a two-year deal ahead of last season following 18 months at Ajax.

Keith Andrews‘ side could now grant him a free transfer to Chelsea as he prolongs his career at the top level.



The Blues are not the only club interested, however, with two other Prem sides believed to be chasing the midfielder’s signature.

Henderson was part of Thomas Tuchel‘s England World Cup squad and was seen as a valuable leader in the dressing room.

This makes him a suitable candidate for Chelsea’s transfer strategy this summer, which has pivoted from almost entirely focusing on recruiting talented young players to aiming for more experience.

Earlier this summer the Blues targeted Sunderland’s 33-year-old former Arsenal midfielder Granit Xhaka.

And today it emerged that they want to add Brighton striker Danny Welbeck, 35, to their forward line.

SunSport also reported last week that the Blues were considering a swoop for John Stones, although the free agent now looks nailed on to be heading to Serie A.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Henderson began his career at Sunderland and played 79 times for the Black Cats before landing a move to Liverpool in 2011.

The boyhood Mackem starred at Anfield for 12 years, succeeding Steven Gerrard as captain and going on to win a Premier League title, the Champions League, an FA Cup, two League Cups and the Club World Cup.

After seeing his minutes decline, Henderson opted to reunite with Gerrard at Al-Ettifaq in the summer of 2023.

The England star received plenty of criticism for his Saudi move and quickly decided to return to Europe, signing for Ajax in January 2024.



Henderson soon got his career back on track in Amsterdam, playing 57 times for the Dutch giants ahead of a Premier League return with Brentford in 2025.

He subsequently helped the Bees to a ninth place finish.

Having been in the international wilderness between November 2023 and March 2025, Henderson has since become a regular in Tuchel’s England squads.



The 90-cap star was picked for this summer’s World Cup, but was limited to just one cameo appearance from the bench.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

During the celebrations of England’s 3-2 win in Mexico, Henderson suffered a broken arm as he fell while vaulting an advertising board.

It remains to be seen when he will fully recover from the injury.

Sports.title: Former Premier League manager left so furious by calamitous pre-season goal he starts vaping on sidelines
Sports.content:
WALTER MAZZARRI was left so glum he started vaping after two goalkeeper howlers in a pre-season loss.

Mazzarri, 64, took over Greek minnows Iraklis earlier this month and oversaw their first friendly against Bologna on Saturday in Italy.



The Elder went on to lose 2-0 in Bolzano after two errors committed by two different keepers.

The Serie A outfit opened the scoring after just seven minutes when Giorgos Athanasiadis committed the first blunder.



Athanasiadis, 33, got such a heavy touch on the ball that he lost it and set up Thijs Dallinga for an easy opener.

The Greece international was replaced by Panagiotis Tsintotas in the second half when Bologna got a penalty that shouldn’t have been given.



Former Norwich ace Jonathan Rowe took it on and doubled the Italians’ lead on 58 minutes.

Tsintotas, 33, got to the ball as he lunged to his right and could have held on to it but it still slipped out of his hands.

That’s when the camera panned in on Mazzarri watching from Iraklis’ bench.

The ex-Watford boss looked bewildered – probably from the two errors as well as the referee’s wrong decision to award Bologna a penalty.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

So much so that the ex-Napoli boss started smoking his vape while the game continued.

The ex-Sampdoria boss’ assistant Ieroklis Stoltidis was also left completely frustrated.

Mazzarri joined Iraklis after two years without a club as his second stint at Napoli ended in 2024.

The ex-Inter Milan boss spent a year at Watford but he left in 2017 despite securing Premier League status after a gruelling relegation scrap.

Sports.title: Premier League and EFL to implement radical new rule forcing teams to play with TEN men starting this season
Sports.content:
ENGLISH football is set to trial a new rule in a bid to prevent goalkeepers “bending rules” by going down for treatment.

Last season saw plenty of instances in which goalkeepers were seen by a physio on the pitch, allowing team-mates to receive instructions from their managers and breaking up the action.



When an outfielder is seen by the physio, they must leave the field – unless an opponent has been carded for the challenge that caused the injury.

The rule was taken on ahead of the 2023/24 campaign but goalkeepers had been immune and could get treatment on the pitch.



According to the BBC, however, that is about to change.

They report that the PGMOL have opted to trial a system that will see teams have to nominate an outfield player to go off for one minute if their goalkeeper has had treatment.

If no player has been selected within 10 seconds, the captain will be forced off.

The trial is subject to being approved by global refereeing body IFAB.

It is set to be used across the Premier League, English Football League, Women’s Super League and National League.

The trial could begin as soon as Saturday, when Tranmere host Rochdale in the Carabao Cup preliminary round.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

After Gianluigi Donnarumma went down during a clash between Leeds and Manchester City last November, Whites boss Daniel Farke said: “If we don’t educate our players in football what to do in terms of fair play and sportsmanship and whatever and if we just try to bend the rules and even do a fake injury in order to do an additional team talk, it is not what I like personally.

“But if it is within the rules I can’t complain.”

In February last year, Bolton boss Steven Schumacher even admitted to using the ploy as a deliberate tactic.

Schumacher said: “I can’t complain about it because I have done it myself, so I’m not immune to it.

“It’s a ploy, a tactic that kills the momentum of the game when the opposition is on top and if you time it right you can really affect the game and there’s a chance to get your team in.



“It happens pretty much in every game now, even in the Champions League. I was laughing last week watching one of the Champions League games and thinking ‘we’ll it’s not just in England then,’ so it’s just part of the game now.”

After using the tactic last season, Plymouth Argyle boss Tom Cleverley admitted: “My thoughts are, to be completely honest with you, I think it’s wrong, there’s an element of embarrassment when you do it.

“Schuey was the same last weekend, but why would you not? I’m here to get results for this football club so if there is something I can do to help that I’m going to do it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Do I feel like it should be taken away from us as coaches? Yeah. There should be a caveat to that.

“That’s my feelings, but whilst I can do something to help our football team I will do it.”

Sports.title: Arsenal's dream attack as Vinicius joins from Real Madrid and £51.7m swap deal agreed
Sports.content:
Arsenal's dream attack as Vinicius joins from Real Madrid and £51.7m swap deal agreed

Arsenal have the chance to send a statement of intent to their biggest rivals by signing Vinicius Junior from Real Madrid

View 3 Images Mikel Arteta is interested in signing Vinicius Junior (Image: Getty )

After a weekend where reports emerged of Arsenal’s concrete interest in Real Madrid talisman Vinicius Junior, the Gunners have the chance to build their own squad of Galacticos.

‌



Arsenal fans everywhere stopped what they were doing and took notice on Saturday after news broke out that a deal for the Brazilian had been approved at all levels at the Emirates Stadium. Gunners chiefs, who have been targeting a major left wing signing this summer, spotted a golden market opportunity after missing out on Morgan Rogers’ signature in disappointing fashion.

‌



Vinicius has just one year left on his deal and has still not reached a resolution with Los Blancos over a new contract. With Real anxious not to lose the Brazilian sensation on a free transfer next summer, there is a real chance that both they and Vinicius could be tempted by Arsenal’s pursuit.

‌



As of now, no official negotiations have taken place between the two clubs or with the player’s representatives, with Arsenal monitoring the situation closely before deciding whether to submit a formal bid. Given his superstar status, Arsenal would have to make the 26-year-old their top earner on a mammoth £400,000-a-week contract in order to convince him, meaning he would overtake Bukayo Saka and break the club’s current wage structure.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Vinicius Junior transfer: Arsenal ready to break salary record to sign Real Madrid star READ MORE :

Arsenal's two conditions for Bruno Guimaraes transfer as Gunners set to make next move READ MORE :

But, as shrewd and well-run as the Gunners are with regards to their finances, this is one player they should be willing to splash out on. In a transfer window where top wingers such as Rogers, Bradley Barcola and Yan Diomande are going for over £100m, Vinicius stands levels above any of them in terms of his quality and accomplishments.

‌



The Brazilian played an integral role in two Champions League-winning campaigns for the greatest club in the world, and was unlucky not to win the Ballon d’Or in 2024. Arsenal need to find a way of making him their biggest ever signing - a transfer that would send shivers down the spines of not only Premier League clubs but also European rivals.

Vinicius’ arrival would hand manager Mikel Arteta the game-changing abilities he has been crying out for up top, most notably after the Champions League final defeat to PSG in May, where they lacked individual moments of magic. The Brazilian has proven time and again that he has such moments in his locker.
