World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms
World.content:
Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud

The US government on Monday filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court seeking authorization to implement President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, which lower courts have blocked. The request comes 99 days before November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The filing followed by two days a decision by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Boston, which refused by a two-to-one vote to stay the injunction issued on June 25 by a district judge. That ruling keeps the order blocked in twenty-three Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.

The order, signed in March, tasks the director of Citizenship and Immigration Services and the commissioner of the Social Security Administration with drawing up a list of eligible voters, and bars the Postal Service from sending ballots to anyone not on it. The plaintiff states argue that the Constitution reserves the conduct of elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, an argument accepted in the earlier rulings.

In its filing before the high court, the administration framed the order as “general policy guidance” and stressed that the Postal Service has not finalized any regulations. The appeals judges had noted, by contrast, that the measure sets rapidly approaching deadlines requiring states to reorganize their procedures immediately, while also ensuring that officials and the public understand the rules governing the September and November votes. A White House spokesperson said the lower courts' decision “is not the final say” and that the administration expects a favorable outcome.

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud. Election officials, courts, and federal agencies concluded that there was no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 elections, when that method saw unprecedented use during the pandemic, and noted that the system includes multiple verification and audit mechanisms.

The initiative is part of a broader set of government actions on electoral matters. The administration is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register on the federal roll and remains stalled in the Senate, and has sued twenty-nine states to obtain copies of their voter registries, which include dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and portions of social security numbers. Courts have blocked access in three states and have yet to rule in the rest.

World.title: Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools
World.content:
Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released

Argentine President Javier Milei announced an agreement between the National Communications Agency (Enacom) and Starlink to provide satellite connectivity to 6,000 rural schools that currently have poor internet access or no connection at all. The announcement was made on Sunday during the main event of the 138th International Livestock, Agriculture and Industry Exhibition in Buenos Aires.

According to the president, Elon Musk's company will donate 6,000 complete satellite kits along with 24 months of its highest-capacity service, which includes priority access of up to five terabytes per month per site. “Yes, it's a huge amount. Thank you, Elon,” he said during the speech.

Once that period ends, the equipment will remain at the schools and the regulator will take on the cost of the service for an additional year, covering the subscription, installation, technical support, and monitoring. Enacom sources said those resources will come from the Universal Service Fund, made up of contributions from the telecommunications sector and earmarked for extending access to areas not covered by commercial provision.

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released. The president also said the initiative adds to the three million users who, he said, already use the company's services in the country.

Starlink accelerated its expansion in Argentina following the easing of the regulatory framework for satellite services introduced by the current government, and now operates across the entire territory. The Argentine market accounts for about 25% of the company's Latin American operation and ranks among the countries with the highest service penetration, with weekly user growth of around 2%. Most customers are households, a concentration that has led to episodes of saturation in certain areas, such as greater Buenos Aires, Córdoba, and the Vaca Muerta region.

The agreement fits into the relationship Milei has maintained with Musk since the start of his term. The two met in February 2025 in the United States and have kept in frequent contact since. In parallel, Tesla is advancing its commercial entry into the local market, after formally incorporating in the country and appointing its first manager for Argentina and Uruguay.

In the same speech, the president projected an expansion of agricultural output and said the country is in a position to double its grain harvest, though he announced no decisions on export duties, one of the sector's main demands.

World.title: Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring
World.content:
Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:00 UTC Full article

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said

Uruguay's government is drawing up a set of contingency protocols for the flooding risk associated with the El Niño phenomenon, which climate projections indicate will have its greatest impact on the region during the southern hemisphere spring. President Yamandú Orsi announced at the Congress of Departmental Governors that the measures will be presented in August, ahead of what may occur from September and October.

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said. He indicated that the protocols drawn up by the departmental emergency coordination centers will be put on the table and that a coordination space will be created with the National Emergency System. “We have a record, going back to 1998, of how floods play out and we know where they will hit hardest and where less. It will not affect every area in the same way,” he added.

The available projections are probabilistic. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the probability of El Niño conditions during the June-July-August quarter at close to 100%, persisting at least through the end of the year. Uruguay's Meteorological Institute does not forecast specific flooding, but projects a higher probability of above-normal rainfall in the country's northeast, with that signal expanding toward the north and part of the center during the spring. Brazilian consultancy MetSul estimates a probability above 80% that accumulated rainfall will substantially exceed historical averages in southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina, and across Uruguay, placing the period of greatest risk between September and December.

A central concern is the effect of rainfall in southern Brazil on the flow of the Uruguay River, which runs along the country's western edge. Rio Grande do Sul has already recorded flooding episodes this month. National Party senator Sebastián Da Silva said management of the binational Salto Grande dam will be decisive and warned about the situation of the Río Negro dams, while identifying the Merín Lagoon basin, the Estero de Pelotas, and the Treinta y Tres lowlands as sensitive areas. He called for machinery and shelter space for potential evacuees to be arranged in advance.

Meteorologist José Serra said the movement of moisture from the equator toward southeastern Brazil and Uruguay has already begun to affect dams in the country's north, and put forward, as his own hypothesis, that a convergence between El Niño and a cooling of North Atlantic waters could amplify the phenomenon's effects.

The region is already going through a season of extreme events. Last week, Chile declared a state of catastrophe in the north of the country over a storm that left at least ten dead.

World.title: De la Espriella to close Colombian embassies in 14 countries and cut ties with Cuba and Nicaragua
World.content:
De la Espriella to close Colombian embassies in 14 countries and cut ties with Cuba and Nicaragua

27th Monday, July 2026 - 20:14 UTC Full article

The announcement draws a distinction between two situations. With Havana and Managua, the president-elect said there would be “no link whatsoever”

Colombia's president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced that his government will close the country's embassies in fourteen nations and will not maintain relations with Cuba and Nicaragua, which he described as “tyrannies.” The measure, released on Sunday night in a video on his social media accounts, will take effect from his inauguration on August 7.

The announcement draws a distinction between two situations. With Havana and Managua, the president-elect said there would be “no link whatsoever.” For the remaining twelve cases he cited budgetary reasons and made clear that the decisions “do not mean breaking diplomatic relations”: those countries will instead be covered through concurrent representation from other embassies in the region. “We cannot maintain such a costly structure, which produces no concrete results for the country,” he said.

The move reverses much of the diplomatic expansion pursued by the outgoing government of Gustavo Petro, which had opened missions in Africa, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe to diversify foreign policy. Colombia will close the missions inaugurated under that administration in Senegal, Ethiopia, Haiti, Barbados, the Czech Republic, and Romania, along with pre-existing ones in Algeria, Azerbaijan, Cuba, Ghana, Hungary, Malaysia, Nicaragua, and South Africa. On the African continent only the delegations in Kenya, Egypt, and Morocco will remain.

The shift regarding Cuba and Nicaragua carries significant history. The island acted as a guarantor of the negotiations between Juan Manuel Santos's government and the FARC that culminated in the 2016 peace agreement. With Nicaragua, Colombia maintains a decades-long dispute over the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago and fishing rights in surrounding waters, largely settled before the International Court of Justice.

The plan also includes merging the dual representations in Paris and Rome, where a single ambassador will take on duties before both the host country and the international bodies based there, the closure of fifteen consulates, and the cancellation of the planned mission in Ramallah, announced by Petro in 2023 but never established. Conversely, the incoming government will reopen the embassy in Israel, with which the outgoing administration severed relations.

The decision drew opposing reactions. Former trade minister Luis Carlos Reyes, a columnist for the Spanish newspaper EL PAÍS, argued the savings will be marginal, since total spending on foreign affairs accounts for 0.35% of the national budget. Governing-party senator Johana Osorio warned about the impact on ties with the global south. Former foreign minister Julio Londoño, by contrast, defended the measure, saying that “the proliferation of embassies and consulates has lent itself to paying political favors,” while acknowledging it is not decisive in budgetary terms.

The announcement adds to other foreign policy decisions by the incoming administration, which confirmed its intention to join the regional security alliance promoted by the United States.

World.title: IMF chief says Argentina is in "a strong position" despite missing its fiscal target
World.content:
IMF chief says Argentina is in “a strong position” despite missing its fiscal target

27th Monday, July 2026 - 19:59 UTC Full article

It is Georgieva's first visit to the country since taking over the institution in 2019 and the first by a top IMF official to Buenos Aires in eight years

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Monday endorsed the economic program of Javier Milei's government during a visit to Buenos Aires and ruled out that the country will need additional financing from the institution next year, when presidential elections are due. “Argentina today is in a strong position,” she said at a press conference alongside Economy Minister Luis Caputo.

It is Georgieva's first visit to the country since taking over the institution in 2019 and the first by a top IMF official to Buenos Aires in eight years. Her agenda included meetings with Caputo, central bank president Santiago Bausili, and a meeting with Milei at the presidential palace.

Among the indicators she said reflect an improvement, Georgieva cited the shift from a fiscal deficit to a primary surplus, inflation falling from 210% annually to around 30%, and the accumulation of some $13 billion in reserves since the start of the year. “I am not worried about Argentina having the money to pay its debt. Keep buying,” she said, referring to the central bank's currency purchases. Asked about the possibility of additional funds to navigate the election year, she replied: “There will be no need for extra financing.”

The endorsement comes, however, at a difficult moment on the fiscal front, the program's central pillar. Falling tax revenue during the first half of the year led in June to the first primary deficit of the current administration and to a breach of the fiscal target agreed with the institution for that period. While reserve accumulation targets have ceased to be a source of tension, the Fund's concerns have shifted toward the public accounts.

Georgieva placed at the center of the discussion the need for growth, currently concentrated in oil, gas, mining, and agriculture, to be “shared more widely.” Sectors tied to domestic consumption, such as construction, industry, and commerce, are in a weaker position. A recent central bank report shows household loan arrears tripled in a year, to 12.8%, their highest level in two decades. She spoke of the need to improve credit conditions for small businesses and families, manage those arrears, and accelerate infrastructure investment.

Argentina is the IMF's largest debtor: it accounts for about 35% of the institution's outstanding loan portfolio, with some $58 billion pending, far ahead of Ukraine, second with $15.4 billion. The current relationship dates back to the agreement signed in 2018 under Mauricio Macri's government, refinanced in 2022, to which a new $20 billion understanding was added in April 2025, the 23rd program between the country and the Fund. According to the financial program presented this month, Argentina faces maturities of nearly $45 billion between this year and next.

Small left-wing parties called a protest against the visit. On Tuesday, the delegation is scheduled to travel to Neuquén to tour the Loma Campana field in the Vaca Muerta formation, before continuing on to Uruguay.

World.title: Mercosur's two largest partners in their worst diplomatic crisis as Brazil recalls its envoy
World.content:
Mercosur's two largest partners in their worst diplomatic crisis as Brazil recalls its envoy

27th Monday, July 2026 - 09:14 UTC Full article

Milei defended his government's alignment with the United States and Israel and again criticized Brazil's judiciary for barring him from visiting Jair Bolsonaro

Brazil on Sunday recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, for consultations and summoned Argentina's ambassador in Brasília, Daniel Raimondi, to provide explanations at the Foreign Ministry, in the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years. The measures, taken by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, follow the speech Argentine President Javier Milei delivered on Saturday in São Paulo at the convention that formalized Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy.

A spokesperson for the Brazilian foreign ministry said the ambassador was recalled “over President Milei's insults” at that event, where he referred to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva using terms such as “thief” and “convict” and disparaged a Supreme Federal Court justice. Bitelli was expected to arrive in Brasília between Sunday night and early Monday. A recall for consultations is a formal signal of displeasure through which a government temporarily brings its representative home.

Hours after the measure became known, Milei broadened his accusations in a radio interview from the Palermo Rural Exhibition. There he accused the Brazilian government of having financed part of what he called an “anti-Argentine campaign”: “Do you know who put the most money into this anti-Argentine campaign? The government of Brazil. Twenty-five percent of the resources came from the government of Brazil,” he said. He extended the accusation to Mexico and to the US Democratic Party. He offered no evidence and did not specify which campaign he meant, and the claim is not supported by any known public documentation.

In the same interview, Milei defended his government's alignment with the United States and Israel and again criticized Brazil's judiciary for barring him from visiting Jair Bolsonaro, sentenced to more than 27 years for the attempted coup and currently under house arrest. The Supreme Federal Court had prohibited visits for political or electoral purposes until the end of the electoral process.

The episode also drew reactions within Argentina. Buenos Aires province governor Axel Kicillof said the country “respects sister nations and is committed to regional integration.” Argentina's foreign ministry had not issued an official response as of this writing.

The crisis involves Mercosur's two largest members, which are also each other's main trading partners. Milei's visit, his third to Brazil since taking office, included no contact with the federal government. There is a precedent from July 2024, when Bitelli was also summoned to Brasília after an exchange between the two presidents, though of lesser intensity.

World.title: De la Espriella to make Medellín Colombia's hub for the Trump-backed anti-drug alliance
World.content:
De la Espriella to make Medellín Colombia's hub for the Trump-backed anti-drug alliance

27th Monday, July 2026 - 08:44 UTC Full article

“We are going to have the main headquarters of the Shield of the Americas, the agreement we will sign with the United States in the fight against crime and drug trafficking,” the president-elect said

Colombia's president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, confirmed that Medellín will host the Colombian headquarters of the Shield of the Americas, the security alliance promoted by US President Donald Trump, and announced he will work part of the time from that city and from Barranquilla. The announcements came during a series of activities in the department of Antioquia, less than two weeks before he takes office on August 7.

“We are going to have the main headquarters of the Shield of the Americas, the agreement we will sign with the United States in the fight against crime and drug trafficking,” the president-elect said after a meeting of more than five hours with Governor Andrés Julián Rendón and the department's 125 mayors. He justified the choice by arguing that Medellín is where “the head of the serpent of drug trafficking and organized crime” lies and that much of the country's criminal structures is directed from its metropolitan area. He also signaled a hardline approach toward those organizations.

The decision marks a shift from the outgoing government's policy. The Shield of the Americas was launched by Trump on March 7 at a summit in Miami attended by right-wing Latin American leaders, among them Argentina's Javier Milei, El Salvador's Nayib Bukele, and Ecuador's Daniel Noboa. Colombia was not invited, amid deteriorating relations between Gustavo Petro's administration and Washington. The alliance, which envisages intelligence sharing and coordinated operations against drug trafficking, currently brings together 16 countries; Mexico and Brazil are not members. Vice-President-elect José Manuel Restrepo has already expressed in Washington an interest in joining, “with absolute respect for national sovereignty.”

Separately, De la Espriella announced he will move the headquarters of ProColombia, the agency that promotes non-mining exports, tourism, and foreign investment, to Medellín. “Colombia will no longer be governed exclusively from Bogotá. The country's future will be built from its regions,” he said on Friday at an event with the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean in Medellín, where a $9 billion investment in the country over the next four years was announced.

His cabinet will include at least three ministers from Antioquia: former senator Paola Holguín in Culture, Juliana Gutiérrez in Sport, and María Nohemí Arboleda in Mines and Energy. Antioquia was decisive in his runoff victory over Iván Cepeda: he took 2,185,834 votes there, about 65% of the total, and won in 108 of the 125 municipalities.

World.title: Cristina Kirchner expands her international legal team to take the Vialidad case abroad
World.content:
Cristina Kirchner expands her international legal team to take the Vialidad case abroad

26th Sunday, July 2026 - 23:16 UTC Full article

The legal team is weighing two possible routes

Former Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner has added Brazilian jurist Rafael Valim to the team preparing a filing before international bodies to challenge her conviction in the Vialidad case, according to sources close to her cited by the Argentine press. Those sources did not specify when he will begin working or what the first procedural steps will be, and the information has not been officially confirmed by her defense.

Valim is a lawyer and professor of public law with more than two decades of experience in constitutional and administrative law and human rights. A doctor and master of law from the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo, he has litigated before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court in cases involving the separation of powers and due process, and has taken part in proceedings before United Nations human rights mechanisms and the inter-American and European systems. He has written on the concept of lawfare, one of the pillars of the argument advanced by Kirchner's political movement since the conviction became final.

According to the same reports, Valim will work alongside Spanish jurist Javier Borrego, a former judge of the European Court of Human Rights and former justice of the Third Chamber of Spain's Supreme Court, who was already part of the international team advising the former president.

Fernández de Kirchner was sentenced to six years in prison and permanent disqualification from public office for fraudulent administration in the awarding of road public works contracts in Santa Cruz province. The sentence became final after being upheld by the higher instances of Argentina's judiciary. Her defense maintains that the proceedings were marked by political persecution and violations of due process, a position Argentine courts rejected throughout the case.

The legal team is weighing two possible routes. The inter-American system requires submitting the case first to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and, if admitted, it may later reach the Inter-American Court. The other alternative is the United Nations human rights protection mechanisms. Those close to the former president have not confirmed which route will be chosen.

Neither body can annul a conviction handed down by national courts. If a petition is admitted and responsibility is found, they may declare the state internationally responsible and order reparation measures, whose implementation falls to the country.

The legal effort is complemented by a political committee set up last year to publicize abroad the movement's position on the case, made up of party figures, former officials, and human rights advocates.

World.title: In canceling La Parota dam, Sheinbaum details a different water plan for rural Acapulco
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Sunday the cancellation of the La Parota hydroelectric dam to instead double down on an alternative plan featuring radial wells, rehabilitated pumping systems and elevated tanks to supply water to the Acapulco area.

“Yesterday I informed the entire rural area of ​​Acapulco that we are no longer going to do [the dam project] because it would have greatly affected the communities,” Sheinbaum said.

The Federal Electricity Commission’s (FCE) proposed 900-megawatt La Parota dam was expected to flood between 14,000 and 17,000 hectares of land, impacting the municipalities of Acapulco, Juan R. Escudero, San Marcos, Chilpancingo and Tecoanapa. However, concerns over the land expropriation process and a lack of agreements with local communities drove Sheinbaum to cancel the project.

Sheinbaum’s water strategy for Acapulco includes three radial wells along the Papagayo River, the rehabilitation of aqueducts, the repair of the pumping system, the construction of elevated tanks and the replacement of leaking water lines.

The works were initially included in the January 2025 federal program “Acapulco Transforms with You,” established in response to the damage caused by Hurricanes Otis and John.

The radial wells are being built on tall towers — high enough to keep them safe from flood waters — and will draw from the Papagayo River through underground collection systems.

In addition, Sheinbaum said, the government will replace drinking water lines in the upper part of Acapulco, starting in the neighborhood of Renacimiento.

Cleanup work is now underway in the Papagayo River, and dredging is taking place to remove sediment and increase the capacity of the riverbeds.

The aim is to reduce obstructions and reduce the flood risk during heavy rainfall as part of Acapulco’s reconstruction and adaptation efforts following the two severe hurricanes.

Residents of towns bordering the river have voiced their concern that the water works will directly serve beachfront Acapulco, instead of increasing their supply.

With reports from El Imparcial, Expansión Política and Infobae

World.title: Formal and informal employment slumped during the first half of 2026
World.content:
Participation in the workforce declined by nearly 300,000 during the first half of 2026 as June employment figures were the second-worst of the year, according to the National Survey of Occupation and Employment (ENOE) carried out by the national statistics agency INEGI.

ENOE data indicates that 319,633 jobs were lost last month and said the decline was linked to a contraction in both formal and informal employment, although more pronounced in the latter.

The negative June figures — topped only by the loss of 705,427 jobs in January — resulted in a deficit of 293,227 jobs through the first half of the year. Economists say Mexico needs to create 1.2 million jobs annually just to keep pace with labor force growth.

The June report is particularly disappointing as there were high expectations for the economy since Mexico was co-hosting the FIFA World Cup.

“Employment figures show the labor market remained weak, despite … the World Cup, which failed to boost job creation, even temporarily,” the financial group Banco Base stated in an analysis. “The event’s effect was marginal and likely concentrated only in the host cities.”

ENOE said Mexico’s unemployment rate stands at 2.9%, its highest figure since September 2025. At the same time, the economically inactive population (EIP) increased by 285,856 people in June compared to May.

Banco Base interpreted the rise in the EIP as an indicator that “some of those who stopped working stopped looking for employment,” suggesting that “the unemployment rate alone does not reflect the magnitude of the deterioration in the labor market.”

The official employment rate for the population aged 15 and over registered at 58.8%, according to seasonally adjusted figures. This represents declines for both month-to-month (–0.2%) and year-on-year (–1.0%).

The economic think tank México ¿cómo vamos? Identified another significant structural challenge: low female participation. In June 2026, the labor force participation gap between men and women stood at approximately 28.3%.

With reports from El Economista and México ¿cómo vamos?

World.title: Sheinbaum denies Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ claim: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇦🇷🇲🇽 Sheinbaum denies Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ claim : Responding to weekend remarks by Argentine President Javier Milei accusing Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party of financing a campaign against his government, Sheinbaum was blunt: “There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world.”

: Responding to weekend remarks by Argentine President Javier Milei accusing Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party of financing a campaign against his government, Sheinbaum was blunt: “There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world.” 🎖️ Militarized schools ‘not authorized,’ says Education Ministry (SEP) : Amid fallout from the case of a student’s death at a so-called “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools fall outside SEP and Defensa jurisdiction and that military-style education in schools is incompatible with Mexico’s constitutional education principles.

: Amid fallout from the case of a student’s death at a so-called “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools fall outside SEP and Defensa jurisdiction and that military-style education in schools is incompatible with Mexico’s constitutional education principles. ⚠️ Zacatecas cartel threat video ‘isn’t real,’ Sheinbaum says : Asked about a video in which armed men claiming to be part of a Sinaloa Cartel faction threatened Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, the president said the Security Cabinet determined the same day it surfaced that the audio had been dubbed.

: Asked about a video in which armed men claiming to be part of a Sinaloa Cartel faction threatened Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, the president said the Security Cabinet determined the same day it surfaced that the audio had been dubbed. 🌎 Self-determination principle invoked again: Sheinbaum tied her response to Milei to Mexico’s long-standing approach to foreign policy, saying Mexico asks other nations for the same respect for internal affairs that it offers them.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum took the opportunity during her Monday morning press conference to share advances of her administration’s investigation into the impact of social media and artificial intelligence on Mexico’s young people.

Education Minister Mario Delgado brought in two experts — Lucía Magis Weinberg and Tania Jiménez García — to present findings on how excessive screen time and social media use affect young people’s cognitive and emotional development.

“We are compiling this information so that it is available to parents,” Sheinbaum said.

“And so that, together, we make a series of decisions to protect children and adolescents during this formative stage of their lives,” the president said, before connecting the issue to the development of the country at large.

Sheinbaum also shared results of a recent survey indicating that 71% of parents consider it necessary that the government regulate minors’ cell phone use in schools.

Other issues at today’s mañanera touched on headlines from Zacatecas to Argentina.

On the international front, reporters pressed Sheinbaum on Milei’s accusation that Mexico had helped fund a campaign against Argentina during the 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup.

Milei’s accusation didn’t come out of nowhere. The president of Argentina has leaned on similar claims before: in May, a leaked call between him and pardoned former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández surfaced, in which Milei was said to have put up $350,000 for a media operation to spread information against leftist governments in Mexico, Colombia and Brazil — an episode that became known as “Hondurasgate.”

Sheinbaum was also asked on Monday about a video threatening Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, which she dismissed as fake.

That video surfaced in the wake of a real and still-unsolved multihomicide. Ten people — among them businesspeople and former officials — were found killed in several Zacatecas municipalities earlier this month, with five bodies located along the Zacatecas-Saltillo highway. State and federal authorities are still investigating who was responsible, with one line of inquiry examining whether some of the victims had ties to extortion by organized crime.

Sheinbaum rejects Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ accusation

A reporter asked Sheinbaum to respond to remarks made Sunday by Argentine President Javier Milei, who told the Buenos Aires-based Radio Mitre that Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party had bankrolled a “campaña antiargentina” — an anti-Argentina campaign — aimed at undermining his government ahead of elections.

Milei’s comments came hours after Brazil recalled its ambassador from Buenos Aires over separate remarks in which he called Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a “presidiario” (convict) and a “ladrón” (thief). Milei alleged Brazil had funded 25% of the supposed campaign and labeled Mexican and U.S. Democratic officials “progressive heads” seeking to derail his economic agenda.

Javier Milei acusó a México y Brasil de financiar una presunta “campaña antiargentina” para desacreditar a su administración Esto previo a las elecciones presidenciales en Argentina 📹 Radio Mitre pic.twitter.com/2l5jYD1zti — Manuel Lopez San Martin (@MLopezSanMartin) July 26, 2026

“There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world,” Sheinbaum said, adding that if anything, “here there is a campaign” against Mexico’s own government, from multiple fronts.

She stressed that Mexico “doesn’t tend to get involved with other countries” and tied her response to Mexico’s constitutional principle of self-determination, a doctrine she has repeatedly invoked this year in response to frictions in foreign relations.

Education Ministry: Military-style schooling ‘not authorized’

Monday’s mañanera also addressed fallout from the case of Dafne Quintos, a student whose recent death has been linked to a “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas. Quintos, 13, reportedly died on July 17 at Academia Militarizada “Doenitz” where she was taking a summer course. According to her mother, Alejandra Quintos, the crime is being investigated as a femicide with drowning as the cause of death.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reiterated a position his ministry first stated Friday: schools branded as “militarized” fall under neither the Education Ministry (SEP) nor the Defense Ministry (Defensa), and delivering military-style instruction in educational institutions is “incompatible with the constitutional aims, principles and objectives” governing Mexican education.

Delgado said Tamaulipas authorities have since identified five additional schools operating under the same model. He said he remains in contact with the Tamaulipas state government and has tried to reach Quintos’s mother directly.

Sheinbaum debunks video threatening Zacatecas governor

A roughly two-minute video circulating on social media shows nine masked, armed men posing behind a tenth who reads out a message on camera claiming responsibility for the killing of 10 men in Zacatecas earlier this month on behalf of a Sinaloa Cartel faction.

The spokesperson asserts — without evidence — that the murders were carried out at the state government’s request. The same message then turns to a direct threat against Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, warning him to “honor and respect the agreements his cabinet has with our organization” or face consequences that would extend to his family.

Asked about the clip, Sheinbaum said the recording is not authentic. She said the federal Security Cabinet informed her the same day the video surfaced that it contained technical inconsistencies, chiefly that the voice track doesn’t match the person shown speaking.

“It’s not a real video — the voice doesn’t even match what the person is saying,” she said, adding that the case is still being investigated.

She said federal authorities are working to determine who produced the video, who distributed it and what the purpose of publishing it was, and that any evidence linking public officials to organized crime would be investigated under the law regardless of the outcome.

Monreal has not commented directly on the video but said separately that Zacatecas maintains permanent security operations involving the army, the National Guard and state police. Last week, state authorities announced the arrest of five people in connection with the homicides.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Hurricane Genevieve gathers strength offshore, casting stormclouds over most of Mexico
World.content:
Hurricane Genevieve briefly reached Category 5 in the early hours of Monday, becoming the first cyclone of this magnitude recorded in the eastern Pacific since Hurricane Kristy in 2024, the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) reported.

As of 9 a.m. CST on Monday, the NHC said Genevieve was located approximately 855 kilometers south-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California Sur, with maximum sustained winds of 250 kilometers per hour and wind gusts up to 305 kilometers per hour.

The system was moving northwest at 20 kilometers per hour on a track that kept it offshore and parallel to the Mexican coast, and is expected to maintain a west-northwest to northwest track over the next two days, gradually slowing its speed.

Despite the hurricane’s strength, forecasters have ruled out any direct impact on Mexican territory, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

However, the generated swells are already affecting Mexico’s southwest coast and are expected to reach southern Baja California, with the risk of potentially dangerous rip currents.

Rainfall forecast for most states

According to the National Meteorological Service (SMN), cloud bands from Genevieve in the Pacific Ocean will increase the likelihood of heavy to very heavy rains in western Mexico, coinciding with the Mexican monsoon in the northwest and Tropical Wave Number 21 in the south, which will intensify the storms.

The SMN said very heavy rains are expected on Monday in at least 17 states, with particular intensity in Sonora, Oaxaca and Chiapas.

Here’s the rain forecast for Monday afternoon:

Very heavy rain with isolated intense downpours (75 to 150 millimeters): parts of Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco.

Heavy rain with isolated and very heavy downpours (50 to 75 millimeters): parts of Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango, Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Puebla.

Showers with isolated heavy downpours (25 to 50 millimeters): parts of Hidalgo, México state, Mexico City, Tlaxcala, Morelos, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

Periods of showers (5 to 25 millimeters): parts of Baja California, Baja California Sur, Tamaulipas, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato and Querétaro.

Isolated rain (0.1 to 5 millimeters): parts of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Aguascalientes.

With reports from Radio Fórmula and the Associated Press

World.title: 2 separate freight derailments prompt emergency responses
World.content:
In two separate incidents on Saturday night, a tank car on a freight train derailed, prompting the mobilization of emergency services while specialized personnel carried out containment efforts.

Authorities declared a Code Red in the northern state of Tamaulipas, Mexico, after a Pemex-owned tank car carrying 70,000 liters of gasoline tipped over when a freight train derailed.

The incident, which occurred in the Kansas City Southern rail yard in Ciudad Madero, triggered hazardous materials response protocols.

Municipal, state and federal authorities cordoned off the perimeter and established a command post. Specialized personnel quickly evaluated the scene to consider the possibility of leaks, fire hazards and explosion risks.

The situation was fraught with danger as the Ferrocarrilera Talleres neighborhood — the site of the accident — is one of the most sensitive railway and industrial corridors in southern Tamaulipas. Its proximity to logistics infrastructure linked to Petróleos Mexicanos — including the Madero Refinery — prompted authorities to consider an evacuation, though it was deemed not necessary.

Local officials urged the public to avoid the area while the authorities continued trying to secure the tanker truck, citing the risk posed by any maneuver involving a vehicle loaded with fuel. Authorities — along with Pemex personnel — were preparing to transfer the fuel to a different tank car on Monday.

As of Sunday night, authorities had not reported any injuries or fuel spills.

Evacuarán a más de 200 personas en Ciudad Madero por retiro de carrotanque con gasolina descarriladohttps://t.co/HiyEL5wEg4 pic.twitter.com/HJXrx1dTuh — Milenio Tamaulipas (@MilenioTam) July 27, 2026

In the second incident, a freight train derailed in the municipality of Naco, Sonora, approximately 20 miles south of the U.S. border.

The derailment occurred just outside the town of Ejido Cuauhtémoc on the railway tracks used by Ferromex, a private rail transport company that operates the largest freight railway network in Mexico.

According to official information from the Sonora civil protection agency, one of the tank cars overturned during the derailment, causing the spillage of a chemical substance.

Although neither the type of chemical involved nor the volume of the spilled material was specified, specialists were inspecting the site to define remediation measures and rule out additional risks.

Emergency personnel were carrying out assessment, monitoring and control work to determine the extent of the spill and reduce any risk to the environment and ensure public safety.

The area remains under precautionary protection while technical operations continue to determine the cause of the accident, to recover the spilled chemical and to ensure safe conditions before resuming rail operations.

The incident occurred less than two weeks before the 12th anniversary of one of the biggest environmental disasters in Mexico’s history. On Aug. 7, 2014, a chemical spill despoiled the Sonora River, affecting more than 22,000 inhabitants across eight municipalities.

With reports from La Jornada, Hoy Tamaulipas, Nación 321 and El Sol de Tampico

World.title: MND Local: Dengue cases drop in Jalisco and Mexico’s first openly gay mayor is killed while visiting Guadalajara
World.content:
This week in Guadalajara, there is good news on seasonal dengue cases, while global challenges are taking a toll on Canadian airline WestJet. Finally, we look at the life and death of Mexico’s first openly gay mayor.

Dengue cases down 90% in Jalisco this year

Dengue cases in Jalisco are down sharply from a year ago, with only 90 reported year to date compared with 917 during the same period last year. Of the confirmed infections this year, seven were classified as severe (hemorrhagic) dengue, 51 were nonsevere cases, and the remaining 32 were classified as cases with warning signs.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Salud Jalisco (@sec.saludjalisco)

The drop in dengue cases in 2026 reflects a concerted public effort to eliminate breeding sites, fog high-risk areas before the rainy season, encourage residents to prevent standing water around their homes through a public health campaign and expand monitoring across the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area to track mosquito density and the presence of the virus.

That said, eight deaths are under investigation statewide, with dengue infections suspected as the cause. According to Jalisco Health Secretary Héctor Raúl Pérez Gómez, the highest risk is concentrated in coastal and tropical forest areas, specifically Cocula, Teuchitlán, Atengo and Chiquilistlán, where most cases this year have been identified.

Gómez also reported that ovitraps — used to detect the presence of the dengue virus — tested negative in areas that drew large crowds during the recently concluded World Cup events, including around Estadio Akron and fan fest sites across the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area. This suggests there is likely no active dengue virus in those locations, despite the presence of mosquitoes.

He added that there are currently no reported cases in Jalisco of two other mosquito-borne diseases — Zika or chikungunya — despite recent outbreaks of chikungunya in Costa Rica and Nicaragua.

Jalisco’s rainy season runs through late October, and infection risk typically rises from late July through September, when dengue cases historically peak.

WestJet suspends nonstop flights between Guadalajara and Calgary

Canadians heading to Mexico this winter will have fewer routes to choose from. WestJet, Canada’s second-largest carrier, is suspending its Calgary-Guadalajara route from Oct. 19, 2026, through April 24, 2027.

The changes come a week after WestJet confirmed 20 route suspensions to the United States amid fare increases driven by rising fuel costs tied to the ongoing war in Iran and weakening demand. Demand-side pressures have also been linked to a widespread avoidance of U.S. travel by Canadians in response to President Donald Trump’s posture toward Canada during his second term.

“These route updates better align capacity with demand while maintaining operational reliability,” the airline said in an online statement.

In addition to service cuts, WestJet is dealing with a labor dispute involving about 4,400 unionized flight attendants, who recently voted to strike after 10 months of unsuccessful contract negotiations.

The flight attendants have been without a contract since the previous agreement expired Dec. 31, 2025.

Mexico’s first openly gay mayor shot and killed in Guadalajara

Benjamín Medrano Quezada, Mexico’s first openly gay mayor, was shot and killed July 7 while leaving an ice cream shop in the Santa Elena de la Cruz neighborhood on Guadalajara’s north side.

The 59-year-old served as mayor of Fresnillo, Zacatecas, from 2013 to 2015 and later as a federal deputy in Mexico’s Chamber of Deputies, representing Zacatecas’ 1st District.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gay Times (@gaytimes)

The assailant shot Medrano Quezada multiple times in the face before fleeing on a motorcycle. Another report suggested there may have been two attackers. Authorities have not announced suspects or a motive.

“We express our deepest condolences to his family and friends, and we accompany them in this moment of grief, wishing them strength in the face of this irreparable loss,” the Fresnillo City Council said in a statement.

In addition to his political career, Medrano Quezada was a singer and owned a gay bar in Fresnillo. In 2022, he was accused of embezzling public funds while serving as president of the board of trustees for the National Fair of Zacatecas in 2019. A complaint filed by the Zacatecas State Public Administration Secretariat alleged he embezzled more than 60 million pesos (about US $3.4 million). Medrano Quezada later missed a mandatory hearing, prompting authorities to issue an arrest warrant.

The Zacatecas attorney general told U.S.-based outlet MundoNow that a judge overturned the warrant in 2025, meaning Medrano Quezada was not a fugitive at the time of his death.

Despite being openly gay, Medrano Quezada held conservative views and opposed same-sex marriage and adoption. In 2013, he said: “Our idiosyncrasies do not allow it. Not because we lack the capacity to do it, but we cannot go against doctrines and customs.”

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Discovering Mexico: San Luis Potosí
World.content:
San Luis Potosí is for you if you like: Nature, colonial architecture, weird British artists.

San Luis Potosí is a state that challenges most assumptions about Mexico’s geography. From its UNESCO-listed capital, where more than 500 historic monuments line 42 streets, to the waterfalls and subtropical canyons of the Huasteca Potosina, it offers a spectrum of landscapes that still feel hidden from both domestic and international travelers. You can spend the morning on the Calzada de Guadalupe — one of the longest pedestrian avenues in the Americas — and the afternoon paddling upriver toward a 105-meter curtain of water, then return to the city for gorditas and an evening walk past Baroque façades and wide, tree-shaded plazas.

What makes San Luis Potosí compelling is not only its visual variety but the way nature, history and a touch of surrealism intersect. In the east, jungle rivers feed emerald pools and cascades at sites like Tamasopo and Puente de Diós, while deep in the Huasteca, a concrete labyrinth at Las Pozas turns a hillside into a walkable surrealist dreamscape. On high desert plateaus, the abandoned mining town of Real de Catorce and the sacred landscape of Wirikuta add pilgrimage routes, ghostly mining ruins and wide, open skies, underscoring that this is a territory with as much spiritual resonance as scenic appeal. Between one of Mexico’s largest urban parks, canyon rivers, cave-like water formations and mountains revered as a place of origin, San Luis Potosí invites visitors not just to see nature, but to engage with a state that deserves to be as recognized as an equal to legendary regions like Oaxaca and Guanajuato.

When talking about the state of San Luis Potosí, it makes sense to start with the capital. A UNESCO-listed historic center of 42 streets and roughly 500 monuments, it pairs colonial architecture with a laid-back urban rhythm that many travelers would never think to seek out here. Plaza by plaza, it reveals itself as a city of wide sidewalks, generous shade and everyday rituals, where grabbing a coffee and wandering past sandstone façades feels less like sightseeing and more like slipping into the local routine.

Beyond the downtown core, a network of former mining villages, vast public parks and quiet neighborhoods extends that sense of lived-in history into the surrounding hills. This is a place where 19th-century industrial heritage sits alongside contemporary art spaces and weekend family outings, giving visitors multiple entry points into the region’s past and present.

Farther afield, the waterfalls and canyons of the Huasteca Potosina introduce a very different version of the state, one defined by jungle rivers, steep ravines and small communities that have built a modest tourism economy around the area’s natural assets. Taken together, these landscapes — urban and rural, desert and subtropical — make San Luis Potosí a destination that rewards curiosity, inviting travelers to look past the usual hotspots and spend time with a corner of Mexico that still feels genuinely undiscovered.

Las Pozas, the Edward James Sculpture Garden outside Xilitla, is best approached with time and a willingness to walk slowly. Set in subtropical forest in the Huasteca Potosina, the site combines concrete structures, waterfalls and pools across several hectares dedicated to both sculpture and ecological conservation. Visitors follow paths and stairways that weave between towers, arches and platforms, with vegetation and water constantly in view, making the experience feel more like moving through a landscape than visiting a conventional monument.

For travelers, the practical side of a visit is straightforward but worth planning. Entry is limited and organized in timed groups with mandatory guides, so advance reservations and early arrivals are recommended, especially on weekends and holidays. The garden sits above Xilitla, a Pueblo Mágico with basic services, lodging and transport options, which makes it a natural base for exploring the area’s other attractions, including nearby waterfalls and viewpoints.

On the ground, the effect of Las Pozas is cumulative rather than centered on a single highlight. As visitors move between structures and natural features, the combination of sound, humidity, plant life and concrete begins to define the visit as much as any one staircase or tower. It is a place where art, landscape and local stewardship now intersect, offering a distinctive stop on a broader San Luis Potosí itinerary for travelers interested in both nature and the traces of one of surrealism’s more ambitious projects.

San Luis Potosí offers a range of hikes that can be tailored to different levels of experience, starting with the Tamasopo area in the Huasteca Potosina. Here, a network of waterfalls, pools and rivers creates a natural setting that functions almost like an outdoor water park, with jumping platforms, bridges and rope swings for those who want more activity, and flatter riverside paths at nearby Cascaditas for visitors who prefer a slower, less strenuous walk. Access involves a roughly three-hour drive from the capital, making it a full-day outing that combines time on the trail with swimming and time by the water.

In the high desert, Real de Catorce serves as the starting point for a more demanding hike to Cerro del Quemado, or Wirikuta, a site recognized as a UNESCO Natural Sacred Area and central to Wixárika cosmology. The route covers around 15 kilometers at altitude and can be done on foot or on horseback, with additional options to visit El Pueblo Fantasma, the ruins of a former silver mine at nearly 3,000 meters above sea level. This part of the state appeals to travelers interested in combining physical effort with an encounter with living Indigenous tradition and the remnants of the region’s mining history.

For those drawn to river travel, the journey upriver to the Tamul waterfall adds another dimension to hiking in San Luis Potosí. After an early start and a stop for breakfast in Río Verde, visitors board wooden boats and paddle against the current for about an hour to reach the base of the 105-meter-high falls, with opportunities to swim and take photos near the cascade and to walk up to La Cueva del Agua, a cave pool set above the river.

For travelers interested in the deeper timelines of a place, the Calera cave system in San Luis Potosí adds a striking layer to the state’s appeal. Known among specialists as the setting for the documentary “Crypt of the Megafauna,” the cave sits in the Sierra del Abra and has yielded fossils of mammoths, giant sloths, saber-toothed cats, dire wolves, camels, bison and other Ice Age animals, after a team led by cave biologist Luis Espinasa went in looking for cavefish and instead found a dense concentration of ancient bones. The work to document the site has involved tight vertical entrances, underwater sections and the use of a remotely operated vehicle nicknamed “Robo-Teddy,” underscoring that this is an active research environment rather than a conventional tourist stop.

While Calera itself is not open for casual visits, its story is accessible through the film and through the broader context of San Luis Potosí’s caves and karst landscapes. For travelers, this makes the region a natural fit for those who combine surface-level hiking and nature trips with an interest in what lies beneath, from cavefish and underground streams to paleontological work that is still ongoing. Local guides and caving clubs occasionally organize specialized trips in the wider Sierra del Abra for experienced participants, which can add a technical component to an itinerary that might otherwise focus on waterfalls and rivers in the Huasteca Potosina.

Even for visitors who never enter a cave, the Calera discoveries contribute to the way San Luis Potosí is understood. Knowing that the same state now known for mezcal routes, hiking to sacred mountains and boating to waterfalls also holds evidence of mammoths and five-ton ground sloths helps situate present-day landscapes within a longer natural history.

In San Luis Potosí’s capital, one of the most compelling stops for travelers interested in art and history is the Centro de las Artes de San Luis Potosí Centenario, housed in the state’s former main penitentiary. The late-19th-century neoclassical complex, once organized as a panopticon with cells radiating from a central tower, has been restored and repurposed as a cultural center, with courtyards, former cell blocks and corridors now serving as exhibition spaces, classrooms and performance areas. Walking through the main gates, visitors move from heavy stone walls into open-air patios and smaller galleries, where rotating contemporary art shows sit alongside traces of the building’s past use.

Within this larger complex, the Museo Leonora Carrington functions as a museum-within-a-museum devoted to one of Mexico’s key surrealist artists. Opened in 2018, it houses an extensive collection of Carrington’s sculptures, jewelry, engravings, drawings and personal objects, with several courtyards dedicated to large-scale works that visitors can view from multiple angles. Inside, former cells have been adapted to display smaller pieces and archival materials, allowing travelers to move between outdoor installations and more intimate rooms that highlight different periods of Carrington’s career.

A visit can be folded easily into a day spent in the historic center, as the complex sits within walking distance of other museums, churches and plazas. Depending on the timing, visitors may also encounter festivals and events such as the annual wine fair held in the courtyards, adding a contemporary social dimension to a space that once served a very different function.

San Luis Potosí, Where Nature Feels Like a Dream / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

By air:

San Luis Potosi International Airport: The airport offers flights to Mexico’s main metropolitan hubs, plus international links to Dallas-Forth Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Chicago.

Aguascalientes: A similar international selection, Houston, Dallas-Forth Worth, Chicago and Los Angeles, plus domestic destinations across Mexico. Located 168 km (104 miles).

Zacatecas: Though the airport is modest, it offers flights to Los Angeles, San Jose, Dallas and Chicago. Domestically, the airport links to Guadalajara, Mexico City and Tijuana.

By road:

San Miguel de Allende: 170 km (105 miles), roughly a 2 hour drive.

Mexico City: 411 km (255 miles), roughly a 4 and a half hour drive

Laredo, Texas: 727 km (452 miles), roughly an 8 hour drive.

Guadalajara: 344 km (213 miles), roughly a 4 hour drive.

World.title: Russia-Africa Information Warfare Exposed in Angola Spy Trial
World.content:
Africa · Southern

Key Facts —Verdict. Igor Ratchin and Lev Lakshtanov were convicted on 21 July 2026 in Luanda. —Sentences. Ratchin received 11 years; Lakshtanov received 8 years for terrorism and espionage. —Alleged network. Prosecutors linked the men to “Africa Politology,” a group with Wagner-era roots. —Payments. Over $24,000 was allegedly paid to local journalists to spread disinformation. —Target. The operation aimed to influence Angola’s 2027 presidential election and destabilise the state.

A Luanda court has convicted two Russian nationals for terrorism and espionage, pulling back the curtain on a new phase of Russia-Africa information warfare that targets elections, media, and strategic minerals.

Angola Spy Trial Exposes New Phase of Russia-Africa Information Warfare (Photo internet reproduction)

The Verdict in Luanda

On 21 July 2026, an Angolan court sentenced Igor Ratchin to 11 years in prison and Lev Lakshtanov to 8 years. The two Russian men faced 11 charges, including terrorism, espionage, and influence peddling.

They were arrested in August 2025 and their trial opened on 24 March 2026. Prosecutors alleged the pair paid local journalists and experts over $24,000 to spread propaganda designed to incite unrest.

The case marks one of the most explicit legal confrontations with alleged Russian information operations on the African continent. It signals that Angola is willing to draw a hard line against foreign interference.

The Alleged Network: Africa Politology

Prosecutors connected the defendants to a group called “Africa Politology.” Investigators describe it as a Russian influence network that emerged from the Wagner ecosystem after Yevgeny Prigozhin’s death in 2023.

Some reporting suggests the network was later absorbed into structures linked to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service. Those claims remain attributed to investigators and have not been independently verified by court documents.

What is clear is the method: low-cost payments to local intermediaries, online narratives, and an attempt to shape political conditions without overt military action. It is a playbook that mirrors Russia-Africa information warfare tactics seen elsewhere on the continent, as detailed in our pillar Africa: The New Scramble.

Angola’s Strategic Pivot

The trial unfolds against a backdrop of profound realignment. President João Lourenço, in power since 2017, has steered Angola closer to the United States and Western partners.

That shift reduces a decades-long dependency on Moscow’s orbit. French and German diplomatic sources frame the verdict as a message that Luanda will no longer tolerate the kind of influence operations it once quietly accepted.

The timing is sensitive. Angola’s next presidential election is scheduled for 2027, and any credible allegation of external interference immediately raises the political temperature in a competitive pre-election environment.

The Lobito Corridor and the Minerals Angle

Several reports connect the alleged influence operation to efforts to undermine the Lobito Corridor. This rail and logistics project links the copper and cobalt belts of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo to Angola’s Atlantic coast.

The corridor is a flagship American geoeconomic project in Africa. It is central to exporting minerals essential for the global energy transition, and Washington has invested significant political capital in its success.

If Moscow-linked actors wanted to slow Angola’s Western integration, disrupting confidence in such projects would be a logical target. Prosecutors’ claims in this area remain allegations, but the strategic logic is unmistakable.

A Transactional, Not Ideological, Play

Prosecutors reportedly said the defendants explored influencing both the ruling MPLA and the opposition UNITA. That suggests the aim was not ideological but transactional.

The goal appeared to be retaining access and leverage regardless of who wins the 2027 election. For a relatively small sum, the alleged operation sought high-value political and economic outcomes.

This pattern fits a broader Russian strategy in Africa. It combines security partnerships, disinformation, private military networks, and resource diplomacy to build influence while working around Western sanctions imposed after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

What Brazil and Latin America Should Watch

For readers in Brazil and across Latin America, the Angola case offers a preview of how great-power competition is evolving in the Global South. Information warfare is cheap, deniable, and easily exported.

Both regions sit on critical minerals, both face pre-election sensitivity, and both are arenas where Moscow, Washington, and Beijing compete for access. The Angola trial shows one government’s decision to criminalise the playbook rather than ignore it.

The BRICS dimension adds another layer. Angola is not a BRICS member, but its realignment away from Moscow complicates Russia’s narrative of a rising anti-Western bloc in the developing world.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who were the two Russians convicted in Angola?

Igor Ratchin and Lev Lakshtanov were convicted on 21 July 2026 in Luanda. They received sentences of 11 years and 8 years respectively for terrorism, espionage, and influence peddling. Prosecutors alleged they were part of a Russia-linked disinformation network called Africa Politology.

What is the Lobito Corridor and why does it matter in this case?

The Lobito Corridor is a rail and logistics project connecting the mineral-rich regions of Zambia and the DRC to Angola’s Atlantic coast. It is backed by the United States as a flagship geoeconomic initiative. Several reports allege the influence operation sought to undermine confidence in the corridor to slow Angola’s Western integration.

How does this trial fit into the wider Russia-Africa pattern?

The case reflects a broader Russian strategy that mixes security partnerships, disinformation, private military networks, and resource diplomacy. The alleged network, Africa Politology, is said to have emerged from the Wagner ecosystem after Prigozhin’s death. The trial shows one African government choosing to criminalise that playbook rather than accommodate it.

World.title: Fintechs LemFi and BVNK Use Stablecoin Rails to Cut Kenya Fees
World.content:
Africa · Eastern

Key Facts —The partnership. LemFi will route cross-border settlement through BVNK’s regulated stablecoin infrastructure, bypassing traditional correspondent banking networks. —The cost difference. Stablecoin-powered transfers can cost 2–3 percent, compared with roughly 6.5 percent for traditional money transfer operators on the Kenya corridor. —The Tether connection. The deal operationalises a strategy that began with Tether’s undisclosed investment in LemFi in May 2026, positioning USDT as a core settlement asset. —User experience. Customers never touch cryptocurrency. They send local currency in the LemFi app, and recipients receive Kenyan shillings via M-Pesa or bank accounts. —Regulatory caution. The stablecoin settlement will roll out market by market, only where local central bank and regulatory frameworks permit it.

LemFi and BVNK have partnered to shift diaspora remittance settlement onto stablecoin remittance rails, a move that promises to cut costs and settlement times for Kenya’s US$4 billion annual inflow while quietly extending the reach of dollar-linked digital infrastructure across Eastern Africa.

LemFi and BVNK partner to rebuild diaspora remittance rails with stablecoin settlement (Photo internet reproduction)

What the LemFi–BVNK deal actually does

LemFi, a UK-headquartered cross-border platform serving African and Asian diaspora customers, announced it is moving its settlement layer onto BVNK’s enterprise-grade stablecoin payments infrastructure. The change replaces multi-day correspondent banking chains with near-instant, lower-cost settlement.

On the front end, nothing changes for users. A customer in London or Houston funds the LemFi app in local currency, initiates a transfer to Kenya, and the recipient receives Kenyan shillings into an M-Pesa wallet or bank account.

Behind the scenes, however, the value is converted into a reserve-backed stablecoin, moved across blockchain networks that operate 24 hours a day, and cashed out into local currency via payout partners. The entire chain bypasses SWIFT and its intermediary banks.

The remittance economics that make stablecoin remittance rails compelling

The global average cost of sending remittances stood at 6.36 percent in the third quarter of 2025, more than double the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal target of 3 percent by 2030. Meeting that target would return roughly US$20 billion per year to recipient families worldwide.

Sub-Saharan Africa remains the most expensive remittance region globally, with average fees reaching 8.78 percent in 2025. For a Kenyan in Houston sending US$500 per month, traditional operators such as Western Union or MoneyGram charge about US$33 in fees, equivalent to 6.5 percent.

A stablecoin-powered route can bring the total cost down to US$10–15, or 2–3 percent. That translates to annual savings of US$216–276 for a single sender, a meaningful sum in a corridor where the Kenyan diaspora sends over US$4 billion home every year.

Kenya as the proving ground: M-Pesa meets new rails

Kenya is positioned as a key early corridor for the LemFi–BVNK rollout, and the reason is straightforward. The country’s mobile-money system, M-Pesa, provides a ready-made off-ramp for stablecoin-settled remittances, allowing funds to reach recipients instantly even if they lack a bank account.

Kenya’s Digital Economy Blueprint, which runs from 2019 to 2029, emphasises cross-border interoperability, pro-innovation regulation, and the reduction of remittance bottlenecks. Analysts note that stablecoin rails align with these policy goals, particularly for diaspora-funded sectors such as healthcare.

The broader pattern across Africa is clear. Stablecoins accounted for about 43 percent of total cryptocurrency transaction volume in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2024, functioning as practical payment infrastructure rather than speculative instruments. This is the landscape that Africa: The New Scramble tracks: a quiet contest over the pipes through which money, data, and influence flow.

Tether, dollar power, and the geopolitics of settlement

The LemFi–BVNK partnership cannot be separated from the strategic investment Tether made in LemFi in May 2026. That undisclosed investment was explicitly aimed at wiring USDT into LemFi’s African and Asian remittance corridors, and the BVNK deal now operationalises that strategy.

Tether controls a USDT float exceeding US$185 billion and reportedly earns roughly US$15 billion in annual profit. Chief Executive Paolo Ardoino has said the company is building a business ecosystem that can survive a future breakdown in legacy financial rails.

Because most major stablecoins are dollar-pegged, every transfer settled via USDT effectively moves value in dollars, even when the end recipient receives Kenyan shillings. Africa already records stablecoin flows equivalent to 6.7 percent of GDP, suggesting a significant layer of de facto dollar infrastructure running parallel to formal banking systems.

What this means for banks, regulators, and the diaspora economy

European and African banks still control SWIFT-based correspondent networks, but research now concludes that in most large African economies, stablecoins are already the cheaper, faster rail for diaspora transfers today. Where local regulators permit it, stablecoin-powered money transfer operators undercut bank wires by tens of dollars per transaction.

LemFi has stated clearly that its stablecoin settlement will only be deployed where local central bank and regulatory frameworks support it. This acknowledges that corridors such as Kenya are more receptive than jurisdictions with outright bans on cryptocurrency activity.

For African central banks, the rise of stablecoin remittance rails presents a tension. Cheaper, faster flows benefit households and small businesses, but they also shift FX exposure and capital-flow visibility onto non-bank, offshore infrastructure that central banks do not directly control.

The competitive field and what to watch next

LemFi is not alone. Other platforms such as NALA already use stablecoins for back-end settlement while keeping users in local currency. AfriVest markets itself as eliminating what it calls a US$48 billion annual remittance tax on Africa’s diaspora, using stablecoin rails and tokenised African assets.

LemFi’s differentiators include its deep diaspora focus on African and Asian remitters, its access to large-scale USDT liquidity through Tether, and its partnership with BVNK, a specialist in enterprise-grade stablecoin infrastructure rather than a retail crypto platform. The next milestone to watch is how quickly the rollout extends beyond Kenya into other Eastern African corridors, and whether local regulators in those markets follow Kenya’s relatively permissive stance.
