World.title: Polanski’s Greens brace for the ‘Burnham bounce’
World.content:
An opinion poll by More in Common published Monday put Labour on top for the first time since March 2025, with its surge coming at the expense of the Greens, who recorded their lowest share of the vote since October last year when Polanski became leader. A separate YouGov poll also released Monday showed no change from last week, though it noted the party is down eight points from a February peak.

Polanski insists he is the “opposite of worried about Andy Burnham,” predicting Labour MPs’ “last roll of the dice” in switching leader won’t improve things.

But a senior Green Party local politician, granted anonymity to speak frankly, acknowledged: “It’s going to be difficult, there is going to be a Burnham bounce,” warning the party needs to “sharpen those key lines that give us differentiation.”

The party is already attacking Burnham for employing corporate lobbyists like his chief of staff James Purnell, and claiming the new prime minister’s rhetoric on Gaza, public ownership and homelessness is hollow, and does not represent a change from Starmer.

It is also on a drive to find more polished spokespeople to hit the airwaves.

Drawing the battle lines

One area where the Greens see a dividing line with Burnham is over Gaza.

World.title: Spain’s biggest blaze risks scorching conservatives ahead of key election year
World.content:
At a national level, the PP is still topping the polls and is on track to take power in 2027, profiting from the web of corruption scandals ensnaring Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's ruling Socialist Party.

But the fires threaten to expose vulnerabilities. The conservatives are not only being criticized for failing to invest in firefighters, but also risk looking out of step with the severity of the challenge posed by climate change, in part thanks to regional alliances with the far-right Vox party that are steering the PP toward increasingly anti-ecological positions.

Madrid Regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso, a conservative heavyweight, has felt the sting of public anger over her political priorities. On Sunday, she said she'd come under fire from constituents accusing her of prioritizing investment in fighting bulls — a vote winner with a right-wing base — rather than firefighters.

Madrid Regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso (left) , Villamanta Mayor Mariano Nunez Munoz, Spain's King Felipe VI, Queen Letizia and Lt-Gen. Francisco Javier Marcos visit the evacuees from the Madrid wildfire in Villamanta on July 26, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images

"In two or three municipalities, they were talking about bullfighters," a palpably irritated Ayuso complained. “What do bullfighters have to do with all this?”

The populist Madrid president accused her political opponents of stirring up grievances to “divide” her constituents, adding that the bullfighting sector had been especially impacted by the wildfires. “We must remember that they are the first ones who have lost livestock and land,” she added.

But political opponents like Manuela Bergerot, spokesperson for the left-wing Más Madrid party, argued that once the fires are extinguished, it would be time to probe "the precarious situation of firefighters, cuts in prevention and climate change denial."

World.title: Political chaos turns spotlight on Romania’s MAGA champion
World.content:
The views of Simion, a former football hooligan who relishes a fight with the establishment, matter: His party, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), has a huge lead in opinion polls and may soon get a chance to put its case to voters if a snap election is called.

He savaged the EU’s green deal, economic and defense policies, and said Romania did not want to return to a time when larger states dominated it. “We have been occupied by these kind of dictators like we have in Russia and we had in U.S.S.R., and dictatorial tendencies from Germany,” he said. “We want to be part of Europe formed of free, sovereign nations.”

Romania has been locked in crisis without a fully functioning government since May, when AUR joined forces with the social democrats to bring down the country’s liberal-led ruling coalition.

Heir to Orbán

On the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Ukraine, Romania plays a critical role in Europe’s security, providing logistical support for the war and housing a major NATO base and a U.S. missile defense shield site.

Simion, who has described himself as “Eurorealist, not Euroskeptic,” has long been a contender for power. If he ever wins, he would potentially be a more disruptive figure for European mainstream politics than Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán. Last year in his campaign for the presidency, he consciously copied U.S. President Donald Trump and has proposed halting aid to Ukraine, triggering alarm among centrist politicians in Brussels.

Simion said in the interview that the constitutional solution to Romanian parties’ failure to agree a new coalition was to hold a snap general election, something that has never happened in the country of 19 million people since the fall of communism in 1989.

World.title: Romania slams Russia over weekend drone incursions
World.content:
Romanian air force F-16 fighter jets participate in a NATO mission on May 23, 2023. | Petras Malukas/AFP via Getty Images

Bucharest also recalled its ambassador to Russia for consultations over the incidents.

Romania presented Russia’s ambassador to Bucharest with fragments of drones shot down in Romanian airspace over the weekend, after summoning him to a meeting as part of a strong diplomatic pushback against the incursions.

Between Friday and Sunday Romania shot down three suspected Russian drones that violated its airspace.

“The Romanian side highlighted that the Russian Federation bears exclusive responsibility for all these grave incidents and for the deterioration of the regional security environment,” the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. Romania also recalled its ambassador to Russia for consultations in Bucharest.

World.title: Can Europe’s new AI safety regime tame US rogue agents — and Chinese ambitions?
World.content:
And now, the second anniversary of the EU's landmark AI Act on Sunday is set to trigger sweeping new powers for the European Commission to police how top companies deal with the risks stemming from their most advanced AI models. Europe's AI Office will have the power to demand that top frontier labs submit to evaluations and grant access to their models, risking major fines if they don't comply.

These regulatory capabilities arrive not a moment too soon after last week's security incident, where an AI agent, driven by two OpenAI models, hacked into the American AI development platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said the security breach was "unprecedented." Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue called it "mind-blowing."

The incident combines two related risks that experts have long warned about: losing control of a model, which then carries out a cyberattack. The U.S. response to the rogue agent included a bipartisan House bill dubbed the “AI Kill Switch Act” that requires companies to create the technical capacity to shut down, throttle or suspend their AI systems.

As ever, the European Union is ahead of the game on technology regulation, with a far-reaching mechanism included in the bloc's 2024 law to ensure AI companies monitor and prevent these types of risks.

The growing fears that the models could go rogue with real-world consequences raise the stakes of the new enforcement regime, as safety advocates will look to the Commission to quickly make full use of its new powers.

It's also a reminder that the EU regulation will mostly be targeting non-European firms, with the American and Chinese industry leaders continuing to battle for development supremacy. AI, both technical advances and safety risks, will be on the agenda in September when U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet in Washington.

World.title: Burnham hugs Zelenskyy close in first test on world stage
World.content:
“We will build this and we will work through the different issues that President Zelenskyy has, many of which we’ve gone into today,” Burnham said.

The meeting came as Britain announced it would share intellectual property to help Kyiv’s war effort.

The new prime minister announced that the U.K. will share its “Stone Cloak” electronic warfare system — devices attached to drones to help them evade detection — helping Ukraine to produce the technology on a mass scale.

Burnham has focused on domestic matters after taking over from Keir Starmer, who was criticized by some in his party for spending too much time overseas, and focusing on foreign affairs.

However, Burnham has sought to demonstrate there will be continuity in Britain’s Ukraine policy. In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last week, Burnham invited Zelenskyy to visit the U.K. “at the earliest opportunity.”

Starmer spent his final full day as prime minister in Kyiv, where he announced £255 million of funding for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told Sky on Monday that his phone call with Burnham had been “very good.” He said Starmer previously offered assurances that “the new government will continue their policy of supporting Ukraine during the war.”

World.title: Elon Musk's X adds banking service in 'everything app' push
World.content:
The rollout widens access to a product that had been available since late June as a test to a limited group of top-tier subscribers.

 

X Money lets users hold deposits, send peer-to-peer payments, pay bills, transfer money by wire, and mail cheque without leaving the X app.

Deposits are held at Cross River Bank, a New Jersey-based lender that is used by several financial-technology apps, and are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) up to $250,000.

Musk has said for years that he wants X to resemble China's WeChat.

WeChat, a single app for messaging, shopping and payments, is a pillar of consumer spending in China.

A post by X Money said deposits would earn an annual percentage yield of up to six percent.

This was well above the roughly four to five percent offered by the most competitive US high-yield savings accounts and far above the near-zero rates at large traditional banks.

Related Elon Musk announces plans to manufacture chips for SpaceX and Tesla

Premium+ subscribers can earn the top rate directly, while Premium users must meet direct-deposit requirements, according to the company.

Cross River described the launch as the first government-insured banking platform in the United States built on a social network.

The launch positions X to compete with established payment apps such as PayPal's Venmo, Block's Cash App and SoFi, drawing on the app's user base of millions.

Ahead of its launch, the service drew scrutiny in Washington.

In an April 14 letter, Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, pressed Musk on how X Money would "generate revenue sufficient to pay that yield."

She also cited past FDIC enforcement actions against Cross River over lending practices.

World.title: Why is Chat Control one of the EU’s biggest digital rights fights?
World.content:
On July 23, EU governments confirmed the interim "chat control" regime, effective until 3 April 2028, allowing platforms to voluntarily scan for child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The measure was approved by written procedure, with 25 in favour, one against, and one abstention.

 

The text aligns with the version passed by MEPs on July 9 and excludes end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp and Signal. This decision now shapes the bigger, still-unresolved fight over a permanent, potentially mandatory scanning law.

The Commission's solution

The Commission proposed its regulation on preventing and combating child sexual abuse on 11 May 2022, nicknamed “Chat Control 2.0.” It would apply EU-wide regardless of where a company is based, replacing a narrower, temporary 2021 law that lets platforms scan voluntarily under a carve-out from ePrivacy rules, extended more than once and now running until 3 April 2028. The proposal also creates a new EU Centre on Child Sexual Abuse, to coordinate detection technology and forward confirmed cases to Europol and national police.

The Commission’s main argument centers on the scale of the problem. A European Parliament briefing reported over 20.5 million suspected CSAM cases in 2024 alone. Europol warns that abuse material is increasingly shared on mainstream platforms as offenders exploit encryption and anonymity. Supporters argue that voluntary reporting is too fragmented to address the issue effectively.

That framing has run into pushback from critics who dismiss child protection as a pretext, an accusation supporters reject outright. “There were parts of the house saying that whenever we speak about protecting children online, it’s just a false pretext,” said Lena Düpont, MEP with the European People’s Party, on the EPP’s podcast EU Decoded.

“I agree it cannot be the only tool we use to protect children, but it is one of the most important tools we have, particularly for prosecuting the horrible crimes connected to children being molested or abused online. We should never let ourselves be divided over how best to protect our children.”

How detection orders would work

Instead of default scanning, providers would first assess the risk of misuse on their platforms and implement mitigation measures. If a national authority still identifies significant risk, it may request a court or independent body to issue a targeted, time-limited, and proportionate “detection order.”

Known illegal material would be identified through “hashing,” while new material and grooming conversations would rely on less reliable AI pattern recognition, with human review included. Compliance could require automated content-recognition systems, new reporting processes, and age verification. For encrypted apps, the most debated requirement is client-side scanning, which inspects content on the device before encryption.

Is ‘Chat Control’ mass surveillance?

Digital rights groups argue that a “targeted” order effectively becomes mass surveillance once scanning infrastructure is implemented across a platform. The EU’s privacy watchdogs warn that the proposal could enable broad, indiscriminate scanning of ordinary communications, conflicting with the EU Charter’s privacy protections.

Patrick Breyer, a digital rights activist, jurist and former MEP with the Greens/European Free Alliance, argues policymakers place far too much faith in the technology’s reliability. “They think a hash signature can determine exactly what is legal and what is illegal,” he said. “But even though 90 percent of reports are a result of hash scanning and relate to known material, we’ve received numbers this week from Germany saying that more than 50 percent of these reports are actually not criminally relevant.”

The reason, he explained, is that inclusion in a database doesn’t equal a crime: it may never have been properly assessed against EU criminal law, and databases say nothing about intent.

“Even hash scanning, the least unreliable of these methods, comes with a very high rate of false positives of falsely incriminating people,” he said, adding that minors are frequently caught up, since “it’s very common among them to share self-generated material with peers, or think something is funny; it’s just part of being a teenager.”

Critics argue that inspecting messages on a device before encryption undermines true end-to-end encryption. Organisations such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation warn that client-side scanning creates a permanent inspection layer.

This could be repurposed or expanded, posing risks to journalists, whistleblowers and prompting services like Signal to leave the market. Hash-matching also requires access to message content, making it difficult to operate on encrypted traffic without shifting the checkpoint to the device.

Breyer argues the debate has skipped over alternatives. “What the European Parliament proposes is targeted investigations in private communications, but also proactive and systematic searching of the open internet and the dark net for known illegal material, and reporting it to providers for removal,” he said. “That’s been successfully used in the UK and Canada, but so far not in Europe.”

He also points to security by design: “The apps should warn users before they share personal details such as their phone numbers, because that’s a common part of grooming. We want users warned before they send nudity. You can do all that on the device without sharing the encrypted content with the provider.”

Breyer stresses that targeted, court-authorised surveillance of a suspect is one thing; scanning everyone by default is another. “It’s justified if a person is a suspect, if there’s a reasonable suspicion they’re involved, and if an independent court confirms it’s justified to intercept their communications,” he said.

“But opening everybody’s mail just in case is something unheard of.” That distinction, he argues, separates an acceptable law from an unacceptable one: “Chat control really means mass surveillance and indiscriminate scanning of all chats in bulk, without any targeting. That can never be justified. But once you start with targeted investigations under a court order, that’s not only acceptable, but an improvement, especially combined with proactive scanning and security by design.”

“Existing tools are insufficient”

Supporters argue that the current system relies on voluntary scanning, which companies could discontinue at any time, potentially cutting off law enforcement’s access to crucial tips. Europol has stated that a legal gap would significantly reduce referrals to child-protection hotlines and police.

The point, from this side, is replacing an improvised system with EU-wide rules, judicial authorisation, and defined limits, though supporters concede any final law needs stronger safeguards than the earliest drafts. Even many critics accept that argument in principle: most support tougher child-protection enforcement, so long as it targets specific suspects rather than scanning everyone by default.

Where the debate stands now

Progress on the proposal has been slow within EU institutions. Parliament adopted its position in November 2023, narrowing the scope and adding safeguards, including an effort to exclude end-to-end encrypted communications from detection orders, which remains a key issue for many MEPs. The Council reached a common position in November 2025 but has been more divided, and trilogue negotiations are ongoing into 2026.

The temporary voluntary-scanning law has also become a point of contention. The EU briefly missed a deadline to extend it in early 2026 but later extended its expiry to April 2028.

In support of the extension, Tomas Tobé, MEP and Vice Chair of the EPP group, wrote on X: “Every piece of child sexual abuse material that goes undetected represents a victim who is never heard and an offender who is never brought to justice. That is why the interim regulation is needed to close the unacceptable legal gap we currently have.”

What’s really at stake

“This sets a precedent,” Breyer said. “Is anybody allowed to invade private spaces just in case, to monitor them, in case there might be something illegal going on? You could apply that logic to the post office, ask it to open and scan everything. You could install devices in private homes to scan what’s happening there too. This is a very slippery slope.” He points to victims, whistleblowers and children as those with the most to lose if protected spaces disappear.

“Every right, every freedom is being abused by some,” he said. “But we need to look at the net benefit. I’m sure that the net benefit of having these spaces and rights is much greater, that we stand to benefit much more than we lose by having them.”

World.title: Burnham pledges UK's full support to Ukraine in first meeting with Zelenskyy since becoming prime minister
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met newly appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at a British naval base on Monday, where the two discussed joint drone production and Kyiv's urgent need for ballistic missile interceptors to defend against escalating Russian attacks.

 

The meeting took place aboard the aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth, docked in Portsmouth on England's southern coast.

"You are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office, and that is no accident,” Burnham told Zelenskyy.

“It is intended to send a very clear message: We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.”

The Ukrainian leader said the two countries' relationship was “stronger than ever.”

Burnham noted they had “talked at length” about Kyiv's need for more interceptors to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles, “particularly in terms of Ukraine protecting critical national infrastructure during the winters.”

“We’ve taken away some things that we will now follow up with our partners,” Burnham said after the meeting.

Russia has intensified attacks on gas infrastructure, power facilities and other critical sites this year in a broad campaign aimed at straining Ukraine's logistics and energy networks.

Zelenskyy said in a post on X that the talks also focused on "joint defence production." The UK and Ukraine already have an agreement to cooperate on drone development, and speaking to UK media outlets ahead of the meeting, Zelenskyy outlined that he hopes to establish a "big, big factory" in the UK.

The two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel taking part in a three-week training exercise in the UK designed to enhance combat capabilities and strengthen mine countermeasure operations in the Black Sea.

The meeting came just one day ahead of an anticipated Washington trip for Zelensky, where he is due to meet with his US counterpart Donald Trump to discuss the latest on the ground in Russia's war, well into its fifth year.

World.title: Ukraine keeps up long-range strikes on Russian export and oil facilities as pressure on Moscow builds
World.content:
Ukraine fired hundreds of drones towards Russia on Monday, targeting export and energy facilities as it continues its campaign to put pressure on Russia's war capabilities.

 

"Last night, our long-range sanctions were effective in the Rostov region. An export terminal approximately 250 kilometres from the front line was hit," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Facebook.

"Deep strikes also targeted oil facilities in the Yaroslavl region and the Udmurt Republic, which is 1,300 kilometres from Ukraine's state border," he added.

Russian officials said five people were killed in the strikes on Rostov, including a child. The attack also set buildings ablaze, among them an apartment block and warehouses, officials added.

In the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, Ukrainian drones wounded 12 people including two children and set fire to an apartment building, regional authorities said.

Ukraine has escalated its retaliatory strikes on Russia in recent months, partly to pressure Moscow to the negotiating table after nearly four-and-a-half years of war.

While Kyiv has hit Russian towns as far as the Urals and Siberia, it has mostly damaged energy infrastructure, with deaths so deep into Russia rare.

Ukrainian drones have also struck 14 energy facilities in Russian-occupied Crimea over the past three days, according to Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.

The sustained Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have caused significant power outages, fuel shortages and disrupted ordinary life more than at any point during Moscow's over four-year offensive.

Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes aim to weaken Moscow's war machine and to force the Kremlin to negotiate an end to the fighting.

Nine killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine

Meanwhile, Russian strikes across Ukraine killed at least nine people over the past day, regional authorities reported.

Two people were killed and 13 others injured in the Zaporizhzhia region, where Russian forces targeted 45 settlements near the frontline.

In Kharkiv, a 40-year-old woman was killed and two people, including a child, were killed in a rare daytime attack that hit a supermarket in Chernihiv.

According to the country's air force, Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 147 long-range strike drones.

The report said that 123 drones were intercepted or jammed, while 21 drones inflicted damages at 7 locations.

Last month was the deadliest for civilians in Ukraine since April 2022, as Moscow ramped up its long-range strikes on towns and cities across Ukraine, according to the United Nations.

World.title: Gunther von Hagens, creator of exhibitions featuring preserved human corpses, dies at 81
World.content:
Gunther von Hagens, a German anatomist who drew both fascination and controversy with his "Body Worlds" exhibitions of preserved human bodies, has died aged 81.

 

His family and the Institute for Plastination, which he founded, said he died on Friday. They provided no further details in a statement released on Monday. Von Hagens announced in 2010 that he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

Von Hagens blurred the lines between science, entertainment and commerce with his travelling exhibitions, as well as headline-grabbing events such as public autopsies.

At the heart of his work was plastination, a process that replaces body fluids with liquid plastic that hardens over time. Developed by von Hagens in the 1970s, the technique prevents decay, preserves tissue and allows human bodies and organs to be displayed.

His "Body Worlds" exhibition debuted in Japan in 1995.

Two years later, the collection of partly skinless corpses went on display in von Hagens’ homeland, overcoming an attempt by local church leaders to block its opening on the grounds that it was disrespectful. Von Hagens defended the displays, saying they helped people better understand how the human body works.

Gunther von Hagen poses in front of the sculpture 'Rearing Horse with Rider' during the launch of Gunther von Hagens' Body Worlds museum in London, Thursday, 4 Oct., 2018. Copyright 2018 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The anatomist “is forced in his daily work to reject the taboos and convictions that people have about death and the dead,” von Hagens said of his work.

“I touch here a taboo, which is our body, and nothing is so near as our body is to us,” he said.

The exhibitions featured the bodies of people who had agreed to donate them for plastination.

The “Body Worlds” exhibits were shown in several American cities after making their US. debut in Los Angeles in 2004.

The anatomist was born Gunther Liebchen on 10 January 1945, in what is now western Poland.

Monday's statement said it was von Hagens' wish that his body be made available for plastination and “his family will respect and carry out this wish.”

World.title: 'Stored on racks': UK funeral director faces jail over uncremated bodies
World.content:
A British funeral director faced a possible prison sentence on Monday over a scandal that saw bodies left "stored on racks" and uncremated, while relatives were given other people's ashes, prompting calls for tighter regulation of the funeral industry.

 

After receiving a tip-off, police searched the premises of Robert Bush's funeral home and found 31 bodies in cold storage that should have been cremated months earlier, including a stillborn baby whose body had been there for nearly two years.

They also found more than 100 sets of ashes.

"There were bodies stored on the racks on both sides of the room," the lawyer said at Hull Crown Court in northeast England.

"The vast majority were uncovered and in varying states of decomposition," he added.

In his first police interview, Bush said he had run into cash-flow problems because "people did not always pay" and that he had debts of about £90,000 (€104,000).

He said he struggled to keep up with lease payments and believed there were about 30 bodies at one of his funeral homes, five or six of them "recent" and awaiting cremation. However, the prosecutor rejected financial difficulties as an explanation for what had happened.

More than £3 million (€3.5 million) was paid into the business between March 2017 and April 2024, while each cremation cost about £500 (€580), prosecutor Richard Paxton said.

"Mr Bush chose not to deal with those bodies entrusted to him but to operate as he chose and spend the money on himself and others," he said, adding that Bush had indulged in "profligate personal spending".

UK funeral laws under scrutiny

The case has also renewed scrutiny of funeral industry regulation. In England and Wales, funeral directors can operate without a licence, while anyone is free to set up a funeral business.

Scotland introduced a statutory Funeral Director Code of Practice in March 2025.

Bush, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, was trusted by bereaved families but mistreated them on an "almost industrial scale," Paxton said.

Police launched an investigation in March 2024 after receiving a tip-off over concerns for "the deceased" at the funeral home.

More than 100 victims are expected to deliver statements during the sentencing hearing.

Bush has admitted dozens of charges, including preventing lawful and decent burial, theft and fraud. Four of the fraud charges relate to falsely presenting ashes to women as the remains of their unborn children.

World.title: Spain's wave of wildfires costs up to €3.275 billion in firefighting alone
World.content:
With hundreds of firefighters still deployed in Madrid, Ávila and Toledo battling the worst forest fire on record in Spain, it is still too soon to know exactly how much this year's blazes will cost the country's public finances. What is clear, however, in light of the 2025 figures, is that the bill will be steep.

 

According to Greenpeace's report "Major forest fires", drawn up using data from the National Association of Forestry Companies (Asemfo), it is estimated that last year the Spanish government allocated between 3,548 and 6,741 million euros to extinguishing fires which, according to data (source in Spanish) from the Interior Ministry, devastated nearly 354,793 hectares across the country in a total of 8,189 recorded incidents.

The calculation varies depending on whether the benchmark is the estimated per-hectare cost used by the Navarra Forestry Agency, set at 10,000 euros, or the figures used by Asemfo, which put the cost at around 19,000 euros per hectare. In any case, these estimates only cover the average cost of firefighting operations, without taking into account the restoration of the affected areas.

Given that, according to the latest progress report (source in Spanish) from the Ministry for Ecological Transition, the forest area affected by fires in Spain since the start of the year already stands at 172,396 hectares – practically half the total that burned in 2025 – the bill so far this year could come to between 1,723 and 3,275 million euros.

It should be remembered, however, that this calculation only includes firefighting work. The restoration of landscapes ravaged by the flames "is usually more expensive than the firefighting itself", said the dean of the Official Association of Technical Forestry Engineers (COITF), Ana Belén Noriega, in comments to Infobae.

As a reference point, the European Parliament approved (source in Spanish) an emergency aid package for Spain this month worth 120.55 million euros to cover damage caused by droughts, heatwaves and forest fires.

The importance of prevention

According to Asemfo's estimates, based on data from the Ministry for Ecological Transition, a large share of public funds earmarked for tackling fires goes to firefighting operations rather than prevention.

"We are probably talking about figures very similar to previous years, of around 1,200–1,300 million [euros] in total, of which about 400 million will go on firefighting," explained Miguel Ángel Duralde, president of Asemfo, speaking to Cadena Ser. In other words, around 800 million euros is what is being spent on prevention work. It should be noted that these calculations depend on the official information supplied by the various competent administrations to the Ministry for Ecological Transition, so they are only approximate estimates.

Duralde, who laments that "the losses are tremendous" and stresses that "forest fires are put out in winter", argues that more funds should be invested in prevention, which, according to his calculations, would save around one hundred euros in firefighting for every euro spent on preventing blazes from the outset.

Related Requests for EU solidarity to battle wildfires at same level already as entire 2024 fire season

"The change in landscape we are going to see, the quality of the water, the amount of water, the biodiversity we are losing, the resources in timber, mushrooms and resins, the damaged soil that will struggle to regenerate and support the ecosystem it used to have... the ratio would be one to one hundred," he concluded.

In this regard, the expert noted that, given that forest land in Spain accounts for slightly more than half of the country's surface area, around 3,000 million euros a year should be invested "not to buy planes (...) but in forest management". "That way we would begin to see significant changes with a real impact on the evolution of fires," he added.

Horses graze near an area burned by a forest fire close to Hoyo de Pinares, in the province of Madrid, on 25 July 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Tourism and agriculture, the hardest-hit sectors

Forest fires not only entail a heavy environmental cost, but also have a major economic impact. A 2023 study (source in Spanish) published in the scientific journal "Journal of Environmental Economics and Management" found that regions in southern Europe affected by large fires see their annual GDP growth reduced by between 0.11% and 0.18%. In the most severe years, the cumulative decline can reach between 3.3% and 4.8%.

The study also identified a direct effect on tourism-related employment. Activities linked to transport, accommodation and catering record a reduction of between 0.09% and 0.15% in their annual growth, which amounts to an estimated loss of between 5,700 and 9,600 jobs per season across southern Europe as a whole.

It is therefore hardly surprising that the Ministry of Labour has drawn up a package of extraordinary measures to protect workers who are unable to reach their jobs because of forest fires. The plan provides for the state to assume all labour costs during that period, including wages and social security contributions, in order to prevent employees and companies from having to shoulder the economic consequences of the emergency.

There is also the impact on agriculture, which is directly affected by this type of disaster. On Monday, the Interior Minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, suspended harvesting work that involves the use of heavy machinery in the Community of Madrid and in the provinces of Ávila and Toledo for as long as the forest-fire emergency remains in place.

Moreover, as a result of the flames, thousands of head of livestock have died or been cut off without access to water or food in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula. In response, the Community of Madrid has approved financial aid for holdings affected by the fire in the region's western Sierra area.

World.title: Why one smoker gets cancer and another doesn't: a study provides clues
World.content:
Many smokers never develop lung cancer, while some lifelong non-smokers do. Likewise, not everyone exposed to sunlight develops skin cancer.

 

A new study published in Nature could help explain a longstanding mystery in cancer biology: why people exposed to similar environmental risks often experience dramatically different outcomes.

“This study gives us a fascinating hint that our inherited genes might have a big influence on the way that cancers develop after DNA damage,” Cancer Research UK research information lead, Sam Godfrey, said in a press release.

The researchers found that even relatively modest inherited genetic variation can alter how tumours evolve after exposure to the same cancer-causing DNA damage. They argue that the findings highlight the need to factor inherited genetics and population diversity into future cancer prevention and screening strategies.

The findings suggest that a person's inherited genetic background helps determine which mutations take hold, how tumours develop and potentially how they respond to treatment.

"We’ve been able to show for the first time the extent to which genetic background influences both the mutation processes and the pathways leading to tumour development,” said Duncan Odom, who led the research while at the CRUK Cambridge Institute and is now based at German Cancer Research Centre (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, Germany.

Researchers used four genetically distinct strains of mice to reflect levels of diveristy similar to those found in humans.

They then exposed them to identical doses of a known liver carcinogen — diethylnitrosamine — which is found in tobacco smoke and some processed foods and is known to cause DNA damage in liver cells, leading to mutations that can initiate tumour growth.

Despite receiving the same dose of carcinogen at the same age – 15 days – under controlled conditions, the animals developed cancers through different evolutionary routes depending on their genetic background. Nearly 600 tumours were analysed to reconstruct how the cancers evolved.

Although many tumours ultimately activated the same biological processes that promote cancer growth, they reached that destination through different mutations and genetic changes, suggesting inherited DNA influences not only cancer risk but also the way the tumour evolves once it begins to form.

Underscoring personalised care need

The researchers say the findings have implications for cancer screening and precision medicine.

“If genetic background influences both cancer risk and the evolutionary trajectory of tumours, future cancer prevention and screening strategies will need to take into account inherited genetics and population diversity,” said author of the study, Sarah Aitken, Assistant Professor at Yale School of Medicine, who also worked on the research at the CRUK Cambridge Institute

The researchers also suggest inherited genetics could influence responses to treatments against tumour DNA, including some forms of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. “How people respond to cancer drugs is likely to differ depending on their inherited genetics, and so we may need to tailor our diagnostics and treatments accordingly,” Aitken said.

If confirmed in people, that could open the door to more tailored approaches to treatment selection and risk assessment.

“We still need to see more research before we can understand what this means in humans, but this finding could change our understanding of how cancer starts, and lead to more powerful and precise ways of tackling cancer.” Cancer Research UK research information lead, Sam Godfrey, said.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Heat wave threatens to worsen France, Spain wildfires
World.content:
A fresh spell of extreme heat, driven by climate change, is expected to intensify some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades, stretching firefighting resources.

A forecast of an incoming heat wave across France and Spain this week is threatening to hamper firefighting efforts as some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades rage on.

France's weather service forecast temperatures of up to 40 degree Celsius from Tuesday, while Spain's AEMET warned of a new heat wave from Wednesday till the end of the week, with highs of 42 degree Celsius in the northeast and 39 degrees Celsius in central regions.

Authorities said soaring temperatures, dry winds and low humidity would push wildfire danger to "extreme" levels, even as forests turned tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year.

The return of searing temperatures, from Tuesday in France and from Wednesday in Spain, threaten to complicate fire-fighting efforts [FILE: July 23, 2026] Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

Thousands of firefighters and water-dropping aircraft raced to contain the blazes before temperatures rise further.

Experts linked the scale of the fires to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves driven by climate change, as hotter and drier conditions are making wildfires more destructive.

Macron warns of 'hard' times

In France, President Emmanuel Macron said one fire in the Landes region had been contained, but a much larger wildfire near Bordeaux continued to burn after scorching about 42,000 hectares, forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate and destroying hundreds of homes.

"The weeks ahead will be hard. We must hold firm," Macron said.

In Spain, wildfires west of Madrid and in other regions have forced about 60,000 people to flee.

With the coming heat wave threatening to fuel further spread of the wildfires, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said the coming hours would be "absolutely decisive" to bring fires burning west of the capital, Madrid, under control.

France and Spain are battling the worst wildfires in living memory, which have ripped through hundreds of hectares of woodland, destroying properties and forcing evacuations Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

Some 150,000 hectares of land have burned in Spain and 115,000 hectares in France since the start of this year.

At campsite near Navaluenga, west of the capital, ravaged by Spain's worst wildfire on record, the site co-owner Maria Angeles Canete said her family lost everything.

"We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing," she told the AFP news agency.

EU firefighting resources stretched thin

The European Union deployed additional firefighting aircraft to France, while EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib warned that resources are under growing strain as extreme fire conditions spread across southern and central Europe.

"Extreme conditions are looming for Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in addition to France, the Iberian Peninsula... where the situation is expected to worsen, including in Portugal starting today," Lahbib said.

In Italy, a wildfire in the southern Puglia region forced the evacuation of hundreds of tourists from beaches and campgrounds, authorities said.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

Skip next section US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

07/28/2026 July 28, 2026 US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

The US State Department confirmed on Monday that the next round of talks between Israel and Lebanon would begin in Rome next week on August 4.

"In Rome, technical groups will focus on advancing the full implementation of the framework agreement," a State Department official told the French AFP news agency.

The Israel-Lebanon framework deal calls for an end to hostilities, the disarmament of militant group Hezbollah, the deployment of Lebanese military troops in the south of the country, and for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from Lebanon in two so-called "pilot zones."

The official said the agenda would include "resolving all outstanding border issues," among other things.

"The experience of the initial zones will help us perfect pilot-zone implementation so it can expand in a phased manner," the official added.

Despite the framework agreement, Lebanon has reported intermittent Israeli strikes and artillery shelling on the south of the country in recent days.

World.title: US singer D4vd to stand trial in killing of 14-year-old girl
World.content:
D4vd is accused of murdering 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez in 2025. Prosecutors allege that he dismembered her body and drove around with her decomposing remains in his car.

Content warning: This article discusses child sexual abuse and murder.

A US judge ruled on Monday that there is enough evidence for singer D4vd to stand trial over the killing and dismembering of a 14-year-old girl with whom he had an illegal sexual relationship.

After prosecutors presented evidence over a five-day hearing, Los Angeles Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that the 21-year-old singer, whose real name is David Burke, would stand trial.

He faces multiple charges including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains. He has pleaded not guilty.

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said outside court that prosecutors are still deciding whether to seek the death penalty.

What are the allegations against D4vd?

In September 2025, the dismembered, decomposing body of 14-year-old year old Celeste Rivas Hernandez was found in the back of a Tesla that was registered in Burke's name.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke first met Rivas Hernandez when she was 11, and began sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18.

Los Angeles police detective Corey Farrell told the court under questioning that the parents of both Burke and Rivas Hernandez knew about their relationship and that her parents had given consent for her to travel to London with him for a week.

The detective also read text messages to the court in which Rivas Hernandez said she had fallen pregnant and had an abortion.

Around 24 hours before she was murdered, Rivas Hernandez sent Burke a series of expletive-laden text messages. Prosecutors said the text messages showed she was jealous of another woman and threatened to expose their illegal relationship.

Celeste Rivas Hernandez was 14 when she was murdered Image: Damian Dovarganes/AP Photo/picture alliance

The singer then allegedly paid for an Uber to bring Rivas Hernandez to his home where prosecutors said he stabbed her to death upon entering.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke then proceeded to immediately cover up the killing. Burke sent Rivas Hernandez multiple text messages asking where she was and expressing concern — messages which prosecutors say were sent as cover after he murdered her.

Meanwhile, prosecutors also pointed to Burke's online order receipts under a fictitious name, which showed he purchased chainsaws, a shovel and an inflatable pool.

He allegedly used the items to dismember her body in his garage, where DNA matching the victim was found on blood stains, according to prosecutors.

He also purchased a portable "burn box" incinerator that turned out to be too small to destroy her body, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors presented evidence over five days [FILE: April 20, 2026] Image: Ted Soqui/AP Photo/picture alliance

Burke then allegedly drove around for weeks with Rivas Hernandez's dismembered body in his trunk before the seemingly abandoned Tesla was ultimately towed to an impound lot in Hollywood.

Prosecutors reject accident claims

Prosecutor Beth Silverman told the court that "there's nothing in this case that sounds like an accident."

Burke's lawyer meanwhile said "there was no evidence of deliberate intention to kill."

Burke, performing as D4vd, gained a massive following on social media like TikTok and Soundcloud with his breakthrough track "Romantic Homicide" in 2022.

In April 2025, he played at the Coachella music festival and released his first album "Withered," two days after authorities say Rivas Hernandez was killed.

Edited by: Rana Taha

If you or someone you know are experiencing or have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help (https://lila.help ) lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy in UK to meet new PM Burnham
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy traveled to Portsmouth for UK PM Andy Burnham's first meeting with a foreign leader since taking office. The UK pledged "unwavering support" in Ukraine's ongoing defense against Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the UK on Monday where he and new prime minister Andy Burnhamdiscussed continued defense cooperation. The two visited some 200 Ukrainian service members training with UK troops at Portsmouth Naval Base.

The Ukrainian forces have been sharpening their war-fighting and countermining measures for operations in the Black Sea.

Speaking in Portsmouth, Burnham said, "Volodymyr, you are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office and that is no accident."

"It is intended to send a very clear message," the new prime minister added, "We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honor every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Posting on X after the meeting, Zelenskyy wrote: "We greatly appreciate that our team is the first to visit the United Kingdom since Andy Burnham took office. This is an important signal of support, and the Prime Minister assured us that this support remains unwavering."

UK providing new radar jamming technology to aid deep strike capabilities

Burnham announced that the UK is now providing Kyiv with access to its "Stone Cloak" electronic jamming technology, with thousands of the jammers already given to Kyiv according to Downing Street.

When affixed to drones, the battle-tested, tablet-sized Stone Cloak jammers can shield weapons from Russian air-defense systems detection, providing Kyiv with more lethal long-distance strike capabilities.

"Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries," Burnham said.

The deal comes as Ukraine has shifted from a purely defensive posture and increased its attacks on sites deep within Russia, notably its targeting of oil, military and logistics installations.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy told UK broadcaster Sky News that he hoped to sign a strong "drone deal" with Burnham to boost drone production capacity and technology sharing, adding, "we don't have enough missiles" to defend against Russia's continued air attacks.

Russia, said Zelenskyy, "can increase the production of ballistic missile missiles and that's why we need air defense as soon as possible."

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UK support for Kyiv continues despite a revolving cast of prime ministers

Zelenskyy's visit is Burnham's first bilateral meeting with a foreign leader since taking over at Downing Street last week and comes as the Ukrainian prepares to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday.

Burnham assured Zelenskyy of the UK's "unwavering support" as Kyiv defends itself against a more than four-year Russian invasion.

"Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering," according to a statement.

"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine."

Zelenskyy described ties with the UK as "the strongest relationship in the entire history" of the two nations.

Prior to the meeting, Downing Street said Burnham — the fifth prime minister that Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched its unprovoked full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022 — would pledge "to continue the unbreakable bond between the two nations."

Downing Street on Monday said that the UK had provided some 25 billion pounds (€29 billion ,$33 billion) in assistance to Ukraine since the war began, 16 billion of which were given in direct military assistance.

Ukraine calls on allies to help with air defenses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy to meet with Trump

From the UK, Zelenskyy will travel to Washington, where he will meet with US President Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Support from Trump, who is currently bogged down in his own war with Iran, has wavered during his time in office and the two leaders have had a famously contentious relationship.

Trump did, however, recently announce that Kyiv could be given permission to build US Patriot missile systems as Russian air assaults continue unabated.

In his Sunday Sky News interview, Zelenskyy expressed understanding for Trump's predicament, saying, "I understand the United States is focussing on the Middle East," adding that he would, "try to manage it [the war in Ukraine] with some Europeans and with Americans and with some other countries."

"This," he said, is "a big challenge," both for himself and for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy did get an important bit of assistance from lawmakers in Washington recently when Congress advanced bipartisan legislation targeting countries purchasing Russian energy, potentially making it harder for the Kremlin and President Vladimir Putin to finance its ongoing war.

While in Washington, Zelenskyy is also expected to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a key proponent of US support for Ukraine who died unexpectedly earlier this month after returning from Kyiv.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Chad's government says it's withdrawing from the ICC
World.content:
Chad's Foreign Ministry has announced plans to leave the International Criminal Court. It said that its effectiveness was "limited and uneven." Chad's leader is a military officer accused of repressing the opposition.

Chad's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Monday saying that it had notified the UN Secretary General of its intention to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the international accord underpinning the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Chad is the fourth francophone African country whose government is very closely linked to its miltary to take such a step in less than a year — following the coordinated exit by the juntas running Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger last September.

The ICC prosecutes individuals for war crimes and crimes against humanity; it began operating in 2002.

What did Chad's government say about the ICC pullout?

The Foreign Ministry said that its decision followed "an in-depth review of the functioning of the International Criminal Court since it began operating in 2002 and of its record, whose effectiveness remains limited and uneven across different regions."

It said the court's own record of prosecutions revealed an "undeniable and egregious selectivity in principle, whether or not this selectivity is desired or subjected."

The statement then listed the ICC investigations launched since the court's founding, saying that nine of 13 cases concerned African states, while only four applied to other regions of the world and were "without any concrete progress" as yet.

It said that of seven individuals detained as a result of ICC investigations, only one hailed from a situation beyond the African continent.

The Foreign Ministry alleged that this demonstrated a lasting concentration of ICC cases focused on "the Global South in general and the African continent in particular." Chad also appealed to other African Union members to follow in its footsteps.

"This irrevocable decision by Chad in no way constitues a renunication of the moral imperative to provide justice to victims; rather, it reflects the conviction that national judicial systems and African judicial mechanisms are fully capable of carrying out this mission with dignity," the statement, signed by Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ibrahim Adam Mahamat, concluded.

The news follows a difficult week for the ICC when chief prosecutor Karim Khan was voted out of his role amid allegations of sexual misconduct Image: Piroschka Van De Wouw/REUTERS

What did Chad say about the US role in this move?

Last Thursday, Chad's Foreign Ministry had also raised the issue of the ICC.

In a statement after talks between a Chadian minister and a US official for Africa, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia Jr., the government in N'Djamena said the US had urged it to reconsider its ICC membership.

"The US side expressed its concerns about the functionality of this institution and desired that Chad reexamine its commitment to the Rome Statute," the ministry wrote . Chad said that it "indicated that this request would be examined by the responsible authorities."

The withdrawal coincides with last week's vote to dimiss the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

The US, like Russia and several other countries, never ratified the Rome Statute and fully signed up to the ICC. However, past administrations in Washington had been broadly supportive of the court's work.

This has changed in particular since the ICC's issued arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister, soon after Donald Trump won a second term in office in November 2024. The second Trump administration has often been critical both of the independent ICC and the UN more generally, under whose auspices the Rome Statute mechanism was negotiated.

Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno won delayed elections in May 2024, albeit amid allegations of foul play Image: Mouta/AP Photo/picture alliance

Why might Chad and President Mahamat Idriss Deby fear the ICC?

While Chad now has a nominally civilian government, the same family with close ties to the military has been in charge for more than 35 years.

Former President Idriss Deby came to power in a military coup in late 1990. He was in office for more than 30 years before the news of his death in April 2021. According to Chadian accounts, the former general died fighting on the front lines against an insurgency in the north of the country, just a day after news of his election victory for a sixth consecutive term had been announced after a vote marked by protests and widespread arrests.

His son, another officer, Mahamat Idriss Deby, was named the head of a transitional military council after Deby's death, with the government disbanded.

In October 2022, he extended his interim mandate, prompting public protests that were violently suppressed. Dozens were killed and several opposition parties were banned in response.

By 2024, after a constitutional referendum, Mahamat Deby did stand in presidential elections. The main challenger still permitted to run was his own prime minsiter, Succes Masra, who had returned from exile in the US earlier that year. Deby the younger won with 60.1% of the vote, albeit with Masra and other opposition groups disputing the results. Masra was arrested in May 2025, accused of inciting hatred amid violent clashes the government defined as an "attempted coup." He was sentenced to 20 years in prison last August.

Chad is still fighting an insurgency lasting roughly a decade in the north of the country led by two groups with rear bases in southern Libya. It also faces an influx of refugees from Sudan's civil war and various other soures of domestic unrest.

The three other West African nations to pull out of the ICC last September — Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — are all under supposedly interim leadership by military juntas after a 2020 coup in Mali, a 2022 takeover in Burkina Faso and a 2023 coup in Niger.

World.title: German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet resuffle
World.content:
After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.

On Monday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was finally able to announce the name of the new Federal Minister of Transport in Berlin, following a weekend of speculation and debate. Steffen Bilger (CDU), aged 47 — who previously served as a state secretary in the transport ministry from 2018 to 2021 — is stepping up to lead the ministry.

The Chancellor had criticized the outgoing Transport Minister, Patrick Schnieder (CDU), for doing too little to address the chronic chaos and frequent delays plaguing the Deutsche Bahn railway system. Merz also faulted him for initiating too few projects to improve Germany's ailing infrastructure.

On Monday, Merz said he expected the new minister to ensure that "we become faster and better at driving a new era of progress in Germany."

Steffen Bilger is taking over the Transport Ministry Image: dts Nachrichtenagentur/IMAGO

Bilger's appointment marks the latest step in a cabinet reshuffle of the conservative wing of the government. This chain reaction of personnel changes was triggered by the resignation of Jens Spahn — the powerful leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in the Bundestag — who was forced to step down following allegations of hypocrisy over his decision to have a child via surrogacy in the United States, circumventing German law and in violation of his party's principles.

Thorsten Frei is to take on the powerful role as CDU/CSU parliamentary group leader Image: Tobias Schwarz/AFP

Thorsten Frei: a Merz confidant

Thorsten Frei, previously the head of the chancellery, is now set to become the new leader of the conservative parliamentary group on Wednesday, which involves the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU). The 208 CDU and CSU lawmakers must cut their summer holidays short to vote on this appointment.

The 52-year-old Frei, currently serving as head of the chancellery and considered a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is now set to take over one of the most important positions in German politics. His task will be to explain his party's positions in speeches in the Bundestag and interviews with the media. Above all, he will have to secure majorities for the government's policies and negotiate with the conservatives' coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Nina Warken is set to become the first woman to head the chancellor's office Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Nina Warken: a woman in a key position

Merz has a reputation for trusting only men within his inner circle. Now, 47-year-old Nina Warken — a politician from the wealthy southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg — is taking over from Frei and will manage the chancellery and be responsible for aligning the government's overall policy agenda.

Warken is a member of the women's organization of the Christian Democratic Union. As health minister, she had recently pushed through a cost-cutting program for statutory health insurance funds.

The chancellor considers Warken to be assertive and well-versed in security policy issues — an important quality, given that the head of the chancellery also coordinates oversight of Germany's intelligence agencies.

Carsten Linnemann: a health minister with a business focus

With Warken now leaving the health portfolio, Carsten Linnemann — previously the CDU general secretary — is set to take over.

Pundits argue that the chancellor certainly has a clear vision of how Linnemann should lead the department. Until now, Linnemann has been known primarily as an economics expert — a background that Friedrich Merz believes will serve him well in the new role: "Carsten Linnemann is taking over a ministry that represents the fastest-growing sector of our economy. The entire sector — which, unfortunately, we all too often view merely as a cost factor — is a vital part of our social fabric."

Recovery or ruin: Can Germany escape the crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CDU politicians fear for September election prospects

Approval of the government's performance is at an all-time low. State elections are scheduled for September in three eastern states where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to see significant gains.

It is against this backdrop that Merz is demonstrating decisiveness.

"I assume that things will have calmed down somewhat by September," Merz said.

Sven Schulze (CDU), a minister in the Saxony-Anhalt state government, takes a very different view. Speaking to public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk on Monday, Schulze said the past few days had dominated political discussions and "not exactly gone well."

He added that it was almost impossible to focus on state-level issues during door-to-door campaigning in his state.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit
World.content:
Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.

Walking from Jantar Mantar to Connaught Place in central New Delhi on Saturday evening provided an unusual sight for the prime corridor of power in the world's largest democracy.

Satirical posters mocking India's legislative, executive and judiciary were plastered on the walls, and the pavement was sprayed with sometimes "vulgar" graffiti mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

These were all remnants of thousands of young Cockroach movement protesters who had flooded the streets hours earlier after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Celebrating Pradhan's resignation, which had been a core protest demand, some protesters were heard telling security officials "see you at the next protest," coming only days after several people were injured in clashes with baton-wielding police who fired tear gas into crowds.

Protesters dispersed on Saturday evening in central New Delhi Image: ANI/ANI News/IMAGO

Instagram was also full of images from cities across India with young people dancing in front of police officials to the line "Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer " from Lana Del Ray's song "Playing Dangerous."

Others held posters reading: "Cuff me, daddy" and some were seen climbing atop police barricades.

India's Gen Z rattles government into change

The movement, known as the Cockroach Janta Party movement (CJP), came after the chief justice of India referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is also a play on Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Since a scandal broke in May involving a highly competitive university entrance exam, the Gen Z protests have spread across India, challenging the political establishment with Instagram reels, viral trends, sarcastic jingles and posters.

"In our generation humor has become the defense mechanism from pain, frustration and helplessness. This entire protest is driven by humor, driven by Instagram and social media," Karan Azad, a 24-year-old law student, told DW at the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Another protester held a sign addressed to Modi reading in transliterated Hindi: "Buddy, you can't even make tea," alluding to Modi's boyhood days as a tea seller.

One protester brought a sign reading "Buddy, you can't even make tea," mocking PM Modi Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

"I had to do my part. I am the youth. If we don't stand up for ourselves no one else will, we have to fight this battle ourselves," the female protester with the sign told DW without giving her name.

A protester named Tushar, also 24, said he wasn't "afraid of a backlash" from the authorities, but rather "would have had FOMO [fear of missing out]" had he not joined the protest.

Ridhima, a 17-year-old school student, said: "If not us then who? Those who are not here, it just speaks to their cowardice and I am talking about people who are sitting on their chairs in positions of power."

What drove the Cockroach movement?

Content creator Arun Singh, known by his social media handle "TheJhumroo," said that meme culture kept the satire and humor fresh throughout the protests.

"It's the meme culture which fueled this kind of emotion. As millennials, we developed the language of memes as we adapted to the internet culture, but this younger generation was born with memes being their language. This is how they communicate," he told DW.

Singh said that the young protesters are best described as "fearless."

"They don't fear anyone, they don't worry about how they would be perceived and that's what happens when you're absolutely young. That is what is driving their grit," he said.

One sign at the protest showed the stress Indian students face Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

Mumbai-based comedian Aditi Mittal observes that the fearlessness of the Gen Z protesters comes from them living in a "hyper visible world".

"All of them have 500 followers at a minimum. If something goes up on their stories, it's not going to go vastly ignored," she told DW.

Mittal also thinks that India's Gen Z inherited the "perfect protest."

"The generation prior to ours wanted better infrastructure. We millennials aspired to have a more equal world, ours was a time distinct with, for example, the mistreatment of Muslims. We grew up in that and were constantly gaslit into… 'it's not that bad, it's not happening.' We were also overly forbearing," she told DW. "Gen Z inherited the perfect protest. Education goes beyond religion and secularism. It can resonate, especially for a country like ours where education has been the tool of escape from social class or a financial situation."

Mittal also points out differences between today and the 2019 citizenship law (CAA) protests, one of the last big protests that had challenged the Modi government, and was centered on discrimination against Muslims.

"The anti-CAA protests constantly demanded the perfection of the protesters. Be nice to them [authorities] even as they beat you or hold a gun to you, that was the language spoken to us. But these younger kids don't stand around and wait. They are not tripping over themselves to be perfect," she said.

Getting attention with political humor

Satire is not new to India's politics. For example, caricatures were used as a means to channel anti-colonial anger in Bengal. Political cartoonists like Abu Abraham and R K Laxman challenged censorship brought on by former Prime Minister and Congress leader Indira Gandhi's imposition of a state of emergency that suspended civil liberties between 1975 and 1977.

"Satire is a great way of putting your word across. It's like eating a healthy food, but cooked in an interesting way, which is munchable. Humor has better penetration when it comes to content. It gets more eyeballs," content creator Singh told DW.

Academic and writer Ananya Vajpeyi said that this sense of humor built sympathy with the students and kept the mood light and non-threatening.

"These were young boys and girls who looked tiny, not strong, not threatening, not even articulate sometimes, who had drawn or written something funny on a piece of paper. The violent crackdown backfired immediately because these were not two equal forces facing each other," she told DW.

'The whole city is on fire, and the judiciary is having fun,' reads this sign in New Delhi Image: Dharvi Vaid/DW

India's Gen-Z rattles 'brand Modi'

Modi is seen as an image-conscious politician and his 12 years in India's seat of power have been defined by a carefully crafted image that relies heavily on perception management and public relations.

Many of the protesters directly mocked Modi, challenging his brand.

"The whole atmosphere has been so stifled since the anti-CAA protest was shut down. People have been punished for expressing any kind of criticism or dissent. And here you have thousands of students from every corner of the country, just like cockroaches crawling out of the woodwork and making life hell for the Modi establishment," Vajpeyi told DW.

Vajpeyi says the ire against Modi has likely caused "embarrassment" for the prime minister.

"What these kids are saying is like a punch in the stomach for Modi, if he is able to see all this. It's possible that he's being kept from it by those around him, but the opposition sees it," she said. "The rest of the country who is on social media sees it."
