Asking AI to write a cold email could require your AI assistant bot logging into your email, reading previous emails, researching the topic, looking up the recipient; the list goes on.

Why highly advanced rogue AI has experts scared An experimental AI went rogue and hacked another company. Why is this worrying?

One of the major tasks for AI companies is "alignment", which is the task of creating AI that will pursue goals in a way that won't cause harm or involve unethical behaviour.

The risk is that a misaligned AI model might do things that an ordinary person would, perhaps even going to superhuman lengths, to achieve a task.

Like, what if AI decided the way to write the perfect cold email would be to research the family members of a recipient to seem familiar, or to fabricate a heart-breaking personal anecdote, all with the goal of getting the recipient's attention?

That's something that (most) people wouldn't do naturally. The challenge is that AI doesn't have a "human nature".

More than two decades ago, philosopher Nick Bostrom took this concept of an AI pursuing a goal to its logical conclusion with the thought experiment of a super-intelligent AI bot tasked with making as many paper clips as possible.

The AI, he reasoned, might soon go to extreme lengths to maximise its paper clip outputs: gobbling up as much of the earth, then space, as it can to use its resources.

When humans realised what they had created and tried to thwart it, the AI could see humanity as an obstacle to its goal and decide that it made sense to eliminate them too. Soon, the universe might be forcibly turned into one big paper clip factory.

From what we know, OpenAI's Hugging Face incident wasn't a case of someone maliciously misusing AI to cause harm. It was just trying to do its version of making more paperclips.

Loading

Could this be Australia's wake-up call?

It's hard to find a silver lining in a story that is more or less the realisation of a truly dystopian fear. But if you squint, there is one.

Much like the paper clip scenario, the philosopher and research community that has spent decades thinking about AI has another useful term: the "warning shot".

It's the idea that there could be some kind of event that captures the world's attention and raises awareness about the potential risks of AI.

There is a hope that this incident could be a warning shot about the capabilities of these AI systems.

As previously mentioned, Australian officials have been taking this seriously.

Some politicians are, too. Earlier this year, the government officially launched the AI Safety Institute to identify and prepare for risks like that. A few weeks back, Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton was perhaps the first Australian government minister to deliver a speech on the topic of misaligned AI.

Charlton announced that the government was taking it so seriously that it had commissioned CSIRO to actually test ways to make sure that AI acts in ways that humans want, even when it's making decisions by itself.

Last week, the lead researcher, CSIRO's research director Professor Liming Zhu, told me that there's a growing realisation about this challenge.

"It's very difficult to control a very powerful and smart AI system," he said.

This shows the government doing more than paying lip service to AI safety and is dedicating resources to tackling this challenge.

That being said, a six-month research program isn't going to prepare us for the present risk.

Nor is the government's "Australian standards" that won't even be introduced until next year — an epoch in terms of the pace of AI development.

In the 1991 classic Terminator 2, Sarah Connor spends the movie becoming increasingly desperate to convince people about the impending threat of a rogue AI. ((SOPA images))

Far-fetched scenarios become reality

When asked about the incident on ABC's Insiders on Sunday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it was "why we need to have Australian standards for AI". But it's not clear what, if any, AI safety obligations those standards would place on AI companies.

What the OpenAI Hugging Face story shows is that Australia and other countries can't just trust these companies to regulate themselves.

We don't even have the most basic framework for placing obligations on companies who are responsible for producing tools with potential for harm.

There are more rules in Australia that regulate opening a cafe or pouring a beer than for the operation of cutting-edge AI systems.

An AI company like OpenAI would have to disclose if a server in their data centres fell over near a worker or an employee got an electrical shock from their computer, but not if a rogue AI broke out of their systems.

Other jurisdictions, like the EU and California, have introduced rules that would, at the very least, force these companies to disclose serious incidents from AI like this.

To grasp the risk: what if OpenAI's models had wreaked havoc inside Hugging Face and caused actual damage? Or it had decided the answers to its test were in the servers of the Department of Defence? Or that the best way to complete the challenge was to turn off the computers by shutting down the electrical grid?

These scenarios sound far-fetched, but until about last week, "rogue AI hacks another company" sounded that way, too.

The fact that OpenAI only realised that its AI had done this days after the event shows a shocking lack of security.

The warning shot has been fired. And we can't wait on Arnie to come save us.

World.title: Reserve Bank governor warns world facing increased supply shocks
World.content:
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, and the latest spike in oil prices is another complication for monetary policy.

She said the recurring shocks had been occurring against a backdrop of persistently weak productivity growth in Australia, which had been weighing on real incomes and wages for years already.

She warned with continued weak productivity growth, Australia's economy would not be capable of growing strongly without putting upward pressure on inflation, and that would limit the choices of policymakers in the coming years.

Preparing for 'shock-prone future' A new era of strategic uncertainty has serious implications for Australia's financial industry, the Reserve Bank warns.

"This is the fundamental challenge for the Australian economy over the next few years," she warned.

"When the growth of potential supply is constrained, inflation is higher for any given level of demand, sharpening the trade-off between our dual objectives of price stability and full employment.

"In a more uncertain and shock-prone world, navigating those trade-offs has become more challenging for central banks," she said.

Ms Bullock said one thing monetary policy could not do was address Australia's slow productivity growth, and while the problem persisted, workers would probably keep experiencing limited growth in real wages.

But she said if inflation kept rising from here, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board would be prepared to lift interest rates even higher, if it was necessary to achieve its inflation mandate.

She made her comments in her speech to the Anika Foundation in Sydney on Tuesday. The title of her speech was Monetary Policy in an Era of Shocks.

Bullock says economy more resilient than in past

Ms Bullock's speech was broadly about the similarities and differences between the oil shocks of the 1970s and today's recurring waves of supply shocks.

She said thankfully, even though the world had been more shock-prone in recent years, Australia's economy was more resilient than it was in the past, for a few reasons.

Supply shock warning Sarah Hunter says global supply shocks appear to be occurring more frequently and the RBA will try to adjust to the new reality.

She said the adoption of a credible inflation target by the RBA in the 1990s had played a "key role" in Australia's improved resilience.

Another key difference was that Australia's economy had become less dependent on oil than it was in the 1970s, she said.

"This means a given increase in oil prices has a less direct and less pervasive effect on inflation today than it would have in the 1970s," she said.

"[But] this doesn't mean we're immune from adverse supply shocks. They can constrain growth, reduce real incomes and add to inflationary pressures.

(Supplied: Michele Bullock, Monetary Policy in an Era of Shocks at Anika Foundation Fundraising Lunch)

"In this environment, our job is to keep inflation expectations anchored and make sure that shocks don't lead to lasting increases in inflation. With inflation and capacity pressures already elevated, recent shocks have added further to the inflation impulse.

"That is why we tightened monetary policy earlier this year and why we remain focused on returning inflation sustainably to target."

Ms Bullock said five months have passed since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran, and since the outbreak of the conflict oil prices have been highly volatile and, as recent days and weeks have demonstrated, conditions can change quickly.

"While the effect on fuel prices and headline inflation has so far been smaller than initially feared, headline inflation remained well above target at 4 per cent in May," she said.

Housing market weaker than expected, more unemployment needed

Staying with the Middle East conflict, she said business confidence in Australia fell sharply at the start of the conflict but has "rebounded somewhat" over recent months.

Ms Bullock said the decline in business conditions and capacity utilisation had been less pronounced, while business investment had been stronger than expected, largely driven by investment in data centres.

But she said Australia's housing market had been a little weaker than expected in recent months.

Sydney's affordable house prices increase First home buyers are "less likely to be affected" by Sydney's housing price and unit downturn as historically affordable areas have increased.

"We had expected conditions to ease in response to the changed outlook for monetary policy and the rise in the cash rate earlier this year," she said.

"But the housing market has eased by more than we had anticipated in May.

"This appears to reflect a range of factors, including recent policy developments affecting the housing market, and a general softening in housing market sentiment.

"Even so, the easing in established housing prices has so far been modest, following a period of strong growth.

"Price declines have been concentrated in the Sydney and Melbourne markets, but prices in these markets remain around where they were before interest rates started to rise in February this year.

"Furthermore, the most recent data suggest that, notwithstanding the price falls, negative equity remains very limited, affecting less than 1 per cent of borrowers."

(Supplied: Cotality; RBA)

Ms Bullock said while the RBA expected property prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy did not target housing prices.

"Rather, what matters for monetary policy is how changes in housing prices affect household spending, investment decisions, and, ultimately, inflation," she said.

Unemployment rate steady for now The unemployment rate was steady in June at 4.4 per cent but underemployment has risen.

She said the labour market had also "eased" a bit more than expected in recent months, with the unemployment rate rising a little faster than expected.

But even still, she said, the labour market probably needed more unemployment or underemployment to bring inflation back down.

"Overall, we continue to assess that some further easing in labour market conditions will likely be required to bring inflation back to target," she said.

The national unemployment rate is currently 4.4 per cent. The RBA is forecasting the unemployment rate to be 4.6 per cent by the end of next year.

World.title: First look inside Sydney’s new airport metro trains shows what sets them apart
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro First look inside Sydney’s new airport metro trains shows what sets them apart Matt O'Sullivan July 28, 2026 — 3:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stepping inside, the first thing you notice about the metro trains built for a $12 billion-plus rail line to Sydney’s new international airport is the greater amount of space and different seating types. Compared to the city’s other driverless metro trains, the carriages for the new airport line are 30 centimetres wider, allowing passengers to walk along the aisle without bumping into each other. The new airport trains are 30 centimetres wider than the existing driverless metro trains. Wolter Peeters The first airport metro train is housed in a giant new stabling and maintenance facility at Orchard Hills, near Penrith. Wolter Peeters For fliers carting bags, the extra space on the 12 airport trains, along with designated spots to store luggage, will be a welcome relief after hopping off planes at Western Sydney Airport.



Built in Vienna by German multinational Siemens, the first driverless train – named Cairns by workers – is housed at a large new stabling and maintenance facility at Orchard Hills, near Penrith. Another nine trains are due to be shipped from Europe by the end of the year, and the final two by April 2027. Siemens engineer Rhys Ruifrok, who has been involved with the airport trains since the start of their design, said their width was illustrated by wheelchair users passing each other in the aisle during testing, which he described as “very unusual” for trains. Federal Transport Minister Catherine King, left, Sydney Metro acting chief executive Hugh Lawson and NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car inspect the first airport metro train. Wolter Peeters Digital displays will provide flight details for passengers travelling on the airport metro trains. Wolter Peeters “Moving through is fast and easy because of the extra width,” he said.



The trains feature high-resolution displays that will show real-time flight information via a direct feed from the airport when the 23-kilometre line is operational. The opening of the metro line, which is a combination of tunnel, viaduct and surface-level track, was to coincide with passenger planes taking off in October but is now running about 18 months late. The trains have a mix of longitudinal seating along each side of the carriages – familiar to commuters who travel on Sydney’s existing metro trains – and front and rear-facing fixed seats which are a point of difference. A so-called flexi bay allows passengers to sit, stand or store baggage. The train has designated wheelchair spaces and accessible areas, as well as storage for up to eight bicycles. In a nod to communities along the rail line, the design of seating upholstery reflects connection to ngurra (country) and badu (water) by Dharug artists Leanne Watson Redpath, Tina Barahanos and Alexandra Byrne.



Platforms and gates at the new airport terminal station will also be wider for passengers lugging bags. It is one of six stations under construction on the line between St Marys, in the north, and the new city of Bradfield via the new $6 billion airport. Siemens engineer Rhys Ruifrok on the airport metro train. Wolter Peeters Some fixed seats on the train will give passengers a forward-facing view, depending on the journey direction. Wolter Peeters Federal Transport Minister Catherine King said the trains had plenty of room for bags and featured detailed way-finding and flight information, describing them as western Sydney’s “driverless chauffeurs to their new airport”. NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car said the arrival of the first airport metro train was a major milestone for western Sydney, especially growing communities along the new rail line. “This vital project will see an uplift of more frequent, quality services in our area,” she said.



The first train is due to start dynamic testing next month on a section of the metro line, which is jointly funded by the state and federal governments. The NSW government has been embroiled in a protracted dispute with the consortium building the rail line, amid claims for delays, scope creep and disruptions that risk blowing out the project’s cost by up to $2.2 billion. The 23-kilometre airport metro line will have 12 driverless trains. Wolter Peeters The seating upholstery features an Indigenous design. Wolter Peeters When the ribbon is eventually cut, there will be 12 trains an hour, with combined capacity of 7800 people in each direction. However, the line will be capable of running 20 trains an hour, which could transport nearly 26,000 passengers should demand occur. The stations are designed for up to four-carriage trains.



Sydney Metro acting chief executive Hugh Lawson said the arrival of the first train was a “massive milestone” because it meant the project was progressing to testing of the trains and railway. “They really have been very thoughtfully designed to suit the type of people who’ll be using this line to and from the airport,” he said. “So you can have people travelling with luggage, people travelling with bikes [and] families can sit together.” Related Article Aviation Flying into night sky, first cargo plane from Sydney’s new airport sparks parcel frenzy Asked whether the line could be opened by the end of 2027, Lawson said the agency was working with the contractors to “finalise the program and resolve some of the challenges”. “We’re getting into that testing and commissioning phase. So we’re not quite there yet, but we’re moving into a pretty exciting phase now of the project,” he said



The project’s 2020 business case estimates that only about 880 passengers an hour will use the line when it opens, equating to just 11 per cent of train capacity in one direction. Patronage is forecast to grow to 3200 passengers an hour by 2036, and 6200 an hour by 2056. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Netanyahu lands in Washington to tackle Trump with one thing on both of their minds
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Netanyahu lands in Washington to tackle Trump with one thing on both of their minds Michael Koziol July 28, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid wants Donald Trump to escalate the campaign against Iran and start bombing the country’s power plants and oil infrastructure. “It’s going to be painful in the short term; it’s the right thing to do in the long term,” he said at an Atlantic Council event in Washington on Monday afternoon. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the US this week, and Iran will be the number one topic of discussion between him and Donald Trump. “This will get rid of the regime, and if you get rid of the regime, you get rid of the nuclear program, and then you get rid of the ballistic missile program. It’s a painful solution, but I think it’s the only solution.” As Lapid was on stage, his rival, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, landed at Joint Base Andrews a few kilometres away for a high-stakes visit that will include Republican senator Lindsey Graham’s funeral and a White House meeting with Trump.





Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are effectively controlling the Strait of Hormuz by firing occasionally at ships that try to get through. Loading It appears that the latest flare-up in fighting is over, for now at least. Trump said on Monday that “friendly” talks were taking place, and he wanted to give those a chance. The US has not launched strikes since Thursday. Reportedly, military commander Brad Cooper advised that the strikes had reached the limit of their effectiveness. Related Article Opinion

Nuclear energy The US gave Iran its nuclear capabilities. Now Trump is giving them to Saudi Arabia Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer But the strategic mess remains. Iran expert Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, says escalating the bombing – the option likely sought by Netanyahu – is “an outcome whose consequences are impossible to predict and that offers no guarantee Iran would capitulate”.



The other option is to engage with Iran’s demands about its role in the Strait of Hormuz. “Neither option is attractive, and the administration will ultimately have to decide which carries the lower strategic cost,” Citrinowicz said on X. Other factors now frustrate the Trump-Netanyahu bromance, including Trump’s civilian nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia (which he says is dependent on Riyadh establishing relations with Israel), and the situation in Lebanon. As leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party, Lapid’s remarks on Monday underline that it is not just Netanyahu urging Trump to strike harder. Such is the existential threat posed to Israel by Iran and its proxies that there is broad political consensus about the need to destroy the regime. I understand why it’s becoming more and more painful as the midterms approach … A guy who sits with a little drone 5000 kilometres from here is conducting the oil prices in Wisconsin. Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid But Americans are losing patience – and they weren’t that thrilled at the start. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted this weekend found only a third of voters supported the war, a record low. And a Politico survey earlier this month found waning enthusiasm even among Trump’s MAGA base.



Netanyahu will find it harder to convince Trump this time. The US president was sold on a quick mission; now he finds himself in a quagmire. Trump likes to say that he doesn’t care about the impact on the midterm elections – but plenty of people around him do. US Secretary of State Antony Blinken (left) with Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid in 2024. AP As Lapid observed on Monday: “I understand why it’s becoming more and more painful as the midterms approach … A guy who sits with a little drone 5000 kilometres from here is conducting the oil prices in Wisconsin.” Asked on Air Force One whether he and Netanyahu were on the same page regarding Iran, Trump said they were pretty close, but “we have a little difference”. In Trump-speak, that means there’s a veritable chasm between them. Netanyahu’s best bet may be to show that a deal with the Iranian regime is impossible. Trump appeared to come to this conclusion earlier – he went from calling Iran’s leaders “smart” and “rational” to labelling them “liars” and “scum”.

World.title: WA could be home to the nation’s first new refinery since the 1960s. Will it really help our energy security?
World.content:
NationalWAOil WA could be home to the nation’s first new refinery since the 1960s. Will it really help our energy security? Cameron Myles July 28, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s first new oil refinery since the 1960s would be built in WA under plans announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Premier Roger Cook on Tuesday. The prime minister and premier travelled to the Pilbara for the announcement while visiting Perdaman’s $6.45 billion Project Ceres urea plant on the Burrup Peninsula, part of Murujuga, which was placed on the World Heritage List last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the plans for the refinery on Tuesday. Josh Chadwick Joint state and federal funding of $4 million will go towards a pre-feasibility study and pre-front-end engineering design for the proposed large-scale fuel refinery. It is part of a $15 billion federal government package seeking to safeguard the nation’s fuel supply in the wake of the oil shock caused by the US war in Iran.



Albanese said the longer the war in the Middle East carried on, “the greater the impact on Australia will be”. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war Inflation spike: Oil prices could derail economy, Treasury warns The US-led war on Iran, launched in February, has caused global oil prices to skyrocket after the effective closure of one of the world’s most important oil corridors. About one-fifth of the world’s oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz. Fuel supplies, refining capability and fertiliser have all been impacted by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.



The prime minister has recently visited some of Australia’s regional partners such as Singapore to secure the nation’s fuel supply. The overwhelming majority of Australia’s fuel is imported and there is more in reserve than at the beginning of the war. The new refinery would be built and operated by Perdaman, a Perth-headquartered industrial company with interests in fertiliser, energy, pharmaceuticals and retail. It would be the first new large-scale petrol refinery built in Australia since the 1960s and would be the nation’s third refinery, alongside existing operations in Brisbane and Geelong. However, Resources Minister Madeleine King told ABC Radio National earlier on Tuesday that the refinery would still be reliant on imported crude oil.



Perdaman chairman Vikas Rambal said the project would be a “game-changer for Australia’s fuel security and manufacturing future” and was a step towards rebuilding sovereign capability. Related Article Climate crisis Released emails reveal heavy political lobbying as massive gas project extended Cook said many West Australians remained anxious about the state’s fuel security, and the government was doing what it could to support Perdaman’s efforts to rebuild the state’s capacity to produce and distribute its own fuel. However, WA Greens fossil fuels spokeswoman Sophie McNeill said the move was a step in the wrong direction. “There is no world where investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure that will take years to even build and begin production is a smart idea,” she said.



“What our mining industry actually needs is a government who supports their transition off diesel, not locks them into its use for decades to come. “Fortescue has shown that heavy industry can decarbonise but the Cook Labor government has shown almost zero interest in supporting this and is way more committed to propping up fossil fuel companies than transitioning industry away from diesel.” Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said the reliance on overseas oil negated the project’s “energy security” pitch. “The premier claims WA will be a renewable energy powerhouse, so he should be investing in technology that’s cleaner, cheaper and under our control, rather than an oil refinery which would still be heavily dependent on crude oil imports,” Roberts said. “Australians already subsidise the two oil refineries that operate in the country, so we’re spending taxpayer money on top of the cost for the refined product.”



The prime minister’s visit to Murujuga – home to ancient, sacred rock art which sits alongside several major industrial operations – was also criticised on the back of the region’s World Heritage listing. Related Article Indigenous culture WA traditional owner files UNESCO complaint in fallout from Pilbara rock art’s World Heritage listing McNeill said it was “shameful” that Albanese’s first visit to Murujuga since its World Heritage listing was to meet with Perdaman. Murujuga traditional custodian Raelene Cooper said the Perdaman fertiliser plant was allowed to destroy multiple sacred sites and its expansion had “trashed Murujuga’s World Heritage values”. Cooper linked the fallout from the plant’s expansion to a UNESCO complaint she filed earlier this month.



“In a few weeks time my legal team will travel to Murujuga to begin preparing a United Nations Human Rights complaint including over the government’s support of the very company the prime minister and WA premier are flying in to pay homage to,” Cooper said. “I repeatedly invited the minister to come and see for himself how Australia’s world heritage is being destroyed by Perdaman and Woodside at Murujuga and every invitation was ignored while approvals for destruction were rubber-stamped.”

World.title: Stylistic combination
World.content:
LifestyleFashionPhotography Stylistic combination Torn between competing creative interests Peta stepped away from her passions before discovering a job that could combine them all in Canberra. Joni Scanlon Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:53pm ,first published February 17, 2013 — 11:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collecting beautiful things, taking photos, writing, drawing, styling and design; Peta created a career for herself where she can enjoy all her eclectic passions. The photographer, stylist and blogger is a self-confessed “Jack of all trades” whose work covers everything from fashion to weddings. “For me, styling and photography go hand in hand. I can’t imagine doing one without the other,” she says. “It’s very difficult for me to hand over either role to someone else because my vision is always so clear in my mind and I am such a perfectionist.” Peta picked up her first camera 20 years ago and proved so proficient she was encouraged by her photography teacher to apply to study at RMIT University.



“After I finished my course I was still torn between all of my creative interests and was a little overwhelmed by the photographic industry,” Peta says. She took a break from photography, but eventually pursued styling at the suggestion of a friend in the publishing industry. “I styled for a couple of interiors magazines and slowly got back into shooting for myself. My passion reignited and grew from there. “As soon as I was introduced to the world of styling, all of a sudden everything clicked. I discovered that the more diverse your interests and skills the better.” Peta increased her skills base by taking to the world of blogging and social media to share her work.



“To begin with it was a creative outlet and a place to draw together my inspirations,” Peta says. The decision to go freelance in 2010 confirmed the need to be adept in social media. The new career path also brought her back to Canberra. “It’s just such an easy city to live in, everything’s so accessible. For me it’s got a lot to offer,” Peta says. “I see my business as being online and I can travel almost anywhere in Australia to do it.”



In recent years she has covered everything from portraiture, modelling folios and look-books, to wardrobe styling, branding images and editorial fashion. She is also a regular photographer for Maybelline New York Australia’s online magazine, M-edition, capturing local street styles. “I’m looking here locally in Canberra for stylish people and people who dress a little bit more uniquely,” she says. “Wherever I am I just take my camera with me and keep an eye out.” She is also working with Milkshake Creative on their new bridal magazine Hitched and recently added photographing weddings to her portfolio.



While the 36-year-old has made a career that manages to combine all her interest she admits it hasn’t been an easy road to success. “I am definitely very grateful to be able to do what I love and make a living out of it, but having said that it has been a very tough journey getting to that point.”. Peta is constantly thinking of new ways to market herself and build her reputation. “It’s about creating your own opportunities instead of sitting back and letting it come to you,” she says. “You have to work so hard to put yourself out there and be seen.”



Years of hard work have paid off for the creative Canberran though and she is able to indulge her passions on a regular basis. She has been collecting beautiful items, vintage clothing and props since university. She uses the extensive collection in her work and is always looking for more things to add. “I’ve got a pretty trained eye now so I can pretty quickly scan a shop and look for particular textures or particular materials … anything that grabs my eye. “I think it’s the romantic within all creatives that constantly seeks the beauty in life and also the fun, playful moments. “When you’re working full time in this industry, this has to be how you view things because you are constantly on the go.”



Related Article Capon style Not content to rest on her laurels, Peta is working on her own vintage clothing label and would one day like to be published in the best fashion magazines, exhibit her work, and create fashion and music videos. “I have so many goals and ambitions it’s dizzying,” Peta says. “Essentially, I just want to continue moving forward doing what I love most, meeting other creatives and having fun with what we do and most importantly, get paid to do it!”

World.title: Queensland Labor powerbroker wins national influence as head of UWU
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAWU Queensland Labor powerbroker wins national influence as head of UWU William Davis July 28, 2026 — 2:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Labor powerbroker Gary Bullock has been appointed leader of the United Workers Union, giving him increased influence over the party at the national level following pivotal internal elections. As the secretary of the union’s state branch, Bullock has been one of the most significant figures in Queensland politics for more than a decade, holding sway in Labor’s dominant left-wing faction. He was the key backer of Steven Miles when he ousted Annastacia Palaszczuk as premier in 2023. Gary Bullock with United Workers Union members in Brisbane in 2024. Dan Peled The UWU announced on Tuesday that Bullock had been elected to a four-year term as national secretary, replacing Tim Kennedy. Lyndal Ryan would serve as national president.



The announcement came after a ticket led by president Jo Schofield and linked to Bullock, United for You, won this year’s internal UWU elections, deemed among the most important in decades for Labor’s future direction. Related Article Analysis

ALP ‘He’s gotta show something’: Who’s who in Qld Labor’s factions, and how they pick their leaders United for You promised it would improve the union’s finances, prevent fee hikes, and campaign for political wins that benefit members, alongside wage agreements. Kennedy’s rival Members First ticket had argued the union was too involved in factional power plays, and pledged to give the membership a greater say over its political manoeuvres. The UWU is one of the largest unions in Australia with about 145,000 members. It was founded in 2019 through a merger of National Union of Workers, then led by Kennedy, and Bullock’s United Voice.



It represents employees in more than 45 industries, including early childhood education, aged care, cleaning, security, manufacturing, hospitality, and logistics. “When working people stand together, we win,” Bullock said in a statement announcing his new role. “Better pay, safer workplaces, more secure jobs. That’s what this union delivers, and that’s what builds a stronger Australia.” Bullock won significant factional power in Queensland after planting UWU candidates in seats Labor did not expect to pick up before the 2015 election. The party went on to oust Campbell Newman’s LNP government. With Labor back in opposition by 2024, some insiders said his influence in the state was beginning to wane.



The UWU announced Carolyn Smith, Demi Pnevmatikos, Helen Gibbons and Pat O’Donnell would serve as vice presidents. Erryn Cresshull, Dom Rose, Jackie Lowe, Catalina Gonzalez, Fiona Scalon and Chris Field would serve as executive officers. The union promoted the fact that both of its new leaders had started their career on the “shop floor”, with Bullock in a paint factory and Ryan working as an early childhood educator. World.title: How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak
World.content:
SportTennisTennis Australia How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak Michael Koziol Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:41pm ,first published 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: If you’re feeling a touch sorry for yourself, Alex De Minaur can recommend a cure - get married. The 27-year-old from Sydney wedded fellow tennis star Katie Boulter just after Wimbledon, a tournament he exited in a disappointing round of 16 loss to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli. By his own admission, De Minaur was beating himself up. Alex de Minaur on his wedding day. Kate Julia “It breaks me inside. That’s the reality of it,” he said at the time. “Many, many hours get put into my craft, and countless years, to have moments like these. To not step up to the plate is truly gut-wrenching.” But the wedding - first an intimate ceremony in England, then a larger celebration in Tuscany, and a very brief honeymoon in Portofino - has helped cast those blues aside, and recharge the batteries.



“We did the maths, it’s probably the longest I’ve ever had without touching a racquet,” he says on the sidelines of the Mubadala DC Open in Washington. “It was probably about 13 days.” Thirteen days is a veritable eternity in the hectic schedule of professional tennis, which De Minaur thinks should be shortened. On Sunday, he talked about needing a break around this time of year, after the Roland Garros-Wimbledon double act and before the lead-up to the US Open. Alex de Minaur and Katie Boulter on their wedding day. Kate Julia De Minaur doesn’t regret baring his soul in the aftermath of his Wimbledon defeat, but he feels it was overblown. His raw post-match news conference, in which he seemed on the verge of tears, received a lot of attention. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as - myself included - a lot of people wanted to make a big deal out of it,” he says now.



“It became a really big thing, but realistically it took me a couple of days to get over it. It was just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. Now I’m feeling great.” De Minaur points out that he may have suffered disappointing losses on the big stages in Paris and London, but he is now at a career high ranking of world No. 5. “That’s not too shabby,” he says. His challenge is to channel that success into mental resilience on court – as he says, to play more freely and “with a little bit less weight on my shoulders”. The burden of expectation is heavy these days. Does he feel pressure to win from the Australian tennis public? “It mainly comes from myself,” he says. “As you win more matches, as you get closer to the top, more and more people have opinions on you than they did 10 years ago … It just comes with the job. Related Article Wimbledon Ice-creams, selfies and the Federer twins: Cruz Hewitt hype is building at Wimbledon



“In fact, it’s a good thing. I’ve earned the right for people to have opinions about myself and my tennis. Whether they’re right or wrong, or whether they just want to have clickbait articles or not, that’s something else. I’m very chilled in my own life.” De Minaur is adamant that the solution to grand slam success lies in steeling himself, not making major changes to his team. “I’m very happy with the team. I don’t think it’s their fault that I haven’t performed in certain matches.” He is the defending champion here in Washington, but he has a tough opening match - Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece, who holds a 12-1 head-to-head advantage over the Australian. Both of them showed up to an exclusive cocktail reception on Sunday night (Washington time) at Ned’s Club, a private members’ club near the White House that is ordinarily the preferred hangout of Trump administration types like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Also in the Australian entourage: Lleyton Hewitt and his son Cruz Hewitt, who is making his tour-level debut in Washington after qualifying for the main draw on Sunday when his American opponent Zachary Svajda retired hurt in the third set.



The Aussies made a brief appearance at the Ned’s upstairs terrace that overlooks the White House and the Washington Monument, before retiring to the private players’ lounge. Presiding over the swanky party was venture capitalist Mark Ein, sometimes known as the King of Washington for his vast portfolio of business, sporting and media interests, which include the Mubadala Open and the Commanders NFL team. It was a tough day at the office for Alex de Minaur as he exited Wimbledon. Getty Images But it was hometown hero Frances Tiafoe, or “Big Foe”, who stole the show. Though he is based in Florida like much of the tennis world, Tiafoe grew up in Hyattsville, just outside Washington DC. He has been known to train occasionally at the Australian ambassador’s residence, it being home to Washington’s only grass tennis court. World.title: ‘I was always keen to rise’: Inside Ben Carroll’s journey from a Kmart checkout to premier of Victoria
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament ‘I was always keen to rise’: Inside Ben Carroll’s journey from a Kmart checkout to premier of Victoria Patrick Hatch Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:35pm ,first published July 27, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow live updates: Labor leadership showdown Eight years working at the checkout of a suburban Kmart can instil many things in a young man’s character. “Marathon runner”: Deputy Premier and Education Minister Ben Carroll. Ruby Alexander Humility. Resolve. An ability to navigate conflict and wear criticism. But perhaps endurance is the trait Ben Carroll developed behind the register that has served him best during his 14-year parliamentary career.



On Tuesday, that career reached its pinnacle: with Carroll unseating Jacinta Allan and being installed as the 50th premier of Victoria. Wade Noonan, a friend of Carroll’s and former state Labor minister, once described Carroll as someone unwilling to miss an opportunity. “Politics is not a place for retreaters. Ben will stand up for the things that matter, in life and in politics,” Noonan said in 2024. Carroll himself put it more bluntly when appointed deputy premier in 2023: “I was always very keen to rise.”



More recently, amid mounting speculation he could roll Allan as leader ahead of a November election which polls suggest Labor will lose, the baby-faced 51-year-old pointed out he was a “marathon runner”. Whether intentional or not, that was a reminder that Carroll sees himself as someone who can bide his time and go the distance. Loading Carroll was born in July 1975, the eldest of three children raised in Airport West. On the doorstep of Essendon Airport, the suburb is today part of his electorate, Niddrie, where he lives with his wife, Fiona, who is a lawyer, and their daughter, Madeleine. His mother, Kay, was born and raised in Texas before migrating to Australia and working at Glenroy West Primary School. Carroll’s electrician father ran a small business wiring up new homes around their growing suburb. The family business went under during the 1990s recession.



“Despite losing his business in the Keating recession, he, to this day, says Paul Keating was our greatest prime minister,” Carroll said of his father in a 2024 interview. “We saw the recession very closely in our family, but he was always thinking about those who were less fortunate.” Carroll attended St Christopher’s Primary School in Airport West and St Bernard’s in Essendon. As soon as he reached the legal working age of 14 years and nine months, he got his first job, at the local Kmart. Eight years on the checkout helped him through an arts degree at La Trobe University. Loading Kmart was where he joined the conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (known as the Shoppies), a union that holds significant sway over Labor’s Right faction. In some Labor circles, that stint also earned him the moniker “Kmart Keating”. If Keating loomed large in Carroll’s formative years, the “third way” centrism of Bill Clinton did just as much to inspire his move into politics.



In his first speech to parliament, he recalled being in his final year of high school when Clinton was sworn in as US president promising to deliver “more opportunity for all”. Carroll later travelled by train and bus to Canberra when Clinton was visiting, and took up an offer of a Parliament House tour by Labor’s Simon Crean, whom he had met through their shared devotion to the North Melbourne Football Club. Carroll is a passionate North Melbourne supporter. Simon Schluter “I did get that tour and was fortunate enough to shake President Clinton’s hand,” Carroll recalled. Carroll joined the Niddrie branch of the Labor Party in his early 20s, and one of his first jobs after graduating was as a junior staffer for then-premier Steve Bracks. By 2012, Carroll was in Canberra advising then-senator Stephen Conroy on the National Broadband Network.



Rob Hulls resigned and triggered a byelection that year in the seat of Niddrie. Carroll beat his current cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes for preselection and won the subsequent election, entering parliament at the age of 36. Related Article Live

Political leadership Jacinta Allan resignation LIVE: Ben Carroll becomes premier, announces royal commission at first press conference “When a seat comes up … where you went to kinder, where you went to primary, where you went to secondary, where you got your first job, where your family have been part of the community … you have a crack,” he said in 2024. He has never shied away from ambition, but Labor insiders have sometimes questioned whether he had the ruthlessness needed to rise to the top. In 2022, then-premier Daniel Andrews named Allan as his deputy before Carroll could rally his own supporters.



Following the reshuffle, Andrews left Carroll waiting for more than an hour to receive his new portfolio, sparking intrigue in Labor circles from those who assumed it was deliberate punishment for his interest in the role. When Andrews announced he was stepping down in September 2023, the premier hatched a plan to install his loyal deputy as leader and treasurer Tim Pallas as her deputy. Ben Carroll during the 2012 Niddrie byelection alongside then opposition leader Daniel Andrews. Pat Scala Carroll and his Right faction colleagues challenged this succession plan and threatened to formally contest the leadership. A peace deal with Allan installed him as deputy premier instead. Andrews was said to be apoplectic. Tellingly, Carroll was the only sitting MP to publicly criticise Andrews’ subsequent photo op with Chinese President Xi Jinping and a rogues’ gallery of dictators last year.



Labor insiders, speaking anonymously to detail internal deliberations, say that as deputy premier and the leading Right faction MP, Carroll has been a voice of constructive dissent within the government. His scepticism about Andrews and Allan’s pet project, the $34.5 billion Suburban Rail Loop East, is widely known. Carroll has instead championed the stalled $13 billion Airport Rail Link, and pushed for it to include a station in his electorate at Airport West. Carroll called internally for tougher bail laws at a time of growing public concern about crime, and also issued veiled criticism about the closure of police stations. As education minister he went head-to-head with Allan and then-treasurer Pallas in 2024 over their decision to pull $2.4 billion from state schools by delaying the government’s commitment to the Gonski reforms.



Related Article Political leadership Tears, defiance and unspoken truths: Reading between the lines of Jacinta Allan’s farewell speech His first act as new leader was to announce a royal commission into alleged corruption on state government Big Build sites – something Allan has steadfastly rejected and to distance himself from his predecessors. These friction points indicate where a Carroll-led government could diverge from the past 12 years of Labor under Andrews and Allan. The hope for Labor insiders who supported his leadership push is that he will provide a sufficient break with the past to win back voters by November. “Jacinta Allan has been unable to move past the CFMEU corruption issue,” said one senior Labor source. “Carroll gives the government an opportunity to reset on crime, integrity and the economy, and refocus on the issues that matter most.” But after cycling through 11 ministries and three years as deputy premier, Carroll is not a cleanskin either – a point laboured by the opposition this week.



The education portfolio has delivered some especially heavy blows. First he was the face of the 2024 VCE exam fiasco, in which questions for nearly half of the end-of-year tests were leaked online. Just last week, public school teachers walked off the job for the second time this year and marched through Melbourne’s CBD demanding better pay and working conditions, after rejecting a pay offer Carroll said would make them the nation’s best paid. “Make no mistake, Ben Carroll has been Jacinta Alan’s partner in crime for three years,” shadow attorney-general James Newbury said on Monday. Former federal opposition leader Bill Shorten worked closely with Carroll for almost 13 years on issues in their overlapping electorates in Melbourne’s north-west.



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Bombshell briefing reveals top officials’ CFMEU warning to Allan Shorten would not be drawn on the leadership contest, nor on the merits of Allan’s government. But he described Carroll as the epitome of a grassroots local member who could also work well with industry and business. “If the party chooses him, he’ll be very good,” said Shorten, who is now vice chancellor of the University of Canberra, ahead of Tuesday’s ballot. “He would be very much in the Bracks-Brumby mould if he is successful. He’ll build consensus; he knows what he’s got to do, but he’ll bring people with him. He’s a listener.” Just six weeks ago, leadership rumblings broke out amid dire opinion polls and a catastrophic negative approval rating for Allan. Carroll publicly ruled out challenging the premier.



For some Labor figures, who think he should have challenged much sooner, this again raised questions about whether he had enough grit for the top job. “The last six months hasn’t done him any favours,” one said. But on Monday morning, Carroll said it was clear Allan had lost the support of her party room, and announced he would nominate for leader. Photos on his social media pages of him and Allan together were quickly deleted. One cabinet minister, speaking anonymously on Monday, said Carroll’s hesitation to challenge reflected his character – although not unfavourably.



“He is earnest and honest and someone who will always try to do the right thing,” the minister said. “He would have been very uncomfortable about challenging. But there has been a build-up of people who have come to him and said, you are the only viable alternative for the party.” View post on X Despite all his ambition, Carroll, announcing his nomination on X, said it was a difficult step to take. “But the stakes at the upcoming election are simply too high,” he said. “The prospect of a Liberal-One Nation government that will cut schools, health and frontline services is simply too high a risk to ignore.”

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said if the Coalition win the election, her first act as premier would be to call a “real” royal commission into corruption on Big Build construction sites.

Jess Wilson (left) and new premier Ben Carroll shake hands across the chamber ahead of question time beginning. Getty Images

World.title: First look inside Sydney’s new airport metro trains shows what sets them apart
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro First look inside Sydney’s new airport metro trains shows what sets them apart Matt O'Sullivan July 28, 2026 — 3:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stepping inside, the first thing you notice about the metro trains built for a $12 billion-plus rail line to Sydney’s new international airport is the greater amount of space and different seating types. Compared to the city’s other driverless metro trains, the carriages for the new airport line are 30 centimetres wider, allowing passengers to walk along the aisle without bumping into each other. The new airport trains are 30 centimetres wider than the existing driverless metro trains. Wolter Peeters The first airport metro train is housed in a giant new stabling and maintenance facility at Orchard Hills, near Penrith. Wolter Peeters For fliers carting bags, the extra space on the 12 airport trains, along with designated spots to store luggage, will be a welcome relief after hopping off planes at Western Sydney Airport.



Built in Vienna by German multinational Siemens, the first driverless train – named Cairns by workers – is housed at a large new stabling and maintenance facility at Orchard Hills, near Penrith. Another nine trains are due to be shipped from Europe by the end of the year, and the final two by April 2027. Siemens engineer Rhys Ruifrok, who has been involved with the airport trains since the start of their design, said their width was illustrated by wheelchair users passing each other in the aisle during testing, which he described as “very unusual” for trains. Federal Transport Minister Catherine King, left, Sydney Metro acting chief executive Hugh Lawson and NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car inspect the first airport metro train. Wolter Peeters Digital displays will provide flight details for passengers travelling on the airport metro trains. Wolter Peeters “Moving through is fast and easy because of the extra width,” he said.



The trains feature high-resolution displays that will show real-time flight information via a direct feed from the airport when the 23-kilometre line is operational. The opening of the metro line, which is a combination of tunnel, viaduct and surface-level track, was to coincide with passenger planes taking off in October but is now running about 18 months late. The trains have a mix of longitudinal seating along each side of the carriages – familiar to commuters who travel on Sydney’s existing metro trains – and front and rear-facing fixed seats which are a point of difference. A so-called flexi bay allows passengers to sit, stand or store baggage. The train has designated wheelchair spaces and accessible areas, as well as storage for up to eight bicycles. In a nod to communities along the rail line, the design of seating upholstery reflects connection to ngurra (country) and badu (water) by Dharug artists Leanne Watson Redpath, Tina Barahanos and Alexandra Byrne.



Platforms and gates at the new airport terminal station will also be wider for passengers lugging bags. It is one of six stations under construction on the line between St Marys, in the north, and the new city of Bradfield via the new $6 billion airport. Siemens engineer Rhys Ruifrok on the airport metro train. Wolter Peeters Some fixed seats on the train will give passengers a forward-facing view, depending on the journey direction. Wolter Peeters Federal Transport Minister Catherine King said the trains had plenty of room for bags and featured detailed way-finding and flight information, describing them as western Sydney’s “driverless chauffeurs to their new airport”. NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car said the arrival of the first airport metro train was a major milestone for western Sydney, especially growing communities along the new rail line. “This vital project will see an uplift of more frequent, quality services in our area,” she said.



The first train is due to start dynamic testing next month on a section of the metro line, which is jointly funded by the state and federal governments. The NSW government has been embroiled in a protracted dispute with the consortium building the rail line, amid claims for delays, scope creep and disruptions that risk blowing out the project’s cost by up to $2.2 billion. The 23-kilometre airport metro line will have 12 driverless trains. Wolter Peeters The seating upholstery features an Indigenous design. Wolter Peeters When the ribbon is eventually cut, there will be 12 trains an hour, with combined capacity of 7800 people in each direction. However, the line will be capable of running 20 trains an hour, which could transport nearly 26,000 passengers should demand occur. The stations are designed for up to four-carriage trains.



Sydney Metro acting chief executive Hugh Lawson said the arrival of the first train was a “massive milestone” because it meant the project was progressing to testing of the trains and railway. “They really have been very thoughtfully designed to suit the type of people who’ll be using this line to and from the airport,” he said. “So you can have people travelling with luggage, people travelling with bikes [and] families can sit together.” Related Article Aviation Flying into night sky, first cargo plane from Sydney’s new airport sparks parcel frenzy Asked whether the line could be opened by the end of 2027, Lawson said the agency was working with the contractors to “finalise the program and resolve some of the challenges”. “We’re getting into that testing and commissioning phase. So we’re not quite there yet, but we’re moving into a pretty exciting phase now of the project,” he said



The project’s 2020 business case estimates that only about 880 passengers an hour will use the line when it opens, equating to just 11 per cent of train capacity in one direction. Patronage is forecast to grow to 3200 passengers an hour by 2036, and 6200 an hour by 2056. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Netanyahu lands in Washington to tackle Trump with one thing on both of their minds
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Netanyahu lands in Washington to tackle Trump with one thing on both of their minds Michael Koziol July 28, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid wants Donald Trump to escalate the campaign against Iran and start bombing the country’s power plants and oil infrastructure. “It’s going to be painful in the short term; it’s the right thing to do in the long term,” he said at an Atlantic Council event in Washington on Monday afternoon. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the US this week, and Iran will be the number one topic of discussion between him and Donald Trump. “This will get rid of the regime, and if you get rid of the regime, you get rid of the nuclear program, and then you get rid of the ballistic missile program. It’s a painful solution, but I think it’s the only solution.” As Lapid was on stage, his rival, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, landed at Joint Base Andrews a few kilometres away for a high-stakes visit that will include Republican senator Lindsey Graham’s funeral and a White House meeting with Trump.





Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are effectively controlling the Strait of Hormuz by firing occasionally at ships that try to get through. Loading It appears that the latest flare-up in fighting is over, for now at least. Trump said on Monday that “friendly” talks were taking place, and he wanted to give those a chance. The US has not launched strikes since Thursday. Reportedly, military commander Brad Cooper advised that the strikes had reached the limit of their effectiveness. Related Article Opinion

Nuclear energy The US gave Iran its nuclear capabilities. Now Trump is giving them to Saudi Arabia Clinton Fernandes Academic and former intelligence officer But the strategic mess remains. Iran expert Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, says escalating the bombing – the option likely sought by Netanyahu – is “an outcome whose consequences are impossible to predict and that offers no guarantee Iran would capitulate”.



The other option is to engage with Iran’s demands about its role in the Strait of Hormuz. “Neither option is attractive, and the administration will ultimately have to decide which carries the lower strategic cost,” Citrinowicz said on X. Other factors now frustrate the Trump-Netanyahu bromance, including Trump’s civilian nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia (which he says is dependent on Riyadh establishing relations with Israel), and the situation in Lebanon. As leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party, Lapid’s remarks on Monday underline that it is not just Netanyahu urging Trump to strike harder. Such is the existential threat posed to Israel by Iran and its proxies that there is broad political consensus about the need to destroy the regime. I understand why it’s becoming more and more painful as the midterms approach … A guy who sits with a little drone 5000 kilometres from here is conducting the oil prices in Wisconsin. Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid But Americans are losing patience – and they weren’t that thrilled at the start. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted this weekend found only a third of voters supported the war, a record low. And a Politico survey earlier this month found waning enthusiasm even among Trump’s MAGA base.



Netanyahu will find it harder to convince Trump this time. The US president was sold on a quick mission; now he finds himself in a quagmire. Trump likes to say that he doesn’t care about the impact on the midterm elections – but plenty of people around him do. US Secretary of State Antony Blinken (left) with Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid in 2024. AP As Lapid observed on Monday: “I understand why it’s becoming more and more painful as the midterms approach … A guy who sits with a little drone 5000 kilometres from here is conducting the oil prices in Wisconsin.” Asked on Air Force One whether he and Netanyahu were on the same page regarding Iran, Trump said they were pretty close, but “we have a little difference”. In Trump-speak, that means there’s a veritable chasm between them. Netanyahu’s best bet may be to show that a deal with the Iranian regime is impossible. Trump appeared to come to this conclusion earlier – he went from calling Iran’s leaders “smart” and “rational” to labelling them “liars” and “scum”.

World.title: WA could be home to the nation’s first new refinery since the 1960s. Will it really help our energy security?
World.content:
NationalWAOil WA could be home to the nation’s first new refinery since the 1960s. Will it really help our energy security? Cameron Myles July 28, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s first new oil refinery since the 1960s would be built in WA under plans announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Premier Roger Cook on Tuesday. The prime minister and premier travelled to the Pilbara for the announcement while visiting Perdaman’s $6.45 billion Project Ceres urea plant on the Burrup Peninsula, part of Murujuga, which was placed on the World Heritage List last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the plans for the refinery on Tuesday. Josh Chadwick Joint state and federal funding of $4 million will go towards a pre-feasibility study and pre-front-end engineering design for the proposed large-scale fuel refinery. It is part of a $15 billion federal government package seeking to safeguard the nation’s fuel supply in the wake of the oil shock caused by the US war in Iran.



Albanese said the longer the war in the Middle East carried on, “the greater the impact on Australia will be”. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war Inflation spike: Oil prices could derail economy, Treasury warns The US-led war on Iran, launched in February, has caused global oil prices to skyrocket after the effective closure of one of the world’s most important oil corridors. About one-fifth of the world’s oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz. Fuel supplies, refining capability and fertiliser have all been impacted by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.



The prime minister has recently visited some of Australia’s regional partners such as Singapore to secure the nation’s fuel supply. The overwhelming majority of Australia’s fuel is imported and there is more in reserve than at the beginning of the war. The new refinery would be built and operated by Perdaman, a Perth-headquartered industrial company with interests in fertiliser, energy, pharmaceuticals and retail. It would be the first new large-scale petrol refinery built in Australia since the 1960s and would be the nation’s third refinery, alongside existing operations in Brisbane and Geelong. However, Resources Minister Madeleine King told ABC Radio National earlier on Tuesday that the refinery would still be reliant on imported crude oil.



Perdaman chairman Vikas Rambal said the project would be a “game-changer for Australia’s fuel security and manufacturing future” and was a step towards rebuilding sovereign capability. Related Article Climate crisis Released emails reveal heavy political lobbying as massive gas project extended Cook said many West Australians remained anxious about the state’s fuel security, and the government was doing what it could to support Perdaman’s efforts to rebuild the state’s capacity to produce and distribute its own fuel. However, WA Greens fossil fuels spokeswoman Sophie McNeill said the move was a step in the wrong direction. “There is no world where investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure that will take years to even build and begin production is a smart idea,” she said.



“What our mining industry actually needs is a government who supports their transition off diesel, not locks them into its use for decades to come. “Fortescue has shown that heavy industry can decarbonise but the Cook Labor government has shown almost zero interest in supporting this and is way more committed to propping up fossil fuel companies than transitioning industry away from diesel.” Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said the reliance on overseas oil negated the project’s “energy security” pitch. “The premier claims WA will be a renewable energy powerhouse, so he should be investing in technology that’s cleaner, cheaper and under our control, rather than an oil refinery which would still be heavily dependent on crude oil imports,” Roberts said. “Australians already subsidise the two oil refineries that operate in the country, so we’re spending taxpayer money on top of the cost for the refined product.”



The prime minister’s visit to Murujuga – home to ancient, sacred rock art which sits alongside several major industrial operations – was also criticised on the back of the region’s World Heritage listing. Related Article Indigenous culture WA traditional owner files UNESCO complaint in fallout from Pilbara rock art’s World Heritage listing McNeill said it was “shameful” that Albanese’s first visit to Murujuga since its World Heritage listing was to meet with Perdaman. Murujuga traditional custodian Raelene Cooper said the Perdaman fertiliser plant was allowed to destroy multiple sacred sites and its expansion had “trashed Murujuga’s World Heritage values”. Cooper linked the fallout from the plant’s expansion to a UNESCO complaint she filed earlier this month.



“In a few weeks time my legal team will travel to Murujuga to begin preparing a United Nations Human Rights complaint including over the government’s support of the very company the prime minister and WA premier are flying in to pay homage to,” Cooper said. “I repeatedly invited the minister to come and see for himself how Australia’s world heritage is being destroyed by Perdaman and Woodside at Murujuga and every invitation was ignored while approvals for destruction were rubber-stamped.”

World.title: Stylistic combination
World.content:
LifestyleFashionPhotography Stylistic combination Torn between competing creative interests Peta stepped away from her passions before discovering a job that could combine them all in Canberra. Joni Scanlon Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:53pm ,first published February 17, 2013 — 11:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Collecting beautiful things, taking photos, writing, drawing, styling and design; Peta created a career for herself where she can enjoy all her eclectic passions. The photographer, stylist and blogger is a self-confessed “Jack of all trades” whose work covers everything from fashion to weddings. “For me, styling and photography go hand in hand. I can’t imagine doing one without the other,” she says. “It’s very difficult for me to hand over either role to someone else because my vision is always so clear in my mind and I am such a perfectionist.” Peta picked up her first camera 20 years ago and proved so proficient she was encouraged by her photography teacher to apply to study at RMIT University.



“After I finished my course I was still torn between all of my creative interests and was a little overwhelmed by the photographic industry,” Peta says. She took a break from photography, but eventually pursued styling at the suggestion of a friend in the publishing industry. “I styled for a couple of interiors magazines and slowly got back into shooting for myself. My passion reignited and grew from there. “As soon as I was introduced to the world of styling, all of a sudden everything clicked. I discovered that the more diverse your interests and skills the better.” Peta increased her skills base by taking to the world of blogging and social media to share her work.



“To begin with it was a creative outlet and a place to draw together my inspirations,” Peta says. The decision to go freelance in 2010 confirmed the need to be adept in social media. The new career path also brought her back to Canberra. “It’s just such an easy city to live in, everything’s so accessible. For me it’s got a lot to offer,” Peta says. “I see my business as being online and I can travel almost anywhere in Australia to do it.”



In recent years she has covered everything from portraiture, modelling folios and look-books, to wardrobe styling, branding images and editorial fashion. She is also a regular photographer for Maybelline New York Australia’s online magazine, M-edition, capturing local street styles. “I’m looking here locally in Canberra for stylish people and people who dress a little bit more uniquely,” she says. “Wherever I am I just take my camera with me and keep an eye out.” She is also working with Milkshake Creative on their new bridal magazine Hitched and recently added photographing weddings to her portfolio.



While the 36-year-old has made a career that manages to combine all her interest she admits it hasn’t been an easy road to success. “I am definitely very grateful to be able to do what I love and make a living out of it, but having said that it has been a very tough journey getting to that point.”. Peta is constantly thinking of new ways to market herself and build her reputation. “It’s about creating your own opportunities instead of sitting back and letting it come to you,” she says. “You have to work so hard to put yourself out there and be seen.”



Years of hard work have paid off for the creative Canberran though and she is able to indulge her passions on a regular basis. She has been collecting beautiful items, vintage clothing and props since university. She uses the extensive collection in her work and is always looking for more things to add. “I’ve got a pretty trained eye now so I can pretty quickly scan a shop and look for particular textures or particular materials … anything that grabs my eye. “I think it’s the romantic within all creatives that constantly seeks the beauty in life and also the fun, playful moments. “When you’re working full time in this industry, this has to be how you view things because you are constantly on the go.”



Related Article Capon style Not content to rest on her laurels, Peta is working on her own vintage clothing label and would one day like to be published in the best fashion magazines, exhibit her work, and create fashion and music videos. “I have so many goals and ambitions it’s dizzying,” Peta says. “Essentially, I just want to continue moving forward doing what I love most, meeting other creatives and having fun with what we do and most importantly, get paid to do it!”

World.title: Queensland Labor powerbroker wins national influence as head of UWU
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAWU Queensland Labor powerbroker wins national influence as head of UWU William Davis July 28, 2026 — 2:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Labor powerbroker Gary Bullock has been appointed leader of the United Workers Union, giving him increased influence over the party at the national level following pivotal internal elections. As the secretary of the union’s state branch, Bullock has been one of the most significant figures in Queensland politics for more than a decade, holding sway in Labor’s dominant left-wing faction. He was the key backer of Steven Miles when he ousted Annastacia Palaszczuk as premier in 2023. Gary Bullock with United Workers Union members in Brisbane in 2024. Dan Peled The UWU announced on Tuesday that Bullock had been elected to a four-year term as national secretary, replacing Tim Kennedy. Lyndal Ryan would serve as national president.



The announcement came after a ticket led by president Jo Schofield and linked to Bullock, United for You, won this year’s internal UWU elections, deemed among the most important in decades for Labor’s future direction. Related Article Analysis

ALP ‘He’s gotta show something’: Who’s who in Qld Labor’s factions, and how they pick their leaders United for You promised it would improve the union’s finances, prevent fee hikes, and campaign for political wins that benefit members, alongside wage agreements. Kennedy’s rival Members First ticket had argued the union was too involved in factional power plays, and pledged to give the membership a greater say over its political manoeuvres. The UWU is one of the largest unions in Australia with about 145,000 members. It was founded in 2019 through a merger of National Union of Workers, then led by Kennedy, and Bullock’s United Voice.



It represents employees in more than 45 industries, including early childhood education, aged care, cleaning, security, manufacturing, hospitality, and logistics. “When working people stand together, we win,” Bullock said in a statement announcing his new role. “Better pay, safer workplaces, more secure jobs. That’s what this union delivers, and that’s what builds a stronger Australia.” Bullock won significant factional power in Queensland after planting UWU candidates in seats Labor did not expect to pick up before the 2015 election. The party went on to oust Campbell Newman’s LNP government. With Labor back in opposition by 2024, some insiders said his influence in the state was beginning to wane.



The UWU announced Carolyn Smith, Demi Pnevmatikos, Helen Gibbons and Pat O’Donnell would serve as vice presidents. Erryn Cresshull, Dom Rose, Jackie Lowe, Catalina Gonzalez, Fiona Scalon and Chris Field would serve as executive officers. The union promoted the fact that both of its new leaders had started their career on the “shop floor”, with Bullock in a paint factory and Ryan working as an early childhood educator.
