World.title: How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak
World.content:
SportTennisTennis Australia How a Portofino honeymoon and 13 days without tennis helped de Minaur move on from Wimbledon heartbreak Michael Koziol Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:41pm ,first published 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: If you’re feeling a touch sorry for yourself, Alex De Minaur can recommend a cure - get married. The 27-year-old from Sydney wedded fellow tennis star Katie Boulter just after Wimbledon, a tournament he exited in a disappointing round of 16 loss to Italy’s Flavio Cobolli. By his own admission, De Minaur was beating himself up. Alex de Minaur on his wedding day. Kate Julia “It breaks me inside. That’s the reality of it,” he said at the time. “Many, many hours get put into my craft, and countless years, to have moments like these. To not step up to the plate is truly gut-wrenching.” But the wedding - first an intimate ceremony in England, then a larger celebration in Tuscany, and a very brief honeymoon in Portofino - has helped cast those blues aside, and recharge the batteries.



“We did the maths, it’s probably the longest I’ve ever had without touching a racquet,” he says on the sidelines of the Mubadala DC Open in Washington. “It was probably about 13 days.” Thirteen days is a veritable eternity in the hectic schedule of professional tennis, which De Minaur thinks should be shortened. On Sunday, he talked about needing a break around this time of year, after the Roland Garros-Wimbledon double act and before the lead-up to the US Open. Alex de Minaur and Katie Boulter on their wedding day. Kate Julia De Minaur doesn’t regret baring his soul in the aftermath of his Wimbledon defeat, but he feels it was overblown. His raw post-match news conference, in which he seemed on the verge of tears, received a lot of attention. “I don’t think it was warranted, as much as - myself included - a lot of people wanted to make a big deal out of it,” he says now.



“It became a really big thing, but realistically it took me a couple of days to get over it. It was just the same feelings and emotions that any athlete has after a tough loss. Now I’m feeling great.” De Minaur points out that he may have suffered disappointing losses on the big stages in Paris and London, but he is now at a career high ranking of world No. 5. “That’s not too shabby,” he says. His challenge is to channel that success into mental resilience on court – as he says, to play more freely and “with a little bit less weight on my shoulders”. The burden of expectation is heavy these days. Does he feel pressure to win from the Australian tennis public? “It mainly comes from myself,” he says. “As you win more matches, as you get closer to the top, more and more people have opinions on you than they did 10 years ago … It just comes with the job. Related Article Wimbledon Ice-creams, selfies and the Federer twins: Cruz Hewitt hype is building at Wimbledon



“In fact, it’s a good thing. I’ve earned the right for people to have opinions about myself and my tennis. Whether they’re right or wrong, or whether they just want to have clickbait articles or not, that’s something else. I’m very chilled in my own life.” De Minaur is adamant that the solution to grand slam success lies in steeling himself, not making major changes to his team. “I’m very happy with the team. I don’t think it’s their fault that I haven’t performed in certain matches.” He is the defending champion here in Washington, but he has a tough opening match - Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece, who holds a 12-1 head-to-head advantage over the Australian. Both of them showed up to an exclusive cocktail reception on Sunday night (Washington time) at Ned’s Club, a private members’ club near the White House that is ordinarily the preferred hangout of Trump administration types like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Also in the Australian entourage: Lleyton Hewitt and his son Cruz Hewitt, who is making his tour-level debut in Washington after qualifying for the main draw on Sunday when his American opponent Zachary Svajda retired hurt in the third set.



The Aussies made a brief appearance at the Ned’s upstairs terrace that overlooks the White House and the Washington Monument, before retiring to the private players’ lounge. Presiding over the swanky party was venture capitalist Mark Ein, sometimes known as the King of Washington for his vast portfolio of business, sporting and media interests, which include the Mubadala Open and the Commanders NFL team. It was a tough day at the office for Alex de Minaur as he exited Wimbledon. Getty Images But it was hometown hero Frances Tiafoe, or “Big Foe”, who stole the show. Though he is based in Florida like much of the tennis world, Tiafoe grew up in Hyattsville, just outside Washington DC. He has been known to train occasionally at the Australian ambassador’s residence, it being home to Washington’s only grass tennis court. World.title: ‘I was always keen to rise’: Inside Ben Carroll’s journey from a Kmart checkout to premier of Victoria
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament ‘I was always keen to rise’: Inside Ben Carroll’s journey from a Kmart checkout to premier of Victoria Patrick Hatch Updated July 28, 2026 — 2:35pm ,first published July 27, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow live updates: Labor leadership showdown Eight years working at the checkout of a suburban Kmart can instil many things in a young man’s character. “Marathon runner”: Deputy Premier and Education Minister Ben Carroll. Ruby Alexander Humility. Resolve. An ability to navigate conflict and wear criticism. But perhaps endurance is the trait Ben Carroll developed behind the register that has served him best during his 14-year parliamentary career.



On Tuesday, that career reached its pinnacle: with Carroll unseating Jacinta Allan and being installed as the 50th premier of Victoria. Wade Noonan, a friend of Carroll’s and former state Labor minister, once described Carroll as someone unwilling to miss an opportunity. “Politics is not a place for retreaters. Ben will stand up for the things that matter, in life and in politics,” Noonan said in 2024. Carroll himself put it more bluntly when appointed deputy premier in 2023: “I was always very keen to rise.”



More recently, amid mounting speculation he could roll Allan as leader ahead of a November election which polls suggest Labor will lose, the baby-faced 51-year-old pointed out he was a “marathon runner”. Whether intentional or not, that was a reminder that Carroll sees himself as someone who can bide his time and go the distance. Loading Carroll was born in July 1975, the eldest of three children raised in Airport West. On the doorstep of Essendon Airport, the suburb is today part of his electorate, Niddrie, where he lives with his wife, Fiona, who is a lawyer, and their daughter, Madeleine. His mother, Kay, was born and raised in Texas before migrating to Australia and working at Glenroy West Primary School. Carroll’s electrician father ran a small business wiring up new homes around their growing suburb. The family business went under during the 1990s recession.



“Despite losing his business in the Keating recession, he, to this day, says Paul Keating was our greatest prime minister,” Carroll said of his father in a 2024 interview. “We saw the recession very closely in our family, but he was always thinking about those who were less fortunate.” Carroll attended St Christopher’s Primary School in Airport West and St Bernard’s in Essendon. As soon as he reached the legal working age of 14 years and nine months, he got his first job, at the local Kmart. Eight years on the checkout helped him through an arts degree at La Trobe University. Loading Kmart was where he joined the conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (known as the Shoppies), a union that holds significant sway over Labor’s Right faction. In some Labor circles, that stint also earned him the moniker “Kmart Keating”. If Keating loomed large in Carroll’s formative years, the “third way” centrism of Bill Clinton did just as much to inspire his move into politics.



In his first speech to parliament, he recalled being in his final year of high school when Clinton was sworn in as US president promising to deliver “more opportunity for all”. Carroll later travelled by train and bus to Canberra when Clinton was visiting, and took up an offer of a Parliament House tour by Labor’s Simon Crean, whom he had met through their shared devotion to the North Melbourne Football Club. Carroll is a passionate North Melbourne supporter. Simon Schluter “I did get that tour and was fortunate enough to shake President Clinton’s hand,” Carroll recalled. Carroll joined the Niddrie branch of the Labor Party in his early 20s, and one of his first jobs after graduating was as a junior staffer for then-premier Steve Bracks. By 2012, Carroll was in Canberra advising then-senator Stephen Conroy on the National Broadband Network.



Rob Hulls resigned and triggered a byelection that year in the seat of Niddrie. Carroll beat his current cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes for preselection and won the subsequent election, entering parliament at the age of 36. Related Article Live

Political leadership Jacinta Allan resignation LIVE: Ben Carroll becomes premier, announces royal commission at first press conference “When a seat comes up … where you went to kinder, where you went to primary, where you went to secondary, where you got your first job, where your family have been part of the community … you have a crack,” he said in 2024. He has never shied away from ambition, but Labor insiders have sometimes questioned whether he had the ruthlessness needed to rise to the top. In 2022, then-premier Daniel Andrews named Allan as his deputy before Carroll could rally his own supporters.



Following the reshuffle, Andrews left Carroll waiting for more than an hour to receive his new portfolio, sparking intrigue in Labor circles from those who assumed it was deliberate punishment for his interest in the role. When Andrews announced he was stepping down in September 2023, the premier hatched a plan to install his loyal deputy as leader and treasurer Tim Pallas as her deputy. Ben Carroll during the 2012 Niddrie byelection alongside then opposition leader Daniel Andrews. Pat Scala Carroll and his Right faction colleagues challenged this succession plan and threatened to formally contest the leadership. A peace deal with Allan installed him as deputy premier instead. Andrews was said to be apoplectic. Tellingly, Carroll was the only sitting MP to publicly criticise Andrews’ subsequent photo op with Chinese President Xi Jinping and a rogues’ gallery of dictators last year.



Labor insiders, speaking anonymously to detail internal deliberations, say that as deputy premier and the leading Right faction MP, Carroll has been a voice of constructive dissent within the government. His scepticism about Andrews and Allan’s pet project, the $34.5 billion Suburban Rail Loop East, is widely known. Carroll has instead championed the stalled $13 billion Airport Rail Link, and pushed for it to include a station in his electorate at Airport West. Carroll called internally for tougher bail laws at a time of growing public concern about crime, and also issued veiled criticism about the closure of police stations. As education minister he went head-to-head with Allan and then-treasurer Pallas in 2024 over their decision to pull $2.4 billion from state schools by delaying the government’s commitment to the Gonski reforms.



Related Article Political leadership Tears, defiance and unspoken truths: Reading between the lines of Jacinta Allan’s farewell speech His first act as new leader was to announce a royal commission into alleged corruption on state government Big Build sites – something Allan has steadfastly rejected and to distance himself from his predecessors. These friction points indicate where a Carroll-led government could diverge from the past 12 years of Labor under Andrews and Allan. The hope for Labor insiders who supported his leadership push is that he will provide a sufficient break with the past to win back voters by November. “Jacinta Allan has been unable to move past the CFMEU corruption issue,” said one senior Labor source. “Carroll gives the government an opportunity to reset on crime, integrity and the economy, and refocus on the issues that matter most.” But after cycling through 11 ministries and three years as deputy premier, Carroll is not a cleanskin either – a point laboured by the opposition this week.



The education portfolio has delivered some especially heavy blows. First he was the face of the 2024 VCE exam fiasco, in which questions for nearly half of the end-of-year tests were leaked online. Just last week, public school teachers walked off the job for the second time this year and marched through Melbourne’s CBD demanding better pay and working conditions, after rejecting a pay offer Carroll said would make them the nation’s best paid. “Make no mistake, Ben Carroll has been Jacinta Alan’s partner in crime for three years,” shadow attorney-general James Newbury said on Monday. Former federal opposition leader Bill Shorten worked closely with Carroll for almost 13 years on issues in their overlapping electorates in Melbourne’s north-west.



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Bombshell briefing reveals top officials’ CFMEU warning to Allan Shorten would not be drawn on the leadership contest, nor on the merits of Allan’s government. But he described Carroll as the epitome of a grassroots local member who could also work well with industry and business. “If the party chooses him, he’ll be very good,” said Shorten, who is now vice chancellor of the University of Canberra, ahead of Tuesday’s ballot. “He would be very much in the Bracks-Brumby mould if he is successful. He’ll build consensus; he knows what he’s got to do, but he’ll bring people with him. He’s a listener.” Just six weeks ago, leadership rumblings broke out amid dire opinion polls and a catastrophic negative approval rating for Allan. Carroll publicly ruled out challenging the premier.



For some Labor figures, who think he should have challenged much sooner, this again raised questions about whether he had enough grit for the top job. “The last six months hasn’t done him any favours,” one said. But on Monday morning, Carroll said it was clear Allan had lost the support of her party room, and announced he would nominate for leader. Photos on his social media pages of him and Allan together were quickly deleted. One cabinet minister, speaking anonymously on Monday, said Carroll’s hesitation to challenge reflected his character – although not unfavourably.



“He is earnest and honest and someone who will always try to do the right thing,” the minister said. “He would have been very uncomfortable about challenging. But there has been a build-up of people who have come to him and said, you are the only viable alternative for the party.” View post on X Despite all his ambition, Carroll, announcing his nomination on X, said it was a difficult step to take. “But the stakes at the upcoming election are simply too high,” he said. “The prospect of a Liberal-One Nation government that will cut schools, health and frontline services is simply too high a risk to ignore.”

World.title: Jacinta Allan resignation LIVE: Ben Carroll becomes premier, announces royal commission at first press conference

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said if the Coalition win the election, her first act as premier would be to call a “real” royal commission into corruption on Big Build construction sites.

“Not a sham royal commission-lite designed to save Labor’s furniture: an unblinking forensic inquiry into this corrupt government,” Wilson said. “I will do this immediately before Christmas.”

Jess Wilson (left) and new premier Ben Carroll shake hands across the chamber ahead of question time beginning. Getty Images

It’s a sign that the Opposition will continue to challenge the government over the CFMEU scandal which plagued Labor and contributed to Jacinta Allan’s resignation, despite new Premier Ben Carroll’s commitment for greater integrity.

Carroll announced earlier today that his priority would be calling a royal commission into alleged corruption in the construction sector, appointing a special prosecutor with commission and giving the state’s anti-corruption body follow-the-money powers.

World.title: Seven race tracks face closure in horse racing industry proposal
World.content:
Listen to NZ Thoroughbred Racing CEO Matt Ballesty just after 5pm

RNZ national

The horse racing industry has proposed shutting down seven race tracks and 12 other venues to keep the sport alive.

The independent Project Stamina report - commissioned by the TAB - found the horse industry's spending was spread too thin across 63 venues.

The governing bodies for thoroughbred and harness racing have now joined forces to implement many the recommendations as a 'One Equine View'.

That includes shutting down 19 venues, including seven race courses such as Wellington's Trentham.

Other courses that would stop holding race meetings were Rotorua, Manawatū, Wyndham, Gore, Hāwera and Ōamaru.

Business cases would be made for five other venues, with the remaining 39 venues kept running.

But the industry bodies said the One Equine View was only a proposal and marked the beginning of the next phase of engagement "rather than the end of the conversation", it said in a statement.

"Doing nothing is not an option," NZ Thoroughbred Racing chair Russell Warwick said.

"Our infrastructure must reflect today's racing landscape and be capable of supporting future growth. This plan gives us the opportunity to invest where it will deliver the greatest long-term benefit for participants, horses and the wider industry."

Harness Racing NZ chair Grant Jarrold said it was "not simply another review".

"It provides a unified direction that links strategy, investment and implementation, giving the industry greater certainty about the future," he said.

World.title: Investigation launched after pōhutukawa trees poisoned
World.content:
Two pōhutukawa trees have been illegally poisoned in the Coromandel, the Department of Conservation says.

There was clear evidence of drill holes around the base of the trees at Hahei Beach Marginal Strip, Hauraki-Coromandel DoC staff wrote in a post on Facebook.

An investigation was underway.

A drill hole at the bottom of one of the trees. Department of Conservation - Hauraki-Coromandel

"Pōhutukawa are iconic coastal trees, often celebrated as Aotearoa's unofficial Christmas tree. But they are much more than a beautiful part of our summer landscape, they are important coastal ecosystems in their own right.

"Their flowers provide nectar for tūī, bellbirds and geckos, while their trunks, bark and canopy offer habitat for birds, insects and spiders. A diverse community of native insects depends on pōhutukawa, and the leaf litter beneath them supports hardy native snails adapted to life along the coast. Shags and white-faced herons often nest or roost in pōhutukawa," staff wrote.

Two pōhutukawa trees at Hahei Beach in the Coromandel have been illegally poisoned. Supplied

The trees' root systems helped to stabilise coastal soils, dunes and cliffs.

Damaging, poisoning or destroying native vegetation on public conservation land is a serious offence, which can result in penalties including fines of up to $300,000.

DoC staff are asking anyone with information about who may be responsible to contact them and quote the reference number: CLE-12213.

World.title: Champion golfer Ryan Fox showcases Claret Jug in hometown celebration
World.content:
Golf's famous Claret Jug is back in New Zealand, and many who witnessed newly crowned major champion Ryan Fox hold the trophy aloft on Tuesday in downtown Auckland were not born the last time the silverware was won by a New Zealander 63 years ago.

Fox's victory at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale last week was dramatic - sinking a 12-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole - and mayor Wayne Brown ranked this achievement alongside the likes of America's Cup victories, golf successes by Fox's predecessors and contemporaries through to the Commonwealth Games gold medal won in the pool by Lewis Clareburt just hours before when announcing Fox to a hometown crowd of thousands at Takutai Square.

The Claret Jug has been put into an overhead luggage compartment and then flew at the front of plane, as Fox made the long and winding journey from Southport, England to Aotearoa to be able to share his first major title win.

The son of an All Black, Fox also took the Jug into camp with the All Blacks on Monday to take a swig of beer from.

Beer is not the only liquid to be consumed from the trophy in the past week. Fox and family enjoyed a fitting beverage - red wine - from it and the champion's 8-year-old nephew apparently also took a sip of water from it.

The storied silverware has been in many places, as 91 golfers took possession of it before Fox, and while a stage sandwiched between hotels near Auckland's waterfront during office workers' lunch break might be one of the more unremarkable places it is been showcased, it is hoped that some in the crowd will have been inspired.

Ryan Fox poses with the Claret Jug in front of fans in Takutai Square. Alan Lee / Photosport

Some had stumbled upon the public celebration for the 39-year-old, others got in early to line the green astroturf carpet that had been rolled out for Fox to walk along, while others took to rooftops and office balconies that overlooked the square to see golf's version of a ticker tape parade.

Fox appeared from around a corner to walk up to the stage, a bit different to walking to the final hole on a golf course on the other side of the world, but there were similarities. Supporters lined either side of the turf carpet and politely clapped or held their phone up to capture the moment that they were that close to the Champion Golfer of the Year carrying the Claret Jug.

Under a sunny sky and surrounded by his family - including his wife, two daughters and parents - and his coach Marcus Wheelhouse, Fox faced his fans.

Ryan Fox carries the Claret Jug back with daughter Isobel after the welcome home celebration in Takutai Square. Alan Lee / Photosport

He wanted to celebrate in New Zealand, even if looking out into a large crowd and soaking up the moment made him slightly uncomfortable.

Golf NZ acting chief executive officer Gregg Thorpe called Fox's win "a landmark moment for golf in New Zealand".

Thorpe knew the impact this latest major win for a New Zealander could have for golfers young, and slightly older, and who could dare to dream about what is possible when the stars align and determination, combined with talent, pays off.

Fox is only the fourth New Zealander to win a major golf championship, joining Sir Bob Charles, who won the Open Championship in 1963, Michael Campbell and Dame Lydia Ko.

Ryan Fox holds the Claret Jug as he waits to attend the welcome home celebration in Auckland. Alan Lee / Photosport

Answering questions on stage, Fox traversed golf's history in New Zealand and his links to the other Kiwi champions.

He was a teenager when Campbell won the US Open in 2005 and that moment inspired Fox to take his golf more seriously.

Dame Lydia video called Fox after his Open Championship win - a conversation he treasured.

Golf fans on the other side of the world are getting a reputation for being rowdy on the course, but in Auckland most fans kept their distance until Fox tried to leave the stage at the end of the celebration. Then they crowded their hero wanting his signature on printed photos, golf balls and other merchandise.

Fox handled himself well as he moved out of the spotlight and down a back alley.

He will leave New Zealand soon - after doing some fishing on Wednesday - to return to his home in Florida with the real and replica Claret Jug in tow.

As he told the crowd who had taken time off school, out of the office or made the trip into the city to see him, he does not know if America will treat him differently now or if can still fly under the radar.

World.title: Battle lines drawn over proposed LNG facility
World.content:
Proposed LNG import terminal unlikely to cause disruption Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

*Correction: This story has been updated to include MBIE and clarify the Port’s role as information provider

Port Taranaki and MBIE have informed nearby residents that initial assessments of a proposed LNG import terminal indicate it is unlikely "risk management zones" will impact on the community or popular recreational areas like Ngāmotu Beach and Breakwater Bay.

In a letter sent to hundreds of local properties, port chief executive Simon Craddock confirmed both shortlisted proposals involved a ship being moored alongside the Main Breakwater.

Opponents of the project argue Port Taranaki is the wrong place for a liquid natural gas (LNG) import facility.

Former oil and gas industry project manager Rob Green's home on Port View Crescent overlooks Port Taranaki.

"I can look straight down on the port, all the ships at anchor here, and I can see all the logs and so on. So, I'm looking straight down on the port at the Main Breakwater and all those berthing possibilities for ships," he said.

"It's very close, all the noises from the port operations I can hear. I'm looking straight at it."

Green was not convinced the port, about 1km from his apartment, was the right place for an LNG import facility.

"I keep hearing that safety is the top priority, but quite frankly I won't believe it until I can see the risk assessment analysis for myself.

"Here we are bulldozing on to a contract the government seems totally committed to regardless to the concerns of the neighbourhood."

Port Taranaki's letter and an article on the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment's LNG webpage explain that the vessel to be moored at the Main Breakwater would store LNG and be capable of regasifying it and distributing it into existing transmission pipelines.

Other vessels from suppliers overseas would deliver LNG - which was frozen - to the moored vessel.

The Main Breakwater was about 200m away from popular recreational areas at Ngāmotu Beach, Breakwater Bay and the Lee Breakwater, where recreational fishers both surfcasted and launched boats.

Port Taranaki referred questions about the safety assessment to MBIE, which was managing the procurement process.

In a statement, MBIE said safety was the bottom-line and the plant would not get built if it could not meet safety standards.

"An initial safety evaluation has been undertaken as part of both of the providers' feasibility work, and detailed health and safety assessments will be carried out through the Safety Case process under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 once the preferred provider is contracted," it said in a statement.

"This includes a quantitative risk assessment which is location-specific and will cover the facility and all phases of its operation, as well as generating risk contour lines (or 'buffer zones') to keep the community safe."

MBIE said it was inappropriate to make the initial safety assessment public as it was commercially sensitive.

In statement, WorkSafe said it had no role in the choice of location, but it would work with the preferred provider on the more detailed Safety Case.

"Before the facility can be built and operated, the preferred provider must submit both a design notice and a Safety Case to WorkSafe.

WorkSafe would assess these to determine whether the facility could comply with major hazard facility requirements and that risks had been identified and appropriately managed.

"WorkSafe will either accept or decline the Safety Case. If it is declined, the facility will not go ahead."

The regulator said it didn't publish safety cases in full.

However, if the LNG project was designated a major hazard facility, prescribed information must be published on the WorkSafe website.

This would include an explanation of activities undertaken at the facility, hazard classifications of substances that could cause or contribute to a major incident, and the characteristics of those substances that made them dangerous.

General information about how the public would be warned in the event of a major incident would also be published, and information on how the public should act and what precautionary steps they should take if a major incident occurred.

Taranaki Energy Watch's Sarah Roberts RNZ / Robin Martin

Taranaki Energy Watch spokesperson Sarah Roberts said that would be a case of too little too late.

"What we're saying is this location is not the right place for an LNG import terminal. We know that there's a known potential worst case fatality distance to approximately 2km from these types of facilities. There are thousands of people and a number of schools in this area."

Roberts said right from the outset former Minister of Energy Simon Watts talked about working alongside the Port Kembla Energy Terminal in New South Wales.

"Over there, they have built a new terminal and they have the 2km separation distance between the terminal itself and the nearest residence."

Roberts worried people in the area surrounding Port Taranaki would be hurt if something went wrong.

"We feel like they're purposely avoiding the RMA and Fast Track legislation to get something through that should have been looked at primarily at the beginning. Looking at the location, seeing if there's any alternatives, and making it publicly available, making the safety assessments publicly available."

MBIE said the exact size and details of the safety buffer zones around the LNG import facility at Port Taranaki would be determined independently to the procurement process, once it had been completed.

"It is inappropriate to estimate the exact size of the buffer zones ahead of this detailed Safety Case process. Until the Safety Case is accepted, the import facility will not be built."

People walking along Ngāmotu Beach and at Breakwater Bay had mixed views on the LNG proposal.

Kevin said he accepted it was necessary: "I suppose we have to have the gas to run the country. There's no great place to put it. Everyone wants it somewhere else, but Taranaki has had all the gas and gas production over the years."

His mate, Denis, wasn't so keen: "I'm not really in favour of the whole thing. It's all imported fossil fuels and a bit close to a residential area."

Don had an alternative idea and reckoned the infrastructure was mostly already in place: "Pipe it in, which would eliminate any need for changes around the harbour area."

Robyn was willing to put her trust in the process: "They've got very stringent safety things, that's the big thing with oil and gas."

Grant worried about access to recreational areas: "Not very happy at all.

"There's a lot of people who use this area here. So, is there going to be an exclusion zone for people walking around here? And what about the cafes here, are they going to remove those?"

Graham said he could see both sides of the dilemma: "It's probably no more dangerous than anything else, but it is an unnecessary addition to danger, and the actual plant itself is unnecessary."

Bernard's home was within 2km of the proposed site: "I think it is a bit risky. It is a highly volatile thing and that. I would prefer them going back to Marsden Point and doing it there."

World.title: Calls for police to revisit ex-officer's other cases after damning sex assault review
World.content:
Two specialist sexual violence support organisations are calling for police to review other cases investigated by a former police officer, following a damning review into a historical sexual assault investigation.

The complainant is also backing calls for a wider review.

RNZ earlier revealed an internal police review found the sexual assault investigation by former Detective Senior Sergeant Darren Folau was "poor", that the complainant was "not listened to and not believed" and that the young man's sporting career was "prioritised over [the complainant] and any offending against her".

The police said that, based on the review of the original investigation, the sportsman did not have a defence and was culpable of sexual conduct with a person under 16 years old.

The sportsman has been granted an injunction after he was approached by RNZ. The injunction means RNZ is not able to report his identity.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Territorial Superintendent Ross McKay earlier confirmed in a statement to RNZ that police had reopened an investigation into historical claims of sexual assault dating back to 2010, after an initial review las year found "concerning management of the original file".

"An independent investigation team from another district is now leading the reinvestigation, and review into the handling of the original inquiry."

HELP Auckland executive director Kathryn McPhillips told RNZ the organisation would welcome any decision to further investigate sexual violence cases handled by Folau.

"The case already identified as requiring review raises legitimate questions about whether other cases he was involved in should also be reconsidered.

"Transparency and a willingness to critically examine whether cases were handled professionally, impartially and with the interests of survivors at the centre are essential to maintaining trust in the justice system.

"The findings in this case are deeply concerning and highlight the lasting harm that occurs when this does not happen," McPhillips said,

She said the organisation's thoughts were with the complainant.

"We welcome New Zealand Police's continued efforts to review and reopen cases where reports of sexual violence have not been handled appropriately. It is important that survivors know concerns can be revisited when failures are identified, and we hope this commitment to reviewing past cases continues."

Wellington Rape Crisis general manager Kyla Rayner said they also wanted to see a "robust review of other cases".

"A young woman disclosed. The investigation found she was not listened to, not believed, and that the sportsman's career was explicitly weighed in the balance. She then spent years - her words - feeling like what happened to her wasn't bad enough. That is what a failed investigation costs a person. The reinvestigation is the right step. But survivors are watching what comes next.

"For many survivors, the greatest harm is not only the violence they experience but the experience of not being believed, not being taken seriously, or feeling that other interests are prioritised over their safety and dignity. Trust in the justice system depends on survivors knowing they will be treated with fairness, respect and impartiality."

Rayner said reopening a file was not the same as restoring trust.

"Trust depends on what happens inside that reinvestigation - whether the survivor is supported, whether prosecutions follow where the evidence warrants, and whether the officer accountability process is genuinely independent."

The complainant told RNZ she believed it was important that Police reviewed other cases Folau was involved in.

"His attitudes towards my reporting show he did not follow correct processes or work in a victim-centric way.

"It's possible that there are other children and young people who were also not believed, not listened to, and not centred in their investigations."

She said Police had told her that the culture had changed in Police.

"To ensure police culture truly changes, they must do everything they can to rebuild trust. Genuinely owning their mistakes and reviewing historic cases is a first step."

RNZ has approached the police for comment.

Folau, who worked in police for 28 years, was awarded a Queen's Service Medal for services in the Solomon Islands in 2004.

He's also held several roles including board member of charitable trust STOP, a community based organisation that says it provides support and therapy for people "who have engaged in, or are demonstrating, concerning or harmful sexual behaviour".

Approached for comment on Friday about RNZ's article, STOP board chair Trisha Edmonds confirmed Folau was a board member.

"Darren brought this matter to my attention on Wednesday this week, and Darren and I immediately agreed that it was appropriate for Darren to temporarily step down from his role as a Board member while this matter is reviewed by the NZ Police.

"We will not be providing any further comment."

Folau has also agreed to step down as a member of the Sport Integrity Disciplinary Panel Te Kahu Aratika.

In a statement to RNZ, the Sport Integrity Commission Te Kahu Raunui said it only became aware of the investigation into Folau today.

"This matter had not previously been disclosed to the Commission".

"Given the nature of the investigation, Mr Folau has agreed to stand down from the Panel. His ongoing role on the Panel will be revisited once this investigation has been completed."

RNZ approached Folau for comment on Wednesday. He said he was "not in a position to make any decisions or commentary".

In response to further questions, Folau said because of the little information he had, he did not think he could make any comments.

"The context I have is that I understand a review of an historical case is underway.

"I am comfortable that any recommendations I may have had input into will have been evidence based."

In May he was announced as the co-chair of the Brainwave Trust Aotearoa board.

The announcement said Folau "contributes to a number of governance and advisory roles, including Oranga Tamariki, STOP Trust, and Moana Vā, supporting Pacific Rainbow+ communities".

Brainwave Trust Aotearoa chief executive Huia Hanlen told RNZ on Friday she was "aware of this situation and have no further comment to make on behalf of Brainwave Trust Aotearoa".

The sportsman said in a brief statement to RNZ he understood police were re-investigating the matter.

World.title: 'Very unwise' for National to push ahead with a social media ban - ACT Party
World.content:
National would be "very unwise" to push ahead with a social media ban on under-16-year-olds "at the expense of coalition unity", ACT leader David Seymour says.

NZ First leader Winston Peters agrees, calling that course of action a "seriously big mistake".

The comments came on Tuesday, after the minister in charge National's Erica Stanford told reporters she was ready to take her proposal to Cabinet and would be doing so "soon".

Stanford said she would take legislation before her colleagues for a "fulsome discussion" and see what happened.

"I'm not going to presuppose what happens at Cabinet. The prime minister will manage that," she said.

"I don't know what's going to happen. People make different decisions at select committees and Cabinet. That's the whole process."

Both ACT and New Zealand First have indicated their strong opposition to the proposal.

But National is also holding briefings with the opposition Labour Party. Between the two of them, National and Labour would have a clear majority in Parliament to pass legislation.

Seymour said National would be making a "mistake" if it ignored two of the three parties in the coalition and a third of Cabinet ministers.

"At this point, we really need to be presenting a united front," Seymour said.

"For one party to pursue a policy important to them at the expense of coalition unity would be very unwise."

Asked whether ACT would "agree to disagree" on the policy, Seymour suggested that National should be the one to do so.

"If you got two parties out of three saying no, it's not a matter of agree to disagree. It's actually the third party that agrees to disagree."

As for National's discussions with Labour, Seymour quipped: "It's not illegal, but... I wouldn't advise it."

Peters said Seymour's argument had merit, especially given the proximity of the election.

He said while National could theoretically carry on, that would be a "seriously big mistake".

"We think that common sense might prevail. Can't... the National Party see now that they're making a mistake? Surely."

Stanford said there had been "really good engagements" with Labour MP Reuben Davidson about her plan so far. She said other Labour MPs would also be briefed on the legislation on Thursday.

"I haven't asked Labour for their agreement. They will be able to see the bill when it's tabled. They'll have plenty of time to make up their mind," she said.

World.title: Ambulance callouts to Auckland homeless 'close to doubled'
World.content:
Ambulance callouts to homeless people in Auckland have nearly doubled over the past four years, according to Hato Hone St John.

The ambulance service attended 459 patients of "no fixed abode" in the most recent financial year, compared to 236 patients in 2022.

Hato Hone St John Auckland District Operations Manager Andrew Everiss said the increase "absolutely" concerned him.

"We are seeing an increase in the number of patients that we are attending of no fixed abode.

"It's come close to doubled."

The callouts were most commonly because the individual had been assaulted, collapsed or fallen unconscious.

Everiss said the ambulance service's data did not record details about the assaults: "That would be information for the police."

Ambulances experiencing delays admitting patients into EDs Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

Those who had fallen unconscious could have done so for a variety of reasons: general medical concern, collapse, a result of diabetes, drugs and alcohol, psychiatric reasons, as a result of trauma, or sleeping in the community.

He presented the figures at a recent meeting of Auckland central stakeholders, including business associations, police, Auckland Council, and Auckland Central MP Chlöe Swarbrick. It was chaired by Minister for Auckland Simon Watts.

Everiss said the increase in callouts involving homeless patients reflected the broader rise in demand across the ambulance service in Auckland and nationwide.

"Last winter, for example, we had our busiest month on record, with just under 70,000 calls for a month."

About 30 percent of that national workload was in Auckland.

World.title: Protection for hoiho around Otago Peninsula to be made permanent
World.content:
A set net ban to protect hoiho off the Otago Peninsula will be made permanent to reduce the risk of fishing bycatch.

A temporary emergency closure was imposed by the Oceans and Fisheries minister last year to protect the nationally endangered yellow-eyed penguin.

Shane Jones said he decided to make the closure permanent.

"I am also establishing a new escalating response framework called a fishing related mortality limit so I can act quickly and decisively to increase protections if needed," he said.

The plan included setting an accidental capture limit of four northern hoiho per year.

Jones called that a "bottom line" and did not rule out putting further restrictions on fishing in place to ensure the limit was not exceeded.

"Last year's risk assessment projected that to stabilise the northern hoiho population we must cut deaths from all causes by half and I consider the new protections will achieve this goal for fisheries bycatch," he said.

Disease, predation and starvation were the major risks to hoiho but the changes to reduce risk of fisheries bycatch would help, he said.

The changes would come into force on 16 September.

Environmental Law Initiative welcomed the ban but senior legal advisor Megan Cornforth-Camden said it was deeply concerned by the bycatch limit of four hoiho deaths per year.

"The announcement does little to change the status quo. Four hoiho were killed in the 24/25 fishing year, five the year before that and 4 the year before that," she said.

"If we were discussing the last remaining 115 breeding pairs of a kiwi species, would New Zealanders accept four birds being killed each year as a result of commercial activity? We believe the answer would be no."

She questioned how the figure was reached and whether the advice given to the minister also considered the looming threat posed by avian influenza on an already fragile population.

"If the northern hoiho population can sustain the loss of four birds a year to fisheries bycatch on top of all the other pressures it faces, we would like to understand the scientific basis for that conclusion," Cornforth-Camden said

It was important to avoid all bycatch deaths because the loss of three or four birds per year would quickly erode an already small breeding population and threaten the recovery of the species, she said.

Seafood New Zealand chief executive Lisa Futscheck said the decision gave fishers in the area more certainty but that was undermined by the addition of a fishing related mortality limit.

"Fishers will continue to do everything they can to minimise risk and avoid hoiho capture," she said.

"We want to see hoiho thrive and have the best chance at recovery and survival."

Futscheck said it was important that all threats to hoiho were addressed using an evidence-based approach.

Seafood New Zealand inshore general manager Tiff Bock said it was unclear what would happen if the limit was reached, even if she believed that was unlikely.

"What they've done in the past in other fisheries, it's essentially an immediate closure of a predefined much wider area for everyone and every method," she said.

"So it becomes quite a high risk for all the other fishers in the area. It provides really good motivation to make sure we don't get there."

The annual bycatch limit of four was "sensible", but scientific modelling indicated six would be sustainable, Bock said.

When Fisheries New Zealand was consulting on the changes last year, it said commercial set net fishing was estimated to be the third largest cause of hoiho mortality in recent years.

World.title: The sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains
World.content:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Archie Goodburn did not win a medal but won the respect of everyone as he competes while dealing with brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport" they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final. But outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"[A dream] where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Abigail Roper won bronze first, but sister Emily got her own an hour or so later. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games that two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her sister who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow. But everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Sabalenka, Djokovic lead mixed doubles teams for US Open
World.content:
Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic headline the initial list of 16 teams entered into the US Open mixed doubles championship.

The tournament was overhauled last year, with a $US1 million ($1.43 million) prize going to the winners, in an effort to get top singles players to compete. Many of those types of stars were listed among the teams announced Monday by the US Tennis Association.

Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud, the runners-up in 2025, are entered again, along with Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, the Japanese duo of Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, along with Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper.

The main draw will be played over two days on August 25-26, with all the matches set to be held in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the two biggest venues at the US Open.

Teams can enter up until August 17, when the six duos with the best combined singles rankings at the time will be automatically entered into the main draw.

That means Sabalenka, the two-time defending US Open women's champion and Djokovic, still ranked number five on the men's tour at age 39, will be safely into the field.

Eight teams will be given wild cards by the USTA, and two other teams will play their way into the field through a qualifying tournament to be held from August 24.

Defending champions win US Open mixed doubles final Italian pair Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori accomplish their "mission" by winning the US Open mixed doubles title for the second straight year in a controversially revamped format.

The remainder of the teams that were entered as of Monday:

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev; Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli; Diana Shnaider and Daniil Medvedev; Amanda Anisimova and Learner Tien; Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime; Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe; Taylor Townsend and Alexander Zverev; Elena-Gabriela Ruse and Nuno Borges; Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori; Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten; and siblings Peyton Stearns and Preston Stearns.

Errani and Vavassori are the two-time defending US Open champions. The Italians needed a wild card to get into last year's event because their singles ranking was too low, and that will be the case again this year.

The US Open was initially criticised last year because the format of the event shut out doubles specialists such as Errani and Vavassori, but the tournament certainly seemed a success, helping draw 78,000 fans to the grounds and selling out Ashe both days.

"Any time you can bring women and men together on the same team, you showcase tennis at its best. This is exactly what the mixed doubles championship does," USTA CEO Craig Tiley said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The mixed doubles championship is an innovation that will engage new audiences and give our fans another opportunity to see the biggest stars compete together."

Errani and Vavassori were the only traditional doubles team in last year's tournament.

There is a chance for more this year — Siniakova and Patten are doubles specialists — with the addition of the eight-team qualifying tournament, which will include six direct entries and two wild cards.

The format will be best-of-three-set matches with sets to four games, tiebreakers at 4-all and a 10-point match tie-break instead of a third set, through the semifinals. The final will be standard scoring with sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all, and a 10-point match tiebreaker if necessary.

World.title: 'A gorgeous human' gets her solo moment and still shares it with her mates
World.content:
There aren't many legacies in sport as dominant as Australia in the women's 4x100m freestyle relay.

The first night of the Glasgow program marked the team's 19th victory in the past 21 major international finals across the Olympics, long-course world championships, Pan Pacs and Commonwealth Games.

It also marked the sixth time Meg Harris had stood on the top step of the podium with her teammates in those events, bridging the gap from the Campbells era to these Commonwealth Games and onwards towards Brisbane 2032.

But on Tuesday morning (AEST), when Mollie O'Callaghan and Shayna Jack joined her up there, they did so with her blessing, of course, after she became the solo 100m champion for the first time.

Meg Harris (centre) pipped superstars Shayna Jack (left) and Mollie O'Callaghan to the wall. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"It's pretty incredible, I've never done that before. I've never been in that position," Harris said.

"Hopefully this is just the start of my journey. I'm pretty happy with that. These girls are absolutely incredible, so any chance I get to stand on the podium with them is great."

The trials in June marked the first time she had made the team as an individual 100m swimmer.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

The 24-year-old admitted to struggling with motivation in the 100m after the Paris Olympics, rediscovering her love for the sport through her pet 50m event, where she won the world title in Singapore last year.

"I've always loved the [100m] race," she said.

"The 50m was something I've always loved and always known I've enjoyed racing that … but the 100m is always the one I've been working towards in the long run. I guess I need to take a step back and enjoy it for a while."

Harris's win was one of seven gold medals on the night for Australia, with Alex Perkins in the 100m butterfly and Jenna Forrester in the 400m individual medley also enjoying a breakout meet.

Jenna Forrester has enjoyed a breakout Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Forrester's victory added to her surprise 200m backstroke victory three nights earlier.

"We all really get around each other, and that's what makes Team Australia really special and successful," Perkins said.

Little did she know how true that was.

Minutes earlier, Harris had made an immediate pivot from star performer to cheer captain, stepping away from her media obligations to cheer Perkins on with every stroke as she powered to victory.

"She's amazing; all those girls are in the 100m freestyle," Perkins said.

"[They're] so successful in that event and [Harris is] just also a gorgeous human. I was really proud; it was really inspiring to watch her before my event."

100m butterfly gold medallist Alex Perkins is a big fan of Meg Harris. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Perkins and Harris are kindred spirits, two swimmers winning their favourite events for the first time after years of toil while in their mid-20s (Perkins celebrating gold on her 26th birthday).

Along with Forrester, Sam Short, Lani Pallister and a slew of other gold medallists on the night and at these Games, it's all part of a moment of transition for the Dolphins in Glasgow.

It's not so much a passing of the baton as simply getting more hands on it.

"We've got a home [Olympic] Games in 2032, we're all trying to do our best and make the most of every moment," Perkins said.

And Harris is a key part of that.

The 4x100m freestyle squad featured eight swimmers in Glasgow: Brittany Castelluzzo (25), Inez Miller (19), Jessica Cole (19) and Hannah Casey (20) in their heat; and Harris, Perkins, Jack and O'Callaghan in the final.

The jewel in Australian swimming's crown is central to the rejuvenation that never really stops for this all-conquering team.

In among the Dolphins, they call themselves "the starfish", according to the retiring Jack.

Swimming is perhaps the loneliest of all elite sport pursuits, so finding that connection is crucial to, if you'll pardon the pun, keeping your head above water.

"Meg's my roommate here, which I'm really grateful for because we do have a lot of events together and being able to share in those moments with her is extremely special to me," Jack said.

"Swimming is such an event that can be quite isolating. That's also why I love the relays because you get to share in those special moments with somebody else, and being able to go 1-2-3 tonight, it's just another moment I get to share with these amazing girls."
